item.content:encoded: continued musings, i feel like modern society has moved greatly towards consumerism as an expression of identity and values, and a self that needs to be noticed will always need something new to show. i dont think the answer is to wear a grey prison jumpsuit or anything, but maybe re-anchoring identity back in relationships, commitments, traditional art, non-consumptive hobbies. can we express ourselves through a small, long-kept wardrobe that avoids the consumer cycle? a good test: does my self-expression depend on constant acquisition (yes, even vintage/thrifted/etc)? if the “art” requires a constant flow of new purchases, it probably aint art. i think very it’s healthy to interrogate forms of self-expression that require us to spend a ton of money, and it’s dreadfully easy to justify consumerism as artistic expression, a moral good, a statement of personal authenticity as long as the things we buy are pretty and give us a dopamine rush. thats why depop and vinted are billion dollar…

item.title: This Week in Stupid: October 17 edition
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: As another stupid week comes to a close here in America, let’s look back at the dumbest fucking shit that happened.Monday: make flushing money down the toilet great again“This is the Trump dollar coin. It will be in the banks next month, and I want to challenge you to go get a roll of Trump dollar coins next month. And then I want you to go to your favorite liberal coffee shop with your Trump dollar coins, buy a cup of coffee, and watch their heads explode. They will not like it, but I love it, and I love this president. I love this coin.”Now hold on there one minute, Mister Actual Goddamned Treasurer of the United States, if that really is your name. Are you telling me to spend $2.50 on a ‘dollar’ coin with Dear Leader’s big, dumb pumpkin face on it, and then turn right around and buy a cup of coffee with the ‘dollar’ coin that I just spent $2.50 to acquire, in order to make some commie have a big sad?Shut the fuck up and take my fucking money.Listen up, you cultist dipshits. If I’m next to you in line at my local coffeehouse, and you pull out a bunch of fake-gold Donnymoney to pay for your cuppa joe, I’m not going to be . I’m going to be laughing in your face at what a credulous nitwit you are. You just spent $12.50 on your five-dollar cup of coffee. Can you believe that MAGA wastes so much time an energy doing stupid shit simply because they imagine they’re No one cares, you fucking dunderheads.Please, I beg of you, trigger me all day long with that kind of stupidity.Oh, and can someone explain to me: why is the Actual Goddamned Treasurer of the United States shilling for Dear Leader’s vanity money in such a blatantly partisan way? Isn’t that some kind of ethics violation? It should be.Tuesday: make incoherent financial advice great againWhat with all the other dumbfuckery being shoved in our faces twenty-four-seven, it’s easy to forget that everyone’s favorite dead-bear-cub kidnapper is still pumping out episodes of his fakakta cooking show that absolutely no one is watching.Bobby Brainwoms: “People can go to the grocery store and to save money.” Question: “Do you have a favorite cut of steak?”Braiworms: “If I had to choose a favorite, it’s a ribeye.”Well, I’m glad we got that cleared up. Oh sure, absolutely. Thanks for that sage financial advice, bro — because when I want tips on scrimping and saving, I turn to the fifth-generation nepo-child of wealth and privilege, who grew up in a private compound on the ocean, and has never done an honest day’s labor in his life.Tell me, Oh Great Slaughterer of Whale Heads, should I use my Donny Coins to buy the ribeye I can’t afford, just to watch the butcher completely lose his shit?Wednesday: make not knowing shit about shit great again “If more women put the same energy into their marriages and into finding a spouse than they do into their careers, you would see society have a lot more babies. That’s what led to the downfall of Rome.”Really? Too many self-actualized women and too few obedient baby factories is what led to fall of the Roman Empire? That sounds super fucking sus to me. No, women stopping having babies did not cause the fall of the Roman Empire. [1]Modern historians attribute the collapse of the Western Roman Empire in 476 A.D. to a complex mix of political instability, economic crises, heavy taxation, civil wars, military recruitment failures, and large-scale invasions by Germanic tribes. [1, 2]No one could have predicted that the wife of the undead White House Deputy Chief of Staff would be so completely full of shit.What happens when a woman gives birth to a vampire’s child depends entirely on the fictional lore or mythology, resulting in either a half-human hybrid (a Dhampir or Daywalker), a full vampire, or pregnancy complications. [1, 2]Daywalkers! So that’s how we ended up with White House Economic Advisor Kevin Hassett.Thursday: make being completely fucking wrong great againThese Daily Mail stories aren’t just tabloid trash, they’re simply made up. Up and down the White House, everyone has been thoroughly impressed with Katie in just a few short days on the job. At the end of this second term, she’ll be remembered as one of the all-time greats.Yeah, right. Let’s just skip straight ahead to the part where we throw our heads back in laughter —Because we all know what happened on the very next day…Friday: the further adventures of Some Fucking Idiot™On Friday, some fucking idiot’s very first public act was to advise his brand-spanking-new press secretary that maybe was ‘not for her.’Who had ‘just under half a scaramucci’ on their Katie Zacharia bingo card? My dude, do you even know what planet you’re on? It sure as shit doesn’t seem as if you do.And, because this whole drama played out far from the press, not one reporter had the opportunity to stand up and ask, ‘what the fuck is wrong with you?’How fucking idiotic is that?And now, let’s put a close to This Week in Stupid and reward ourselves with some Daily Claudia.Here are three selfies taken by Ms Spouse while wandering around the neighborhood on May 17, 2020.Have a non-stupid Saturday, everyone.here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future:practice self-care. do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: Life on Foot
item.content:encoded:
It’s been transformative, and I wish I’d done it sooner!Unlike a city, a village has homes with yards. Unlike a suburb, a village has businesses and parks intermixed with homes. It’s the best of both worlds.Being able to walk or bike places has trickle-down effects.Instead of driving 20 minutes one-way to get groceries, I can ride my bike there in 5 minutes.
Because the grocery store is so close, I don’t need to “stock up.” I go every day and buy less with each trip.Because I’m only buying what I need for that day or the next or so, my meats and produce are much fresher.Because I can ride my bike there, I’m getting more exercise every day and spending less time sitting.Because there are so many shops nearby, its easier to go out and do things.
Because it’s easier to access entertainment out of the house, I buy less stuff and spend less time at home.Because I need fewer things at home to keep me from being bored, I can give away a lot possessions.Because I have less stuff, it’s easier to keep my house clean and tidy.Another trickle-down effect of getting out of the house more is that I have a lot more conversations with strangers.I’ll see a cute dog on the bike path and start talking to its owner. I’ll compliment someone’s shirt in the market and we’ll strike up a conversation. I’ll say hi in passing or wave at a stranger while riding my bike, and they’ll wave back.These kinds of random interactions are common place in cities, but virtually nonexistent in most suburbs.A village makes them far more common, and they nourish my soul! It’s something I wasn’t aware I was missing until we moved down here.I wasn’t really a fan of urbanism because I hate cities.But now that I’m aware of the village layout—now that I’m basically living in my own Sesame Street—I’m sold! This is my happy place!

item.title: Friends Don’t Let Friends Watch the Early Vote
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: One collection of data people obsess over in the weeks before a big election is the early vote – a relatively new feature of American elections. You can’t know who people voted for but you can know who is voting by different metrics and you can draw inferences from that. Take all this early vote data with a huge, huge grain of salt. On the one hand it’s just way to easy to interpret the numbers through the prism of one’s hopes. But there’s a bigger and more immediate reason for skepticism today. To understand what early numbers mean you need to have some theory of who is going to vote early and who late. And basically, I think, we don’t. Or not a good one.

item.title: Why Ghosts Wear White Sheets
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: There was one time I actually went trick-or-treating as a ghost wearing a bed sheet with two eye holes. Just once. I learned that it's impossible to keep the eye holes in the right place when you're walking, or doing anything. I guess that's why Charlie Brown had multiple eye holes cut into his sheet. When my kid wanted to be a ghost, I insisted on using a white bathrobe with a (non-pointy) hood and plenty of white face paint. She changed that to a black robe with white face paint and was much scarier. But why are ghosts depicted as being covered in a white sheet? The art that makes them look like that goes back further than the trick-or-treat costume. Even today, when very few kids want to be a ghost for Halloween, we hang up balloons with white fabric over them to decorate our porches, because that says "ghosts" to us. Dr. Emily Zarka of Monstrum explains why.

item.title: Jim Crow returns…one congressional district at a time.
item.author: bounce-mc.us1_388705.10708631-d186966748@mail66.atl71.mcdlv.net
item.content:encoded: One of the defining issues heading into this year’s midterms is how redistricting has rapidly reshaped electoral maps across the country. When the Supreme Court gutted much of the Voting Rights Act earlier this year, a number of states redrew maps eliminating majority-Black districts, weakening Black political power potentially for years to come. But what does this shift feel like for someone working on the ground to expand voting access for Black communities when the promise of equal representation itself is under assault? Ask LaTosha Brown, co-founder of Black Voters Matter Fund, a group that’s been working to increase voter participation within minority communities in the rural South, especially where turnout is low. “There are people who are openly white supremacists that are consolidating power at record speed in such a way that they are stripping away all of the rights, opportunities, and access points for you and your family,” she says, referring to communities of color in the South. “If that don’t move you, it ain’t nothing that I can say that can move you.”, Brown talks with host Al Letson about her winding path into politics, her fight against ongoing voter suppression efforts in the South, and why it’s important to mobilize Black voters now more than ever.

item.title: Voters face flurry of ballot measures that could transform elections across the country
item.author: SRS0=la73=IH=bh1234.vbnewsletters.votebeat.org=bounces+misc=muneer.top@eforward.registrar-servers.com
item.content:encoded: In another setback for Trump’s efforts to inject more federal control into elections, a federal judge last week to check state voter rolls against federal immigration databases. Judge Sparkle Sooknanan’s found the U.S. Department of Justice’s efforts to collect voter rolls from states and use them to check for noncitizens illegally casting ballots is illegal. Most states refused to comply, often citing privacy laws, though some states agreed to give the Trump administration unredacted voter rolls. Courts have so far dismissed 26 Justice Department lawsuits seeking to force states to comply. The ruling constricts the Trump administration from using its Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, program, a federal tool the administration was using to verify voter citizenship once it obtained the voter rolls. This week, Votebeat spoke to Jonathan Diaz, director of voting advocacy and partnerships at the Campaign Legal Center, about the implications.

item.title: Saturdays 80s Jam – Right Here Waiting – Richard Marx
item.author: Schill
item.content:encoded: Released in 1989, Richard Marx’s “Right Here Waiting” became one of the defining romantic ballads of the late 1980s. It was the kind of song that could turn a quiet moment into a full-blown emotional crisis, complete with longing, separation, and the promise that no matter how far away someone might be, one person would still be waiting.The song came from a surprisingly personal place. Marx wrote it while his future wife, actress Cynthia Rhodes, was filming a movie in South Africa. The two were separated by thousands of miles, and Marx began writing a letter to her. Instead of finishing the letter, he turned his feelings into a song.That personal origin is a big part of why “Right Here Waiting” feels so direct. There is no complicated story to follow. The song is essentially about missing someone so badly that distance becomes almost unbearable.Marx recorded the song for his second studio album, , released in 1989. Although the album contained several more upbeat pop-rock songs, “Right Here Waiting” stood apart. Built around piano, keyboards, acoustic guitar, and Marx’s increasingly emotional vocal, it was deliberately simple compared with many of the huge productions dominating pop radio at the time.Marx had already established himself as a successful singer and songwriter, but “Right Here Waiting” took his career to another level. The song became a massive international hit, reaching number one on the Billboard Hot 100 and topping charts in numerous countries.It was also an enormous adult-contemporary success, fitting perfectly into the radio landscape of the late 1980s. At a time when power ballads were everywhere, Marx managed to make his version stand out by keeping the focus on the melody and emotion rather than overwhelming the song with production.The lyrics were also unusually conversational for a major pop ballad. Marx wasn’t presenting some elaborate poetic fantasy. He was describing the frustration of being separated from someone he loved and the determination to remain emotionally connected despite the distance.That made the song incredibly easy for listeners to adopt as their own.It quickly became associated with long-distance relationships, breakups, weddings, slow dances, and just about any situation involving romantic longing. For an entire generation, “Right Here Waiting” became one of those songs that could instantly transport someone back to a particular relationship or moment.Marx’s vocal performance is crucial to that effect. He doesn’t begin by throwing everything at the listener. Instead, the performance gradually builds, allowing the emotion to become more intense as the song progresses.By the final chorus, the arrangement has expanded, but the central idea remains unchanged: distance may be painful, but the commitment remains.The song also benefited from arriving at the perfect moment for the romantic ballad. The late 1980s were packed with enormous pop productions, but there was still a huge audience for songs that could work with nothing more than a singer, a melody, and a story.“Right Here Waiting” proved that a ballad didn’t need elaborate tricks to become enormous.More than three decades later, the song remains one of Richard Marx’s signature recordings. It helped establish him as one of the major adult-pop songwriters of his generation and became a permanent part of the late-1980s romantic soundtrack.Its appeal is remarkably simple.Someone you love is far away.You don’t know exactly when you’ll be together again.But you’re still waiting.Sometimes the simplest idea is the one that connects with the most people, and “Right Here Waiting” turned that feeling into one of 1989’s most enduring pop songs.

item.title: Quoting Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?"Asking that question also changed review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague.Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny.

item.title: The Brewers had the means to end the Dodgers
item.author: bounce+2edd00.7bdc18-5mr68b7cb43ac2h04ai5=kill-the-newsletter.com@m.ghost.io
item.content:encoded: “They may have a bunch of Hall of Famers, but we’ve got a bunch of gamers.” - Pat Murphy, Brewers managerThey’ve gotten good at it.Since 2018, when Christian Yelich arrived and kickstarted the current era of Brewers baseball into motion, they have the fourth-most wins in baseball. Since 2023, when top executive David Stearns stepped down and handed the reins to Matt Arnold, they’re second behind the Dodgers. Since 2024, when Craig Counsell left and Pat Murphy stepped into the manager’s role, they’re first.In the meantime, they ran into failure, and they learned and got better and ran into failure again. They tried things that worked, hit limits — three times dressed in Dodger blue — and pushed and found more things that worked and pushed until they discovered exactly where they stopped working.The whole process was not easy, was better and more productive for not being easy. You’ll see Brewers players talk about it, about Murphy’s standards and the expectations that can grate on them over the longest, most rigorous season in sports.“You have to be a certain kind of player to play for Murph and to play here,” Yelich told reporters in August, after Murphy pulled rookie shortstop Cooper Pratt from a game for a lack of hustle. “You couldn’t coach that way throughout the league. You really couldn’t.”You can see it in Murphy’s strategic needling of his own team, cutting violently away at anything that might dull their focus. And you can see it in his gentle praise, his doting in moments of doubt.“All I know is that on Aug. 12, we have the best record in baseball,” Murphy said right after the Brewers got swept by the Padres, right before they went to Dodger Stadium and took a confidence-building three of four. “And if you've got the best record in baseball, you're still going to go through times like this when things aren't very good, and everything seems to go against you. But it's in your head that things are going against you.”They practiced, got called out when they fell short, and practiced, and got praised when they hit their marks. Last year, it led to 97 wins in the regular season, the most in baseball, but they got trounced four times in a row against the Dodgers. This year, the Brewers won 103 times in the regular season, the most in baseball, again. Faced with the Dodgers, again, they won four times in a row, and they’re going to the World Series.“The end justifies the means. But what if there never is an end? All we have is means.” - Ursula K. Le Guin, If a genie or a god or a world-altering dream granted median baseball fans three wishes this spring, I think the most common ask would have been for their team to win the World Series, and the next most common would have been for the Dodgers to win the World Series. A particularly enraged few might have asked for the Dodgers’ demise ahead of all else. And an even smaller, more conspiracy-brained sect would have sought the opposite: A third straight championship for the Dodgers, with the conviction it would create more conducive conditions for the introduction of a salary cap and a lasting shift in fortunes for their team.Watching a physically compromised Shohei Ohtani lunge and flail through this postseason, watching him do everything but break down in the batter’s box, I was struck by the foolishness of those wishes, of the human impulse to overestimate our understanding of what we want. The Dodgers being out is not the good part, not really. To seek a good outcome above all else is to disregard how you get there.Baseball is too hard and too interesting to be squished into the tiny form of a pawn on a chessboard. It isn’t a game of design and construction so much as sculpture. The season sands teams down to an essence that can only be partly planned. It grinds away at players who absorb the losses, then struggle to shape what’s left into something productive.The Brewers practiced and practiced. Through grit and grind and greatness, they sharpened themselves into a winning instrument that will be judged by the intrinsic value experienced on the field and on the screen, not for the money spent in creating it.It must be said that the Dodgers did a version of the same, repeatedly molding and wielding the game’s heaviest blunt force object to generationally great effect. Last season, the Dodgers overwhelmed the Brewers, but needed every ounce of might to get past the Blue Jays. Only in that struggle did we achieve our fullest appreciation of what they could do, of their means. The end came at the last possible moment, and still far too soon.When the Brewers came calling for this year’s rematch, the weakened Dodgers were the ones overwhelmed. The Brewers won this round decisively, but it didn’t feel like a grand conclusion. It felt like a simple demonstration of physics, like a wasted wish.“There is no avoiding the fight, because stupid will blame the sheep for inciting the wolves.” - Spencer Hall, Major League Baseball, and the team owners whose interests it represents, has spent the year trying to convince the viewing public that baseball is like Rock, Paper, Scissors. The brute force of high payrolls and big markets will always crush the scissors of leaner operations, and no one in their billionaire’s club has the paper to overcome the rocks.Scissors slicing up rock on the sport’s biggest stage won’t change a damn thing about what they want or what they do next. They’re going to chase the financial boon of self-imposed spending limits, possibly at the expense of playing the games, and they’re going to go on saying that the fans want them to do it. They were going to do and say that all along, whether anyone wanted it or not.That they have successfully misled so many interested onlookers is the saddest, most infuriating part, and that it's so immaterial to their only interest (money) makes it worse. The sport earns its interest so relentlessly that they can self-sabotage to grow their margins. There are baseball fans spending their precious emotional energy on rooting to watch less of Ohtani in his prime, on rooting for or against a flattened caricature, on trying to channel their interest through a convoluted string on a deranged cork board that never pointed to anything except more guaranteed riches for the richest people involved. Worse, there are fans convinced they didn’t want to watch at all who will be stunned — “stun” is the Brewers-inspired euphemistic verb of the moment for the Brewers, briefly supplanting “loom” as it relates to the lockout — that the best team in baseball just dispatched the Dodgers.The pennant-winning Brewers are only stunning if you have missed the whole point, if you have been convinced to follow a boring, pointless shadow puppet routine staged 10 stories above the action. They are not a stand-in for small markets or a team-building philosophy or a piece in a billion-dollar game.They are just a great team that practices what remains the oldest and best advice available in baseball: Keep your eye on the ball. ⚾️The part where I ask for your supportThis is a project by and for the passionate. It’s undertaken on mornings, nights and weekends. On trains and planes and holidays. Around the responsibilities of a full-time job.I recognize the building subscription creep, the proliferation of good writers operating independently and charging independently in an unforgiving industry. I don’t expect The Bandwagon to be your only destination for baseball writing, but I hope it makes your emotional investment more enriching.

item.title: Elizabeth Holmes' fiance is the worst man in America. Now we have him on tape.
item.content:encoded: NOTE: This review contains spoilers for “You Can See Everything.”Sometimes the best journalists are people who don’t even purport to be journalists. The late Anthony Bourdain was one such accidental herald, as was “Borat” star Sacha Baron Cohen before the gonzo comedian became recognizably famous no matter his alter ego. Let’s go ahead and add writer/performer Nathan Fielder to the list. You and I know Fielder best from “Nathan For You” and “The Rehearsal.” Everyone else is about to know him for “You Can See Everything,” a tag team effort with documentarian Lance Oppenheim that is not only the best film of 2026 so far, but also one of the finest works of journalism I’ve ever seen.This movie arrives in theaters with plenty of deserved Oscar buzz. But in this case, a mere filmmaking award seems insufficient in recognition. As far as I’m concerned, this thing deserves a Pulitzer (categories be damned). And maybe a Nobel Prize.Article continues below this adBut I’m getting ahead of myself. In case you haven’t seen the film’s trailer, “You Can See Everything” is a portrait of infamous Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, who was convicted in 2022 of defrauding her company’s investors and is currently in prison in Texas. You can read all about Holmes in John Carreyrou’s book “Bad Blood,” an essential tick-tock of the Theranos scandal. The book not only tells the story of how Holmes led people to believe that her company’s revolutionary blood-testing hardware worked (it did not), but also of how the greater Silicon Valley culture inspired Holmes, and in some cases perhaps abetted her. The Theranos scandal was one of the highest profile financial scandals of this century, and Holmes was the haunting, unblinking face of it.Holmes went dark for years after her malfeasance was exposed, until she and her fiance, Billy Evans, agreed to let Fielder and Oppenheim into their slipshod rental cottage in Del Mar for weeks on end and film the couple (and their two very cute children) as they prepared for Holmes to report to prison. Fielder and Oppenheim were allowed to film the Holmes family nearly 24/7, with Fielder at one point agreeing to stay with the family for an extended period of time. Hence, the film’s title. You will, indeed, see everything. Almost too much of everything, given that this doc runs nearly three hours, and given that the camera stays uncomfortably tight on its participants, Fielder included, for the bulk of that time.You’ll also see Billy Evans’ penis, so be warned or titillated as you see fit.Article continues below this adAs Fielder ingratiates himself with Holmes and Evans, he gets them comfortable enough to ask the hard questions: about Theranos, about prison, and even about themselves. The resulting footage is often shocking. You will see Elizabeth Holmes, who still maintains she did nothing wrong, answer “no” when Fielder asks her if she’s ever lied in her life. You will hear Billy Evans, the real villain in this particular story, tell everyone in the room that he carries a gun on him 24/7. You will see Fielder screen the legendary “Who’s on first?” sketch for Holmes and her partner, with Holmes missing the central joke of the sketch entirely. You will see Fielder explain to Holmes that “Who” is the name of the guy on first base, with her still not really grasping it. And you’ll see Holmes’ partner tell her, “You see the world differently,” in a skin-crawling attempt to turn her seeming cluelessness into something laudatory. The Silicon Valley mindset at work.Speaking of the Valley mindset, you will also see Holmes and Evans spend a great deal of time in this movie attempting to boot up Theranos 2.0. They even go so far as to drag out some of the original Theranos blood testing apparatus, which looks like a bunch of random parts from TigerDirect they hooked together, to show Fielder what their product can do. We do not see it doing anything on screen, but the couple assures that it would if it was, like, hooked up properly. These scenes are extremely funny, but funny isn’t what Fielder is looking for. He’s trying to figure out if this woman is a clueless naif, if she believes her own lies, or if she is playing the of an innocent woman, and doing so with such effectiveness that, to paraphrase Fielder, she might be the most manipulative person in the world.Article continues below this adThe answer proves fabulously elusive, and so Fielder and Oppenheim go to extremes in their attempt to find it. They hold the camera on Holmes’ rubbery elfin face for what feels like hours at a time, to see if she’ll blink (figuratively literally!). They interview Holmes’ visiting parents, with the father, former Enron exec Christian Holmes, casually telling Fielder that everything changed for his daughter “when she was raped.” To the furthest extreme, they bring in actress Amanda Seyfried — who Holmes in the Hulu TV show “The Dropout” — to recreate any dialogues Fielder had with Holmes herself that couldn’t be recorded on camera. Seyfried is so convincing in mimicking Holmes that you, the audience, might forget which scenes were Seyfried talking to the camera and not Holmes herself. I know I did.It gets crazier. After Holmes reports to prison, Seyfried joins Fielder on a trip to visit Billy Evans in a clandestine attempt to get Holmes’ partner to admit that, without Holmes’ knowledge, he demanded (and for a moment, received promise of), monetary compensation from the A24 studio for the couple’s participation in this documentary.A brief pause here. Billy Evans is scion to the San Diego-based Evans Hotels family fortune. Evans met Holmes well after she’d become notorious, but tells Fielder early in “You Can See Everything” that he didn’t recognize her when the two first met. In fact, he fell in love with Holmes within an hour of meeting her, then found out who she was, still wanted to be with her anyway. Do you buy this story? Of course you don’t. This man is full of s—t, and that becomes even more apparent when he’s confronted by both Fielder and Seyfried after Holmes has reported to prison. That’s when we hear Evans sneer, “I’m better read than you,” at Seyfried — who, as a reminder, is one of the most skilled people in the world at her chosen profession. He also taunts Seyfried for getting “owned” on Twitter after she derided the late white supremacist Charlie Kirk, whom of course Evans actually admired. This man is an absolute piece of s—t.Thankfully, Seyfried says as much, becoming audience surrogate after that alarming sequence and telling Fielder that Holmes’ partner is “bats—t crazy.” Amanda Seyfried might be the coolest person in Hollywood. As for Fielder, he’s left wondering if Holmes has been victimized by her own partner, by her former Theranos paramour Sunny Balwani (also now in prison, and whom Holmes also accused of raping her), and by God knows who else. Was this woman, once a billionaire, more pawn than mastermind? Fielder shows some (platonic) fondness for Holmes over the course of this film, but by this point in the story it’s hard to know if , the interviewer, is also playing a character in order to get what he wants.Article continues below this adFielder, to his credit, acknowledges the thorniness of all this. He’s openly uncertain of having Seyfried dramatize Holmes’ words on camera because, no matter how talented the actress is, it’s still not Holmes herself saying those words to the camera. He also doesn’t know if he’s surreptitiously fallen for Holmes’ graciousness, to the point where he questions himself to Seyfried for believing Holmes when she told him, almost on a lark, that she had no clue Evans was making money moves behind her back. That leads to Seyfried herself wondering if her own Hulu portrayal of Holmes was truth, blurred truth, or just fiction. By the end of the film, Seyfried isn’t sure what the word “fiction” should even mean.That’s what makes this film a masterwork. “You Can See Everything” refers plainly to the extensive footage that Fielder and Oppenheim were able to obtain. But here’s a documentary that also shows you, the audience, its whole methodology. It allows you to see the potential flaws in its reporting, and how those flaws might impede the filmmakers’ attempt to find real answers. It’s that truly radical transparency that differentiates this documentary not only from the tacit sponcon docs that now plague your television (Billy Evans cites Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s deal with Netflix as a reason that he should be paid by A24 for appearing on camera), but also from a lot of the best pure documentaries ever filmed. Here is a movie that exists on a level with Banksy’s “Exit Through the Gift Shop” as a superlative example of how the truth can be not just impossible to find but, with great determination, can be eradicated altogether. I’ll never forget it.Article continues below this ad

item.title: A searchable archive of everything
item.author: Jack Baty
item.content:encoded: I wrote something down recently, and later I couldn't find it. If you know me, you know why; I put my notes into too many different apps.Once in a while I declare loudly that "I'm using only this app, from now on! I mean it!" and then change my mind a month later. It's just the way I am. This most recent failure was the last straw and finally forced me to deal with it properly.Instead of fixing myself, I built a software crutch. I spent today vibe-coding an indexer and search engine for all of my stuff. Here's the initial version of a web UI:I also hacked together a TUI and an Emacs package. Those access the data via Tailscale SSH so I don't need to worry about installing things on other machines. Just the wrapper script.Here's the list of sources being indexed (so far):./archive index baty.net: 1272 items (0.9s) archive.baty.net: 2791 items (1.1s) linux.baty.net: 26 items (0.0s) blot.baty.net: 678 items (0.3s) jackbaty.com: 581 items (0.1s) notes: 2287 items (1.0s) dayone: 2507 items (1.4s) thebrain: 1177 items (0.5s) mail: 1 updated, 0 removed (since revision 43773) (1.6s) duplicates: 786 items in 381 groups (10.2s) One nice thing about this is now I can search all of my Denote notes from my phone.Everything is plain files and it uses boring, durable tools, so the archive should outlive whichever apps made the content that week. Even an AI layer, if I add one, sits on top of the search instead of being built into it. The database is disposable because it only takes 10 seconds to reindex everything.Maybe now I'll be OK with all of my app churn.

item.title: An Owl Uses Sound to Hunt Under the Snow
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: If you're a rodent out in the forest, there's nothing more frightening than a hungry owl. They stare at you with those super predator eyes and glide in silently for the kill. Under a thick blanket of snow, however, they can't see you. The great grey owl will find you anyway. These birds have superpowers, and they can hear voles moving underneath the snow. They have excellent hearing, and their whole face is designed to enhance that ability. We need special effects to detect what the owl can hear. They also use physics to fine-tune their attack on a fast-moving vole they cannot see. The owl's survival depends on it. This nature sequence is from the CBC show , from a series called Secret World of Sound. If you're interested, you can see how they got this amazing footage in a behind the scenes video explaining the acoustic camera. (via kottke)

item.title: Some Caveats on Dems Retaking the Senate
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: Democrats’ prospects across the board look about as good as they have at any point in the 2026 election cycle, and about as good as could have reasonably been imagined at any point since late November 2024. House, Senate, governorships, state legislative races, really just about everything is looking pretty rosy. The point of this post isn’t to rain on any of that. But for the last week or so I’ve been wanting to write a post about just how close many of the frontline Senate races are, despite the fact that it’s plausible that Democrats could come out of this election with a majority in the low or even mid-50s. What I’m talking about here is no more than the inherent uncertainty around all polls and all elections. But it’s still worth absorbing.

item.title: La Liga President Says Real Madrid Is Moving Like Joseph Goebbels
item.author: Luis Paez-Pumar
item.content:encoded: It was clear that the relationship between Real Madrid and La Liga president Javier Tebas was heading toward disaster when the two parties started bickering in the press less than a month ago, but we've now reached the stage where one is earnestly comparing the behavior of the other to an infamous Nazi.After Jose Mourinho printed out images of perceived missed calls from the Madrid derby, Tebas blasted Real Madrid for what he felt was a bit of image manipulation, calling the club out for believing itself to be bigger than La Liga itself, all while utilizing the press to drive forward its messaging. In response, Madrid called out what it felt was Tebas's fixation on belittling the winningest club in Spanish soccer history. As I said in September, I thought cooler heads would prevail after how embarrassing that whole situation was for both sides. Boy howdy, was I wrong!As is proving to be his custom, Tebas woke up on Friday and decided to send yet another ballista bolt at Real Madrid. Specifically, and repeatedly, Tebas attacked the media surrounding the club for what he believes are biased articles and debate segments on Real Madrid TV. His targets this time were Tomás González-Martín and Jesús Urdiola, journalists with , the same Spanish publication he attacked last time. Tebas raised two specific articles as issues: One, by González-Martín, details Real Madrid's continued fight with the league over the Negreira referee scandal; the other, by Urdiola, is about how Real Madrid feels personally attacked by La Liga's schedule-making.

item.title: The CFP Is Expanding For The Same Reason The PCSA Is Gaining Momentum
item.author: Israel Daramola
item.content:encoded: ESPN is reporting that ESPN and the College Football Playoff are close to a deal to expand the playoff field to 24 teams in 2027. This news arrives merely two years after the field already expanded from four teams to 12. Not only was this expansion inevitable, but it is unlikely to be the last we see.For now, we are on the cusp of a 24-team playoff, which comes as ESPN and the CFP have been negotiating a big new deal for the network to continue broadcasting the games. According to ESPN's reporting, this new deal will do away with Power 4 conference championship games and start the season a week earlier. Details are reportedly being finalized, but ESPN describes the current composition for the 24-team field as 19 at-large bids, the Power 4 conference champions "as determined by each league," and the highest-ranked Group of 6 team.The Big Ten has been a leading proponent for this change, and its commissioner Tony Pettiti pushed back against complaints that further expansion would dilute and devalue the product and the games. He argues that the new system would include "tiered incentives." According to ESPN, seeds 1 through 8 would get a first-round bye, followed by a home game. Teams seeded from 9 through 16 would get a first-round home game, while teams seeded 17 and lower should be vying for a higher ranking, both to stay in competition and to get that first-round home game. Cool.

item.title: Trump DOJ Takes Election Interference to Next Level
item.author: David Kurtz
item.content:encoded: Do You Get Morning Memo Via Email?Beginning next week, we’re going to be using a new email provider to send out Morning Memo each day. If you already receive Morning Memo by email, you don’t need to do a thing. Morning Memo will still come to you the same as usual, but directly from TPM instead of from Substack. You’ll still be able to read Morning Memo in the email version or on Substack or at TPM.Trump DOJ Sues CaliforniaI’ve had my hair on fire the last three days on the Trump administration’s unprecedented new interference in the midterm elections because it represents a high water mark in its effort to intrude in state-run elections.Sequestering and not counting already-cast ballots — on the dubious grounds that the Trump administration has identified alleged noncitizens who received mail-in ballots — is a dramatic escalation of its month-long attack on state-run federal elections. (It also fits perfectly into the thematics of a GOP campaign largely being run on racist and xenophobic themes in the absence of any affirmative arguments for more of the same.)But we haven’t really talked about the administration’s end game here, which has now become a little more clear.At this stage, the administration doesn’t appear to be advancing a strategy to tilt the outcomes in particular elections by disqualifying a significant number of ballots or by suppressing the overall vote. Even if that was its goal, the numbers involved at this point just aren’t big enough.We learned yesterday in the lawsuit that the Trump DOJ filed against California that its list of “likely noncitizen voters” contained in the vicinity of 20,000 names. I had assumed that the DOJ list was specific to Los Angeles County since acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter sent his list on an encrypted thumb drive (along with a sticky note containing the password). But the lawsuit says the 20,000 names is a statewide list — “with many addresses listed in Los Angeles County.” (That’s down a wee bit from the noncitizen voters that the Trump administration previously claimed California had.)Even if you account for the atmospherics of the DOJ suing to weed out alleged noncitizen voters having some dampening effect on minority voter turnout, the number of alleged noncitizen voters aren’t anywhere near big enough to have either a significant or predictably pro-GOP effect on election outcomes in California.So what does that leave as plausible goals for the administration?Goal #1: Get a federal court somewhere to rule that the law provides a role for the federal government in making sure noncitizens don’t voteGiven what the law says, including the Constitution, legal experts insist it’s a long-shot bid. But it’s a gambit with a high upside and not much political downside. You don’t make shots you don’t take, etc.That being said, I’m struggling with why the Trump DOJ would pick California as the venue for this gambit versus a reliably red state in a federal circuit that is more obviously MAGA-tilted than the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, which covers California.(For what it’s worth, the Trump DOJ is trying to get the California case in front of the Trump-appointed judge who presided over Hunter Biden’s tax fraud conviction, arguing that this case is related to an election case he’s already hearing. But there’s nothing about U.S. District Judge Mark C. Scarsi that marks him as a radical MAGA-coded judge. Already fighting back, California wants the case assigned to a Clinton-appointed judge who is already hearing a election case that it claims is more related than Scarsi’s is.)Ultimately prevailing in the California lawsuit — or in yet-to-be-filed cases in other states — would open the door wide to the Trump administration being able to intervene in the election in much more robust ways under the guise of policing the virtually nonexistent problem of noncitizen voting.But with less than three weeks until voting ends, it might make more sense to view this as a long-term bid with bigger potential impacts coming after the 2026 election — except in one regard, which brings us to the next goal.Goal #1A: Create election chaosIn the short term, with Republicans almost certain to lose the House and the Senate increasingly at risk, sowing chaos has mostly upside for the GOP. In that sense, the California lawsuit is less a legal strategy than a political one.Noncitizen voting is the Big Lie of 2026, so think of this as a prelude to a post-election refusal to accept the results, fights over close individual races, and desperate attempts to salvage a majority in either chamber. Conflicting court rulings, emergency appeals, and a last-ditch bid to get the Supreme Court to decide the election somehow all gin up a crisis atmosphere that’s then used to justify extraordinary interventions of one form or another.The point isn’t to fear-monger here, but just to note that chaos favors the sure loser desperate to do anything to avoid their fate.Goal #2: Delegitimizing a Democratic winRegardless of the outcome of the California lawsuit, the Big Lie of noncitizen voting will inevitably be sustained past the election into the new Congress — as a GOP hand-wave to minimize its own losses, dismiss the Democratic mandate, resist a post-election narrative of MAGA’s demise — and soothe the wounded ego of a certain former reality TV star.The lawsuit in California helps to fortify that rhetorical argument, even if the Trump DOJ ultimately loses. Time and again, MAGA has seized on setbacks and losses as proof of is own victimhood.One caveat to all of the above: California may not be the only place that the Trump DOJ decides to do battle on noncitizen voting while voting is underway. It laid the same groundwork in some two dozen states as it did in California by requesting voter information over the past several months in its pursuit of the mythic noncitizen voter, ultimately losing repeatedly in court. If you see evidence of this happening in other states, please let me know. My contact info is linked at the bottom of this post.And now the Trump administration is attempting to strip Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar, who was born in Somalia, of her citizenship so as to deport her. This is more than just another persecution of one of Trump’s political enemies. Rather, his government is tacitly declaring the citizenship of all foreign-born people provisional, their Americanness something that can be revoked. It’s a frontal attack on the idea of constitutional equality.Uneven Playing Field AlertYour occasional reminder that U.S. elections are, by law, tilted in favor of monied interests to a greater extent than at any point since at least the Gilded Age:NYT: Avalanche of G.O.P. Cash Keeps the Party Competitive Despite Its ProblemsPolitico: Megadonors are powering Republicans’ spending advantageNYT: Most of Ken Paxton’s Money Can Be Traced to One Man: Elon Musk

item.title: Do Not Rage At Your Most Online Fans
item.author: Ray Ratto
item.content:encoded: It's been a tough year for Texas A&M and head coach Mike Elko, who celebrated the Aggies' 27-6 loss to Missouri last Saturday by calling the team's leading social media outlet a "cesspool" and, two days later, apologized for calling the team's leading social media outlet a "cesspool." Elko also said that he is the reason Texas A&M is struggling, which is probably what the team's leading social media outlet was saying about him after his team lost at home by three scores. This is that rare case where someone can be right all three times, making Saturday's showdown with The Citadel a must-watch game, just to see what Elko says afterward if his Aggies don't cover the 45.5-point spread. Otherwise, it's just another weekend in college football's version of paradise, if that's what you consider your afterlife goal. We are near midseason, and exactly as we predicted the most exciting programs in the sport are Will Stein's Kentucky and Bob Chesney's UCLA. Bill Belichick's UNC team keeps losing, but they're too scrappy and full of energy to make fun of or even care about. Deion Sanders's Colorado team is a complete mess but are too dull and incompetent to fuel much schadenfreude. Lane Kiffin cannot get the stank of the Brian Kelly era off LSU in one offseason, it turns out. And all the best teams are just kinda humming along uncontroversially, save for the occasional bad referee call. Texas lost the Red River Shootout to a mid-to-bad Oklahoma team, but that's just something that happens in that game.

item.title: Going 94 MPH on a Skateboard (New World Record)
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: Diego Poncelet recently set a new world record for the fastest speed on a skateboard. The old record was 146.7 km/h (91.2 mph) and he hit 151.8 km/h (94.3 mph). There are a couple of parts you can skip, but watching most of the video is worth it because you see the process and can compare how truly insanely fast he is moving during the final run — I found myself holding my breath for the last minute or so.Also, I cannot believe how closely the camera car is following him — looks like only a few feet away. Bonkers.I just found the first time I posted about speed skateboarding on KDO: this post from 2008. Less aerodynamic, more gonzo, and the cameraman is also on a skateboard going equally fast.

item.title: Smart Can Win
item.author: Ray Ratto
item.content:encoded: And so ends the Los Angeles Dodgers' reign as baseball's most overwhelming boogeyman. The poster kids for the omnipotence of money, the belief that having the best player means being the best team, the power of the big market over all it surveys—all of that feels less important at this moment than the ability to do the things the Milwaukee Brewers do better than anyone else. The same old song has been replaced, for the moment, by this: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7Xzmeye6MaY Yes, meet your new overlords. The Brewers pack extraordinary amounts of baseball into every game, play it better than anyone else, and supposedly have no interest in hitting home runs. It was fitting, then, that they gave the nation a little tweak on the cheek Thursday night en route to sweeping the Dodgers out of the postseason when the final run they scored in their 6-4 win came on a moonshot from noted Boston Red Sox ex-pat and devoted homer avoider David Hamilton. The Brewers did all the things that made them the best team in baseball this season, and mostly kept the Dodgers from doing the things that won them the last two World Series—and then they did the stuff that contemporary winning baseball teams do, too, in a typically unpredictable way.

item.title: The Village
item.content:encoded: About 14 years ago, we moved out into the rural suburbs. I loved the quiet, the abundant wildlife, and our proximity to farms.I didn’t realize just how often doing at all would require a car.Absolutely was walkable. We lived at the very top of a very high hill, so things weren’t really bikeable either.Groceries, restaurants, entertainment, friends, the library, and so on… you need to get in a car and drive at least 15 minutes for all of it.And as a result, we became homebodies, and spent a lot of money buying a lot of stuff to make our home a place we had to leave as little as possible.In a city, any particular block will include a mix of apartments, businesses, and maybe a park or school or playground. No matter where you live, you can walk or bike to get around and get what you need.By contrast, suburb zoning laws in North America usually prevent this kind of mixed-use development.Homes are allowed on one side of town. Businesses are allowed on another. They’re typically pretty far from each other.This means that unless you’re right on the border of these two zones, you a car to do anything.Walk and bike places, but live in a noisy, busy, crowded space.Get quiet and peace, but need a car to get anywhere.But there’s a third option!In much of Europe (and small pockets of America), you can find villages.These are suburban spaces. They’re relatively quiet, and have homes with lawns and lots of wildlife around.But they’re also walkable and bikeable.The zoning of these spaces allows for small businesses to coexist alongside homes. More restricted commercial use than a city, but far less so than a typical sprawling suburb.They often have narrower roads, which slows down car traffic, making them more pedestrian friendly, too.We recently decided we were done with the sprawl, and moved from a rural suburb in Massachusetts to a small coastal village in Rhode Island.The change in lifestyle that comes from being in a walkable/bikeable area has been transformative, and I’m going to talk all about it in part two!

item.title: The Not-So-Great Defector Bake Off Exults, Eventually, In The Freedom Of Audience Choice Week
item.author: Kelsey McKinney
item.content:encoded: The Not-So-Great Defector Bake Off, where Kelsey and Chris attempt to complete the technical challenges from the newest season of The Great British Bake Off in their own home kitchens, with the same time parameters as the professional-grade bakers competing on the show.It's nice having Nigella Lawson in the tent. She is cheerful and radiates serenity, and she takes those big glorious bites. She makes you want to bake and to eat. She even makes you want to share the things you bake with others, so that they too can take a huge cheek-bulging bite of something messy and crumbly and you two can giggle together at the decadence of it all.

item.title: What Is The Mob Movie Donald Trump Saw With A Gangster Named “Alan Jones” In It?
item.author: David Roth
item.content:encoded: The model of Donald Trump currently on display is fussy and sour, poached to glossy and unappetizing gumminess in his own luxurious bathwater; he is also, to all appearances, miserable. It is hard to say whether the adoration of his admirers or the revulsion of a large and growing portion of the American populace has been worse for him in that regard, but neither seems to have done him much good. The Trump currently maundering and free-associating through 110-minute performances at various swing-state event spaces is manic or wan but mostly just dull—a mean old dunce listing his gripes, telling weird lies, and talking about dumb stuff he saw on TV. People suffer and die as a direct result of how much he sucks, every day, and he is still somehow the most boring old rich guy imaginable. Not to put too fine a point on it, but it is humiliating in the extreme to live in a society that produced someone like this at all, let alone put him in charge of everything. Trump remains very well-insulated from the consequences of his actions, moment by moment thanks to a team of chittering courtiers and Renfield types and more generally because protecting him from those consequences is the only thing that a number of hugely important political institutions really do anymore. But also you can tell that he knows, at some level, that everyone can see that he is failing.There's another version of Donald Trump that only comes out when he feels safe, and while that version also sucks ass and is stupid as hell, it is notable as the last vestige of the character who once charmed America's most credulous and least exacting voters. The other version of him, the one that speaks in front of smaller, more carefully curated crowds, does not seem to know that everyone can see that he is failing. That Trump is making innumerable lives around the world harder, crueler, and worse is not something that would bother him, because his own life remains pretty much the same. The trouble comes when he is perceived, correctly, as a preening and delusional failure, and in front of a crowd of people who believe he can do no wrong, all of whom are visibly, clammily yearning to give him more of their money, Trump is untroubled. He knows he can get up there and just say whatever, and so he does.

item.title: The History of Domino's
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: The original title of this video is How Domino's Became #1 With Bad Pizza, but I'm not using that because many folks like Domino's pizza. I haven't eaten one in I don't know how long and besides, pizza is like sex. Anyway, Domino's is the number one pizza chain, and often it's the only name people can remember. Most of that is the work of Tom Monaghan, who founded Domino's in 1960 with his younger brother Jim. Success came from hard work, streamlining the restaurant's menu, delivery, and inventing of the pizza box. Name recognition came, too. In the last 60 years, there have been many Domino's Pizza news stories that you will recall once you hear them again. Not all were detrimental to the company. but they all add up to a pizza place that everyone knows, even if they don't particularly care for the pizza.

item.title: New from Chicago: An urgent call to turn from broken economics
item.author: 555618737.1998257.813949133233@e2ma.net
item.content:encoded:
Acclaimed economist James K. Galbraith sounds an urgent alarm: how conventional economic ideas and policies are unequipped to account for the most daunting challenges of our geopolitical moment.Amid a mounting sense of American decline, Americans live with a new kind of dissonance: economists announcing that everything is fundamentally fine. Where growth is steady, unemployment is low, prices are (somewhat) stable, and stocks are high—what’s there to worry about? shows that this dissonance reflects a failure to evolve. James K. Galbraith’s incisive history of economic policy in this century is grounded in the fundamental problem that today’s experts are still deploying tools from all yesterday’s wars: obsolete economic ideas, measures, and doctrines focused on market functioning and crude economic indicators like output and prices. These methods, many of them honed a century ago against a vastly different social landscape, offer little hope in the face of today’s more existential threats.
Such conventional policies, Galbraith argues, are increasingly ill-equipped to counter the daunting challenges of our moment—from inflation to trade sanctions, industrial cold wars, and climate change—and, left unacknowledged, are accelerating the end of the US economy as we know it. Shortcomings include the weak responses to the inflation of 2021–2022; the sanctions war against Russia; the rise of China; the weak and ineffective attempt at industrial revival; and the impending demographic crisis. All have roots in a flawed body of outdated economic thought that has been sustained for ideological rather than practical reasons. They now promise to hinder the United States in the emerging multipolar world. As Galbraith makes plain, for all the virtues of the market system, governments and their policies make markets possible. The ideas behind the policies—for better or worse—will determine the fate of the US economy—and new and better ideas are urgently needed. The alternative—sticking with economic ideas and policies we know and currently use—brings the power to destroy us all.

item.title: We're tracking 76 ongoing anti-voting lawsuits (and counting)
item.author: 1axbn3qnmubd8o3t6lh6ovkj3rby1u13akv9gj@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: To say there’s a lot going on with voting in North Carolina would be an understatement. A state board of elections meeting could yield anything from voter suppression by Chick-fil-A’s weekend hours to voter suppression led by partisan operatives to voter suppression manifesting in threats to arrest student meeting attendees.Notice a trend? You aren’t alone. So did the nearly a dozen voters, experts and election officials I spoke to marking the start of early voting in the Tar Heel state.In short, hurdles to voting access are not one-off instances. For marginalized communities, they’re embedded in the very fabric of the state. This fall, the GOP-controlled elections board for students and majority-Black neighborhoods, slashed Sunday voting hours in half, a slew of confusing letters asking for various levels of voter identification information, and made it easier to reject mail ballots.Mail ballot restrictions are facing fierce , and we’re awaiting a ruling any day now that would either block or uphold a rule that voters must seal an inner envelope tucked, as one voter described to me, “like an eighth of an inch” away from the outer envelope.It’s a nearly impossible task for those with tremors or other mobility constraints. But it’s already spoiling ballots, according to multiple county election officials who spoke to me for this story. And we didn’t even get to the fact that North Carolina is a major battleground in this election.The stakes truly couldn’t be higher.

item.title: Charanjit Singh
item.author: Flow State
item.content:encoded: It’s Friday so we’re listening to something more upbeat. Today we’re listening to Charanjit Singh, an Indian composer and electronic musician from Bombay. Earlier this week Synthesizing: Ten Ragas to a Disco Beat. He was born in 1940, his parents instrument makers, and he played many different instruments growing up. His versatility earned him plenty of gigs in Bollywood as a session player, though by the early 1980s he’d grown bored of the formula. Around that time, the Japanese corporation Roland released the TB-303 bass synthesizer and TR-808 drum machine. Singh was attracted to these newfangled devices as a way to pursue a new musical direction. He used them, along with the Jupiter 8 synthesizer, to make Ten Ragas to a Disco Beat, which was released in 1982 to little fanfare. Decades later, the album was rediscovered and recognized as an incredibly prescient realization of electronic dance music, especially its acid house-style use of the 303. The record was recently reissued by the label Light in the Attic. A few years before Singh passed away in 2015, he told of the Roland and Jupiter instruments, “At home I practised with the combination and I thought ‘It sounds good – why not record it.’”

item.title: Paid Vacation
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: You will not be surprised that that United States has no mandatory paid days off for workers. But you might be surprised that we are the ONLY nation with over a million people that does not mandate any paid days off for workers. Gig work doesn't have any paid time off at all. In radio, most stations I worked for gave you a week's vacation if you lasted a whole year. However, they always made you feel bad for taking it. And you had to work extra hours for anyone else who took one, so we paid for it during the year and management wasn't out any cash. The rest of the world doesn't expect everybody to work all the time forever.

item.title: When trees fall in a golf course, do they make a sound?
item.author: bounce_4e2016e8-e7c8-f111-bf5b-000d3a4fbe83_prod@bounce.myngp.com
item.content:encoded: Thanks to committed plaintiffs, good lawyers, and a federal judge carefully applying the law, the destruction of hundreds of trees at a public golf course is now being heard across the country. Earlier this year, the DC Preservation League and two frequent golfers at East Potomac Golf Course sued the Department of the Interior and the National Park Service, challenging plans by the President to transform the existing historic public golf course into “an elite champion-style course.” Through multiple court hearings, the judge initially declined to enter injunctive relief. Instead, she directed the government to provide advance notice of substantive construction work and accepted the government’s assurances that it would do so. However, in the early morning of Saturday, October 10, as noted in a subsequent order by the court, the government “…razed nearly 430 trees, none of which were hazardous or posed safety concerns.”With each thud of the 430 trees needlessly destroyed during that holiday weekend, there was a corresponding blow to the justice system. A judge had expected that the government would act in good faith and in accordance with commitments made in a court of law. Instead, that government rushed to bypass those assurances in order to reshape a public resource in line with the President’s vision, with many questions unanswered, including about future public access and affordability. On October 13, the judge issued that temporary restraining order. For the government, it was another severe blow to the presumption of trust and honest dealing that Department of Justice lawyers previously had brought with them into the courtroom. As the judge stated in her opinion: “Breakneck speed to clear trees that posed no harm. The reason? Disputed. The budget? Unclear. The environmental impact? Unstudied. The urgency? None. Next steps: bulldoze hundreds more.”This is not simply a case about whether trees were removed in noncompliance with regulatory programs that would apply to a massive overhaul of a public space. Rather, this is an example of what happens when respect for the rule of law erodes. This case demonstrates how difficult it is for the courts to keep up with an administration that ignores rules that apply to everyone else, spurns judicial directives, and then sends government lawyers to appear before judges, caught between trying to please their employer and possibly risking their own license to practice law in doing so. Joyce Vance, Distinguished Professor of the Practice of Law at the University of Alabama School of Law and a former United States Attorney, has written about the importance of holding on to the moral compass that allows us to distinguish right from wrong. Recognizing how exhausting it is to watch “attacks on democracy unfold every day,” she urges that we “never be quiet about it”. Indeed, that is a responsibility we all share. Speak out. Protect the rule of law. Defend judges who apply the law, even as they risk attacks from their own government.When trees fall, be the sound that is heard everywhere.Lawyers Defending American DemocracyP.S. Thank you for your ongoing support of LDAD. Please help us protect the rule of law and the freedoms we hold dear by volunteering for our Meeting the Moment initiative and donating to our work.

item.title: The law might finally be catching up to DOGE
item.author: delivery_20261015091552.47947129.281@bounce.slate.com
item.content:encoded:
Believe it or not, it’s been over a year since Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency tore through the U.S. government, infamously shuttering the U.S. Agency for International Development while falsely claiming it had saved America $52.8 billion. Throughout its 10-month run, DOGE was dodging a Freedom of Information Act request from a public interest group, which eventually led to a lawsuit that sought to force the agency to hand over internal records that would reveal how it was making decisions. The dispute has been simmering for over a year now, ping-ponging between lower courts, appeals court panels, and the Supreme Court as the Trump administration has been pushing to protect DOGE from any public disclosures. But now, this fight might finally be coming to an end, as the Supreme Court agreed this week to consider the case, for a second time—the first time, SCOTUS sided with the Trump administration by forcing a lower court to reevaluate its order forcing it to hand over DOGE’s records—and Its decision stands to impact what responsibility all federal agencies have to the public—if any.
On Tuesday, the Supreme Court agreed to hear arguments in U.S. DOGE Service v. U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, where the justices will weigh in on whether DOGE should be classified as a federal agency, and therefore subject to FOIA requests—a federal mandate that gives any person the right to access records from federal executive branch agencies. The Trump administration has been insisting for the past year that DOGE was not a federal agency, but a presidential advisory body, and therefore not subject to FOIA. However, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, the watchdog group suing, is calling foul, noting that DOGE was given taxpayer dollars to the tune of $41 million to fund its operations. DOGE also incorrectly sought to apply the standard—a 2004 case that shielded the executive branch from complying with public records requests—in order to maintain autonomy of its office and safeguard confidentiality of its communications, the lawsuit argues.
This case will be critical in holding DOGE accountable for not just the utter destruction it caused within the U.S. government, but in setting a clear precedent for how U.S. presidents can or cannot bypass federal disclosure laws. For decades, journalists in particular have relied on FOIA to unearth waste, abuse, and ethics violations committed by the U.S. government, something that’s become alarmingly common under Trump.
CREW first filed FOIA requests with DOGE in January 2025, around the time President Donald Trump established the agency via executive order. The watchdog group noted that Musk was tasked with running DOGE even though he never received official congressional approval and was operating “seemingly unchecked, with no clarity on its structure, staffing, budget or operations, including whether it is following federal ethics and transparency laws or even acting within its legal authority,” CREW said in a statement. The group’s goal was to arm Congress with critical information that could inform its upcoming appropriations cycle. However, things did not go to plan.
The Trump administration flatly refused to comply with CREW’s records request, while DOGE fired tens of thousands of federal employees, collected Americans’ most sensitive data, and dismantled core agencies like USAID, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the Department of Education, and more. By February 2025, CREW had filed a lawsuit in order to force DOGE’s cooperation. In court the Trump administration argued DOGE was not legally required to comply with FOIA requests because it was not technically a federal agency. U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper disagreed with that assessment and concluded that DOGE was likely subject to FOIA “because it is endowed with and is apparently exercising ‘substantial authority independent of the President.’ ”
Unsatisfied, the Trump administration tried to appeal Cooper’s order but was rejected by the D.C. appeals court panel. Come May 2025, the administration decided to knock on the Supreme Court’s door, asking the justices to stay Cooper’s order, and they agreed. In an unsigned order, they said Cooper’s order was overly broad and needed to “counsel judicial deference and restraint in the context of discovery regarding internal Executive Branch communications.” In response, CREW amended its FOIA request to exclude any information about recommendations DOGE staffers made directly to the White House. Lower courts declined to block its records request, effectively forcing the Trump administration to hand over the bulk of CREW’s original FOIA request.
Still dissatisfied with having to give even an inch, the Trump administration did not comply with that ruling, and instead came back to SCOTUS this year, asking the justices to consider the case on its merits and assess all of CREW’s FOIA requests of federal agencies, from DOGE and beyond. It accused Cooper of continuing to approve “intrusive discovery against a presidential advisory body without adequate consideration for the separation of powers, the FOIA statute,” and the Supreme Court’s order from last year. The administration wants SCOTUS to apply the standard, while CREW has argued “this case looks nothing like ,” and if it did it would effectively foreclose discovery in this case, which is not what SCOTUS said in last year’s order.

item.title: The Secret History Of Dodger Stadium’s Mysterious Concrete Murals
item.author: Nate Rogers
item.content:encoded: L.A. Material is an independent news organization aimed at filling some holes in the Los Angeles news landscape and making that fascinating, fragmented city more legible. You can learn more, and subscribe, at lamaterial.com. This story originally ran at the site on Sept. 30.I had been going to Dodger Stadium with my dad for about 30 years before he pointed them out to me. “See that?” he asked, gesturing toward two rectangular panels of concrete on a far wall of the main seating structure. They looked almost like friezes, carved with inscrutable designs. My dad had been wondering about them for decades.Turns out the pieces he’d spotted are just the beginning. Eventually I’d locate more custom bas-relief sculptures around the park—about a dozen in total. Smaller ones visible from the field-level entrances. Massive, multi-story pieces that wrap around certain outside corners of the building. They’re subtle: abstract scenes unadorned with color, camouflaged into the rest of their concrete environments, in some cases obscured by trees and bushes.

item.title: It’s Jake Bauerses All The Way Down
item.author: Kathryn Xu
item.content:encoded: After a flyout and a strikeout in his first two attempts, Jake Bauers's third time facing Blake Snell in Wednesday's Game 3 of the National League Championship Series went like this: Bauers took a slider down the middle of the plate for strike one. He took two non-competitive pitches down low to make the count 2-1. He foul-tipped a changeup, and then, sitting on two strikes, four pitches into his at-bat, he decided that he simply would not strike out again.So Bauers fouled off a slider in the zone, then a curveball. He laid off an inside fastball to draw the count full. Then he managed to foul off a high fastball, and, immediately after, slowed down to catch a changeup in the zone. As the pitch count for this at-bat ticked over into double digits, Bauers pulled a slider that sat up in the zone a bit too much, sending it into the stands past the right-field foul pole. On the 11th pitch, Bauers made no mistake. Snell threw a middle-middle, 98-mph fastball, and Bauers smoked a no-doubt, two-run homer that carried over 400 feet into right field to give the Milwaukee Brewers a 3-2 lead.When Bauers's teammate Garrett Mitchell hit his own home run off Snell just two pitches later, it was, comparatively, an anticlimax. Spiritually speaking, a guy hitting a home run one pitch after just missing out on another home run counts for two home runs. Bauers had already won the game; Mitchell's own homer was just overkill on Snell's way out.

item.title: Would You Rather Have Sex Or Live Forever?
item.author: Sabrina Imbler
item.content:encoded: Hydras, the tiny freshwater invertebrates that resemble tentacular palm trees, are often considered immortal. They fasten themselves to rocks with their sticky foot, stretch out their tube-shaped body, and unfurl the stinging tentacles that halo their mouth to catch prey that passes by, an activity they can do ad infinitum if given the right conditions. Although they can be felled by predators or disease in the wild, in the lab, the little animals seem resilient to anything. If you cut off their head, they will simply grow a new one (and sometimes the decapitated head will regrow the rest of its body). If you mince or dice a hydra, each segment will regrow into a hydra. If you blend a hydra and run the resulting mush through a centrifuge, that mush will reorganize and regrow into a hydra.But hydras do not just regenerate lost body parts. They regenerate their own cells, turning over their entire bodies in less than a month. In the lab, hydras can renew their cells indefinitely, replacing old and worn cells with shiny new ones. We replace our cells too, but as we get older we start to make mistakes and lose our ability to replace cells that no longer work. But the hydra renews its cells from three different populations of stem cells and makes extremely faithful copies. This means the creature keeps "all its characteristics unchanged for an almost unlimited time," per a 2014 paper. This quality has earned the hydra the nickname "the eternal embryo," and thrust the creature into the spotlight of anti-aging research.At least, this is the lot in life for all hydras. The brown hydra is not so lucky. When the water is warm, the brown hydra defies aging like any other of its ilk. It reproduces by budding, creating clones of itself that pinch off and become new hydras. This asexual lifestyle allows the hydra to reproduce without any signs of aging. But when temperatures dip to around 50 degrees Fahrenheit, according to a new paper in the journal , the brown hydra stops budding and instead produces sperm and eggs. In other words, the hydra transforms and prepares itself for sexual reproduction. But this milestone comes at a brutal tradeoff. After the hydra reproduces sexually, it loses its immortality. It begins to die. Sex! But at what cost?

item.title: How Hunting Owls Use Sound to “See” Under the Snow
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: The great grey owl basically has a sound cone for a face, which helps it hunt down voles burrowing through snow in the winter.The owl’s large facial ruff, formed of dense feathers, helps amplify sound and funnel it towards his ears. Through half a meter of snow, the sound of scampering feet is inaudible to us. But not to him. With the help of a special acoustic camera equipped with 60 highly sensitive microphones, we can see what the owl is hearing.The footage in this video is amazing — and so is the owl’s sense of hearing. A YouTube commenter says “Cat software in Bird hardware. Bad news for the Rodents.” You can watch a short video on the science behind owl hunting techniques and watch the whole episode this is from about how animals use sound (but only in Canada, it seems…VPN works fine tho).The only problem with this video is that now I want two hours of just closeup footage of the owl’s face and it flying directly towards the camera. Those eyes! And its mid-flight loaf-of-white-bread-shaped body! I would also like the owl to be my friend.
