item.title: The Verdict Is In: Bo Nix Stinks
item.author: Drew Magary
item.content:encoded: If you watched the Broncos-Chargers game on Sunday, first of all, my apologies. You shouldn’t have had to see that. Second of all, you might have come away from that game saying, “Good Lord, Justin Herbert has gone from being overhyped to being actively shitty!” I can’t blame you for that gut reaction. Herbert’s play has deteriorated to the point where no one would blame that team’s brass for staging a full reset at quarterback. But the bigger story from that game had nothing to do with Herbert or his winless team, but with this fine fella: https://bsky.app/profile/profootballtalk.bsky.social/post/3mxsjm57kyk22 That’s Broncos QB Bo Nix, who led his team to the AFC title game a season ago, seemingly proving to all the haters and losers that he was a viable franchise quarterback. NOT SO FAST, MY FRIEND. Turns out that even with Denver head coach Sean Payton commandeering play-calling duties last week, Nix couldn’t hit an intermediate route if he was playing against air. The metrics have been saying it, and this week’s episode of helps explains why the tape agrees.

item.title: Inviting friends to your house is just "too exhausting"
item.author: Minnesotastan
item.content:encoded: "I really loved hosting at home years ago, before I had kids, when my house wasn’t filled with toys and I had lots of time to plan and shop,” says Rehanna, 41, from Birmingham. Now, if she’s catching up with friends, she would rather go out... When you host, quite often it feels like you’re just a spectator to your friends’ evening,” says Simon, 37, from Glasgow. In the past, he’s found that, as host, he spends so much time making sure his guests are catered for that it can be difficult to connect with them on anything other than a superficial level...“One reason is that our social networks may have become more scattered as cities have got larger,” he says. “If we live in smaller villages and towns, it is easy to visit for casual get-togethers. There is a thing called the 30-minute rule: if someone lives more than 30 minutes away, we pretty much stop seeing them regularly. The time/effort required becomes too great.”..In May this year, the claimed the dinner party was also being killed off “by the modern curse of the ‘dietary requirement’”; both food intolerances and voluntary restrictions appear to have increased over the past 20 years, and so cooking for others might certainly feel like more of a challenge...I’d venture that the rise of tablescaping has a lot to answer for... Whereas hosts might once have simply given surfaces a quick wipe and emptied the bins, there are now tips for curating the perfect playlist, and rules for creating an aesthetically pleasing “theme”...Caz has two children under the age of 10 and says her house is therefore always “a complete nightmare zone”. Of course, her friends don’t actually care about the mess. “I know this deep in my heart,” she admits, “but it doesn’t stop me from feeling shame every time anyone comes over.”..“Until the 1960s, things like homework from school was limited, and children kind of looked after themselves – playing in the street together and turning up only when they needed to get fed. Now the little darlings are under your feet until they go away to university.” In addition, he notes that there is now an “endless stream” of extracurricular clubs and activities that children are encouraged to take part in, which means “families have to be free to do a lot of ferrying”.Thompson also touches on the idea that it’s now “too much fun to be home alone”. Whereas we might once have invited friends over to stave off boredom – and faced social pressure to attend such events, even if we did not much care for the hosts – today we are “cocooned within personalised entertainment fortresses”.

item.title: Friday night has become "just another weeknight"
item.author: Minnesotastan
item.content:encoded: Americans have been spending less and less time with their friends over the past two decades, a trend that started well before the isolation of the coronavirus pandemic, and has continued long after restrictions were lifted. But looking across the week, Caren found that, starting in the mid-2010s, the biggest loss of friend time happened on Friday nights. (Saturday hangs have also declined a bit, but are still “nearly double the weekday level,” he wrote.)...But it seems that the vibe of Friday night is evolving... people of all ages have been reporting a strong preference for staying home on evenings and weekends. In a 2020 Gallup poll, Americans’ favorite way to spend an evening was “staying home with family.” The runner-up was “watching television or a movie at home.” Only 3 percent of people named “entertaining/visiting friends” as their favorite evening activity. In a 2026 Harris poll on Gen Z, 73 percent said that staying home was their default weekend plan...Friday nights in particular might be suffering because of their association with hitting the bars; drinking has fallen out of favor in the U.S... Or people might simply be too exhausted at the end of the workweek... For whatever reason, “the cost of going out on Friday nights—people aren’t finding this worthwhile anymore.”

item.title: Trump’s new QAnon press secretary exposes his desperation
item.content:encoded: Even by first-day-on-the-job standards, Donald Trump‘s new press secretary is shockingly incompetent. Katie At her first White House briefing on Tuesday, Zacharia kicked things off by haltingly reading a lengthy statement about how she hopes to “only build on, only amplify, and only multiply, to the extent possible, all of the wins” of Trump’s second term.The situation only grew worse. Zacharia took questions from just three reporters. Even though they were from friendly media outlets — Fox News, Breitbart and the Daily Mail — she still seemed overwhelmed. Her response to a softball question about her family was painful to watch; she said “my president” before correcting herself and saying “my husband.” After about seven minutes of questions, Zacharia threw in the towel, directing reporters to the tarmac where Trump would be boarding Marine One. “You can ask him all of the questions there!” she announced.Reviews of her performance were brutal.“Nikki McCann Ramirez, a political reporter for Rolling Stone, dubbed it a “Chat-GPT-ass first speech from the new press secretary.”But Zacharia found a defender in the only audience that ultimately matters. “I thought she was very good,” Trump shouted minutes later over the roar of Marine One’s engines while Zacharia, taking a spot usually held by presidential aide Natalie Harp, stood smiling over his shoulder. Of course the president thinks she’s great. Zacharia has the only traits that matter to Trump: She’s blonde, skinny and she appears to worship him passionately. Harp had better watch out; she’s got real competition for the role of most fervent Trump devotee. The president confirmed this by praising Zacharia not for any special skills but for being a “devoted fan” with “an unblemished record of support” for himself. But taking a step back, Zacharia’s hiring is revealing — and encouraging. It’s yet another sign that the president is putting his own cravings for adulation over political considerations.But taking a step back, Zacharia’s hiring is revealing — and encouraging. It’s yet another sign that the president is putting his own cravings for adulation over political considerations like winning the upcoming midterms for his party. “When stressed, Donald Trump retreats to his comfort zone,” investigative journalist Lindsay Beyerstein told me. Beyerstein, who is working on a book about conspiracy theorists called “Angry Minds,” noted that “Zacharia has a long history of pushing QAnon.”The term “QAnon” may seem like a blast from the past, and for good reason. According to a February 2022 report from PRRI, tens of millions of Americans — including 25% of Republican voters — affirmed the QAnon conspiracy theory that Democrats sexually abuse and kill children to drink their blood. In the haze of the Covid-19 pandemic and the disaster of Jan. 6, millions of Trump supporters turned to the myth that Trump was God’s emissary sent to earth to destroy this Satanic cabal of child-killers. After Trump blocked the release of Justice Department files on his long-time friend, convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, the fantasy that the former reality TV host is a holy warrior against pedophilia lost a lot of public appeal. But as far as Trump is concerned, QAnon is forever. Even as many of his voters quietly pretend the whole QAnon thing never happened, the White House was trying to revive the conspiracy cult over the summer. As The Bulwark’s Will Sommer reported in June, “The Trump administration launched a bizarre QAnon-themed social media campaign,” with various departments tweeting QAnon slogans. Sommer followed up his report by telling CNN that even “as the president faces persistently low approval rating,” the White House is trying to tell his voters something else: “[R]emember when you thought Trump was going to save the world?”As a political move, it’s a bad idea. Trump’s apparent narcissism and corruption were easier for voters to laugh off when the economy was doing well. But now that he’s goosed inflation with tariffs and the war on Iran, his methods are not so funny anymore. For his part, Trump seems increasingly less concerned with political realities and more worried about saving face and fluffing his own ego, even if that means pulling deeper into a bubble where he’s only surrounded by people who flatter him all day with pleasing lies about his greatness. “He’s reliving QAnon because it represents the bygone days when his supporters worshipped him like a god,” Beyerstein said. “Trump may not realized how played out QAnon has become because he doesn’t live in the real world.”Zacharia’s QAnon history is deep and troubling. As Popular Information’s Judd Legum reported, “Zacharia repeatedly used Truth Social to promote Pizzagate and other fringe conspiracy theories.” (Pizzagate is the original QAnon conspiracy theory — that Democrats sexually abuse and cannibalize children.) She repeatedly accused John Podesta, who headed Hillary Clinton’s 2016 presidential campaign, of being a “pedophile,” posting in 2022, “The radical left Hollywood elitists are sick pedo cannibals.” Zacharia also reposted the false claims of another Trump sycophant, Ali Alexander, who wrote, “Democrats want to mask and rape your children. That’s their satanic platform.”Popular Information also looked into Zacharia’s claims that she was a lawyer and found “there is no evidence that [she] ever passed a bar exam.” The press secretary is not a member of the bar association in any state where she’s worked. In fact, according to Legum and his team, there is no whiff of documentation that she’s licensed to practice law anywhere.When she was standing next to Trump after her disastrous briefing, a reporter asked, “Where did she pass the bar exam?”The president looked quizzically at Zacharia, who replied, “When I moved to China.” Sharp readers will notice that China has no authority to grant law licenses anywhere in the United States. Such a clumsy diversion would never have happened under Karoline Leavitt, Zacharia’s predecessor who was, if nothing else, good at her job. A smooth character and fast talker, Leavitt deployed cartoonish Christian piety and a non-stop act of aggrieved victimhood to keep reporters too discombobulated to hold her feet to the fire about the administration’s various failures. There was little sense that she legitimately worshipped Trump; instead, she appeared to see him as a stepping stone for her own ambitions. This theory got another shot in the arm when Leavitt left the White House, implying she was going to be a housewife, only to walk right into a cushy job as a Fox News commentator. Trump reportedly floated Harp as Leavitt’s replacement, a move that was spun as a “joke” — even though “jokes” are not about humor for the president but instead a way to test boundaries. While press secretaries have long been spin doctors, under Trump the job morphed into one where blatant lies and gaslighting are readily employed to create over-the-top praise for the president. But clearly, this outward-facing propaganda was not enough for the president. Being Trump’s press secretary isn’t as much about distorting press coverage or bamboozling the public anymore. The position has been refocused on the task of giving the president more of the hardcore Natalie Harp treatment. Even as the midterms grow closer, Trump is abandoning the task of winning the public over, choosing instead to retreat deeper into a fantasy world.There, everyone loves him most of all.

item.title: When the restaurant wants your phone number
item.author: Minnesotastan
item.content:encoded: A man walks into a restaurant. He doesn’t have a reservation, but that shouldn’t be a problem; there are ample seats at the bar, visible just over the hostess’s shoulder. “Of course,” she says, smiling. “We can seat you right away.” As she gathers menus, he absorbs the pleasant hum of a busy dining room, breathes in the tantalizing smells from the semi-open kitchen. Then, the hostess stops, Columbo-like, to interrupt with one more question: “And what’s your phone number?”...Like pretty much everyone else, I am well aware that my information is strip-mined wherever I go, in more ways than I can count and in many that I will never know... Much of the data collection has been justified in the name of customer service—a way to track allergies, preferences, birthdays, and so on, thus bringing technological efficiency to a job previously handled by a heavily notated reservation book or the encyclopedic mind of a gifted maître d’. “We try to build a database on everybody and get as much information as possible,” Vilkhu told me when I called him a few weeks after my dinner. His restaurant uses OpenTable, and he knew, for instance, which bartenders had served me, the friend who had joined me, that I had complimented the cocktail list and enjoyed the crawfish dumplings. This information, he assured me, was shared with the Kingsway’s sister restaurant but nobody else: “We just want to be able to curate the experience as best as we possibly can.”...Most striking was OpenTable’s promotion of a feature, currently in beta, called Global Insights. Until now, as Vilkhu had told me, whatever data a restaurant collected through the reservation platforms remained confined to that restaurant or restaurant group. Global Insights, which is available to OpenTable Pro subscribers, is the first feature to jump that garden wall and allow other restaurants access to the same information—in OpenTable’s words, to “get an idea of how your diners behave at other restaurants across the OpenTable Diner Network.” With an account, any restaurant can identify big spenders, diners who tend to linger at a table, diners who order a lot of drinks, frequent late-cancelers, and chronic “no-showers."...Curious to see what insights on me OpenTable might share with that hypothetical restaurant, I sent the company a request for my personal data....

item.title: Brian Flores’s Racial Discrimination Lawsuit Reveals Racist Recruiting Memo
item.author: Tom Ley
item.content:encoded: A memo prepared for the Las Vegas Raiders by the recruiting firm Korn Ferry was entered as an exhibit in Minnesota Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores's ongoing racial discrimination lawsuit against the NFL and multiple teams. The memo was unsealed by the court Tuesday, giving the public a rare look at how coaching candidates are evaluated by teams. As it turns out, this particular evaluation was pretty racist.The memo, first reported on by Front Office Sports, contains a list of Flores's strengths and weaknesses, based on Korn Ferry's evaluation of him. There are some harsh things listed under the weaknesses section, including one anonymous team executive calling Flores "the worst hiring decision we’ve ever made." But it is one of Flores's apparent strengths that is likely to be most relevant to his case. Korn Ferry decided to describe Flores this way:Polished and a good presenter despite growing up in Brownsville, Brooklyn (same as Mike Tyson). He was able to build a strong friendship with a billionaire's son which gave him opportunities to socialize and learn how to build relationships with white-collar and upper-class individuals.

item.title: The Flintwhistle Job Interview
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: Finding a job these days means candidates must jump through many layers of hoops, including at least one humiliating "interview" with an AI agent because the company hasn't got the time or personnel for redundant, drawn-out hiring tasks. Graham Dot Zip doesn't need a job, but he goes through the process to highlight the idiocy of AI interviews. In this one, he calls himself Chick Bongo and makes up corporate jargon to match what the agent is giving him. AI, knowing no better, is annoyingly agreeable and downright gullible. Graham mentions the word "flintwhistle" enough that the agent eventually incorporates it and even lies about offering it, first as a corporate strategy, then as a real whistle. The whole series of such interviews is at Graham's YouTube channel, including the newest one in which he brings his own AI agent to the interview. (via Boing Boing)

item.title: Skyrocketing prices for some technology company shares
item.author: Minnesotastan
item.content:encoded: The U.S. equity markets have been hitting all-time highs despite an ongoing war on Iran and relentlessly-increasing prices for gasoline, diesel, and other oil-derivative products like fertilizers. The rise seems to be driven almost entirely by huge increases in the share prices of AI-related companies (producers of the technology and of the materials necessary for the "build-out" of the process) - justified in the minds of investors by the potential for enormous gains in productivity and profits at some time in the future. The financing of these investments and the issuing of new shares to finance growth has sucked money out of other investments. These developments are alluded to in a recent statement by the CEO if Sun Microsystems, reproduced here in a post from Facebook several months ago:For old-timers like me, the numbers look crazy. I'm old enough to remember the Black Monday stock market crash of 1987, when the DJIA . I was an investor back then, and I've told people I "slept like a baby" through it (i.e. "woke up every hour and cried").This ongoing and totally unjustified war by the U.S. and Israel on Iran is having widespread rippling effects through the world economy; the U.S. has been relatively spared but is unlikely to escape unscathed. Full disclosure: I established bearing options positions on the S&P index yesterday. Further disclosure: I tend to be a "perma-bear" predicting market falls that typically don't occur.

item.title: The cost of water
item.author: Minnesotastan
item.content:encoded: US households are paying 62% more for drinking water than they did a decade ago – outpacing inflation, grocery prices and household incomes, according to a new study.Food & Water Watch, a Washington DC-based non-profit, analyzed 2025 billing data from the 500 largest community water systems in the US, which together serve about 155 million people, or 45% of the country’s population. The analysis compared current rates with data from a similar Food & Water Watch survey conducted in 2015. The study does not include wastewater or storm water charges, which are often billed separately from drinking water service.In 2025, the average household using 60,000 gallons of water paid $531 for drinking water service, according to the study. However, costs varied widely, with annual bills ranging from $133 at the cheapest system to $1,416 at the most expensive.I've been keeping careful financial records since moving into this house 26 years ago, so I looked up our numbers. In 2015 our house used 60,000 gallons of water at a cost of $158 (excluding stormwater and sewer as per above study). In 2025 our usage dropped to 41,000 gallons (in part because we have mostly stopped watering the lawn and gardens) at a cost of $177.Adjusting those costs for usage, in 2015 we were paying $2.60 per thousand gallons of water. For 2025 the cost was $4.31 per thousand gallons. That's an increase of about 70% in ten years. Some of that increased cost may have resulted from the community replacing lead-containing distribution pipes in the circuits. Presumably the rest results from their costs for salaries, maintenance, water treatment, and other infrastruture upgrades. The Guardian article has informed commentary on the reasons for the national increase, noting "corporate water abuses" (in years prior to datacenters), federal disinvestment, and climate change, and expecially the "major disparity between publicly owned and for-profit water systems."Corporate-owned utilities charged the average household $823 a year, compared with $494 for publicly owned systems – a difference of $329, or 67%. Corporate systems accounted for just 11% of the 500 systems the study analyzed but represented 44% of the 25 most expensive systems. The study added that 70% of the top 10 were owned by for-profit corporations.I'm not angry about our increase; I'm delighted that fresh clean (good-tasting) water is available at the turn of a tap. I wonder if any readers here have similar long-term data.

item.title: Ten Hours of Street Harassment in Two Minutes
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: In 2015, Shoshana B. Roberts walked around Manhattan for ten hours (probably not all at the same time) with a guy in front of her carrying a hidden camera to record any interaction from strangers. That has been edited down to a couple of minutes in this video. This is the kind of thing women go through every day. Read about the project at Hollaback! If you go to the YouTube page, you’ll see that the majority of commenters do not believe this is harassment, and they are offended that it is portrayed as harassment. However, if you read the comments at Metafilter, it’s a completely different story. That’s why I prefer Metafilter to YouTube. Okay, that’s not the only reason, but you know what I mean. The comments at reddit are a mixed bag.

item.title: Tyreek Hill Found Liable For Two Counts Of Battery
item.author: Diana Moskovitz
item.content:encoded: A jury found former Kansas City and Miami receiver Tyreek Hill liable Tuesday night for two counts of battery in his civil trial. The same Miami jury found him not liable on another five counts of battery, one count of assault, one count of intentional infliction of emotional distress, and one count of continuing domestic violence.The jury awarded Hill's estranged wife, Lakeeta Vaccaro, $500,000 in compensatory damages, but did not award any punitive damages.The trial came about as part of the couple's ongoing divorce in which Vaccaro said Hill physically and verbally abused her during their marriage, including once trying to punch her in the stomach while she was pregnant with their daughter. Hill told jurors that that he did verbally abuse his wife, whom he in turn accused of stealing his money, but the NFL wideout said he did not physically hurt her.

item.title: I owe you a thank you
item.author: 1axb2levevzi9w9n1roire2udyx7yq6d2p43oj@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: It is true that the future of free and fair elections is playing out in courthouses across the country. But it is not enough for lawyers to litigate. They have an obligation to speak publicly and plainly about these cases.This is not a new frustration for me. For years, I have watched Republican lawyers take center stage promoting election-denial conspiracy theories while those charged with defending democracy hide behind their legal filings.During the Biden presidency, this disagreement spilled into public view when some in the White House criticized me for “fighting on every possible front — filing a flurry of lawsuits and exerting public pressure through the media.”Since Trump’s return to power, those critics have largely gone quiet. Yet too few people are willing to take on Trump directly, without caveats or false equivalence.Meanwhile, I have redoubled my efforts. I have continued to litigate, arguing in federal and state courts, including before the U.S. Supreme Court last term.My law firm is currently litigating nearly 90 voting and election cases in 41 states. They include some of the most consequential cases for the future of democracy and free and fair elections. The firm is also preparing for what may come next: post-election litigation, recounts and election contests.Even so, I refuse to stop speaking out. I won’t simply let my legal filings do the talking.That is why I write for Democracy Docket several times a week. It is why I travel and give speeches. It is why I have expanded my video essays on YouTube.I make time to share my opinions on the state of voting and democracy, along with my analysis of what is happening in court, because educating the public is as important as arguing before judges.Usually, that means writing late at night or on weekends. It means recording podcasts at odd hours.Those hours add up, and earlier this week, I admitted to you that I was tired.So many of you wrote back to tell me you were rooting for me, to ask how I was holding up and to remind me to take care of myself. Some of you said you were tired, too. I read those messages, and they meant more to me than I can say. Thank you.Over the past six years, Democracy Docket has grown beyond my wildest expectations. It now includes daily and weekly newsletters, opinion pieces, breaking news, investigative journalism, a podcast and more.With more than 500,000 free newsletter subscribers and millions of monthly visitors to our website, our reach and influence continue to expand. That is all good news.But here is the thing: Democracy Docket is reader-funded. There are no corporate owners or outside investors. We rely on people like you to grow.If now is not the right time for you to become a premium member, I offer my warmest thanks for staying informed and remaining part of this community.If, however, you simply haven’t gotten around to upgrading, or aren’t sure whether to do so, I ask you to consider what Democracy Docket means to you and to the pro-democracy movement. With the midterms less than 30 days away, our mission is more urgent than ever.Democracy will not protect itself from Trump’s lies. It requires people willing to stand up and speak out — loudly, persistently and in plain language. That is what I try to do. It is what the Democracy Docket team does. I hope you will stand with us.

item.title: Death By Firing Squad
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: Jesse Welles has a few things to say about putting a military execution on public live streaming platforms. Whatever you think about capital punishment (I'm against it), making it into a spectacle is barbaric. Pete Hegseth says that a public execution will be a deterrent, but people already know murder is wrong, even those who do it. If you've ever met people, you know at least half will consider watching a firing squad blow someone away as entertainment, and will want more. It was true in ancient Rome, it was true in medieval Europe, and it was true during Jim Crow, regardless of the person's guilt. When I was a child, there was a historical photograph of a lynching displayed at my local state park. The substantial crowd was well dressed for the time, and all turned to the camera to smile, even the children. The victim was barely a dark blob hanging from a tree. We may like to think we are better than that now, but recent history shows that we are not.

item.title: Humpday Hottie: Dove Cameron
item.author: Schill
item.content:encoded: Dove Cameron is an American actress, singer, and performer who became widely known through her work with Disney Channel before developing a broader career in music, film, and television. Born Chloe Celeste Hosterman in Bainbridge Island, Washington, in 1996, she adopted the professional name Dove Cameron in honor of her late father.Cameron became a major young television star through the Disney Channel series , which premiered in 2013. The unusual premise allowed her to play both Liv Rooney, an actress returning home, and Liv’s identical twin sister Maddie, an athletic teenager. Cameron’s ability to portray two distinctly different characters helped establish her as one of Disney Channel’s most recognizable performers.She expanded her audience through the film series, beginning with in 2015. Cameron played Mal, the daughter of Maleficent, and reprised the role in the subsequent films. The franchise became a major part of Disney’s late-2010s youth culture and gave Cameron opportunities to combine acting, singing, and dancing.Music eventually became an increasingly important part of her career. Her solo work moved away from the Disney sound and toward contemporary pop, with songs exploring relationships, identity, and personal experiences. Her 2022 single “Boyfriend” became an international breakthrough, gaining substantial attention through social media and streaming platforms.Cameron has also pursued acting outside Disney, appearing in projects including and the film . Her career demonstrates the transition from child and teen television star to a more independent performer working across several areas of entertainment.With her distinctive voice, versatile acting abilities, and strong connection with younger audiences, Dove Cameron has established herself as a performer whose career extends well beyond the Disney Channel platform that first made her famous.

item.title: Your Quick Primer on Katie Zacharia’s False Claim to Have Taken the Bar in China
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: Since I was revising the post below as I got more information, here’s the latest on White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia’s apparent claim to have taken the bar exam in China. Judd Legum revealed yesterday that notwithstanding Trump’s and Zacharia’s claim that she was an attorney, it doesn’t appear that she ever took or passed the bar in the U.S. Today reporters pressed her on whether this was true. Had she passed the bar? In what state? Zacharia responded that she took it “when I moved to China.” Reporters took that, understandably, to mean that she took the Chinese bar exam when she lived there between 2011 and 2013. The Washington Post reported, for instance, that Zacharia “said she had passed a bar exam in China, a country where noncitizens aren’t allowed to practice in courtrooms.” But it’s more than that. Foreign nationals are not allowed to take the Chinese bar exam or practice law in China under any circumstances. Her LinkedIn bio says she worked at a Chinese law firm, Zhong Lun, while living in China. And that is possible. I assume it’s true. Foreigners can work at Chinese law firms but only for the purpose of advising on the law in the countries in which they are licensed to practice law. They are specifically barred from advising clients on Chinese law. I don’t know whether not having passed the bar in the U.S. would have been an issue on that front or not. Bottom line: In her first day on the job Zacharia gave everyone the impression that she took the bar exam in China. But that’s not true. Because she would not have been allowed to.

item.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months.In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day.This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity."Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion.They had some pretty extreme requirements:The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day.The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months.When asked on Hacker News about the lack of offline support, Scion engineer Nick G replied:Since Claude is by far the heaviest user of Scion and is necessarily online, this just wasn't important to do.As an aside, I've been trying adversarial review in my own projects recently, where you have a model try and find flaws (I often play Claude and GPT off against each other). This note from the article reflected my own experience with that:Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns.

item.title: llm-gemini 0.35
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: I added support to llm-gemini for the new Gemini 4 Argon model, made available today via the Gemini API and for customers of their $100/month subscription plan.Here's the "high" illustration, which cost me 17.166 cents:The pricing is interesting. At launch, Argon is $2/million input and $10/million output - the same price as GPT-6 Sol, half the price of Claude Opus 5.5 and 1/5th the price of Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra.But on December 1st Argon is set to double in price - so it will be the same price as Opus 5.5.Prices like this aren't really comparable these days since what really matters is how many tokens a model takes to achieve a goal within an agentic harness.One useful clue for that comes from Artificial Analysis, who publish the total cost to run their benchmark using each model. Argon is looking very good there - costing $2,407 to run the benchmark, putting it close to GLM-5.3 and significantly cheaper than OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta's latest models.When the price doubles it will still be a little cheaper than GPT-6 Astra.(I used ChatGPT to edit that chart! The data is all correct, I checked - I needed to get that Gemini 4 Argon info box to display without overlapping the other numbers.)

item.title: Zacharia Claim About Chinese Bar Exam Is False
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: As I noted in the earlier post, new Press Secretary Katie Zacharia claims she passed the bar exam in China and to thus be an “attorney” despite never having passed the bar in the U.S. A Post article said that foreign nationals aren’t allowed to appear in Chinese courts. And I took that to mean that perhaps you could take the bar exam but not appear in court. (Many U.S. attorneys never appear in court. That’s only one part of practicing law.) But it looks more stringent than that. And it looks like Zacharia’s claim is false. It’s difficult to confirm a technical point like this about a foreign country. But numerous websites which provide information about practicing law in China say thatforeign nationals can’ttake the bar exam under any circumstances. Starting in 2021 there appears to have been a pilot program which would allow foreign national to take the patent bar. But even that required foreigners to have permanent residence which is apparently quite difficult to get. Foreign lawyers can work in Chinese law firms, but only to provide guidance about the law in the countries in which they are licensed to practice. (She appears to have worked in that capacity.) They’re specifically barred from interpreting Chinese law or acting in the capacity of a Chinese lawyer. So it’s pretty tight.Again, maybe there’s some technicality that made this possible for her which doesn’t come up in any of the explanations I’ve found. But it seems like a pretty across-the-board ban.Perhaps Zacharia was being cagey. She was asked at her appearance today where she’d passed the bar, in what state. She responded, “When I moved to China.” Reporters understandably took that to mean that she took the Chinese bar exam. But perhaps she was trying to hoodwink them.: This just-published article in the South China Morning Post says definitively that at the time Zacharia claims to have passed the bar in China foreign nationals were barred from taking the bar exam.Foreign nationals were therefore ineligible to take the examination, a step towards qualification to practise mainland Chinese law.Employment at a Chinese law firm does not, by itself, establish that someone holds a licence to practise Chinese law. SCMP has asked Zhong Lun to clarify Zacharia’s role and qualifications. The firm did not immediately respond.

item.title: Ready for their close-up
item.author: bounce+2edd00.7bdc18-5mr68b7cb43ac2h04ai5=kill-the-newsletter.com@m.ghost.io
item.content:encoded: Under a microscope, we observe reality in extremis and in mundanity. We observe it in that instant. The usual gets replaced by the current. The specific overwhelms the general. October baseball is nothing if not a microscope.It presents us with no context, just the guts of the matter at hand. And we never get any better at wrapping our heads around the chaos in magnified form. Among 6-foot-4 lefty batters, is Nathaniel Lowe a stronger hitter than Shohei Ohtani? Observably, yes. Is Cade Smith made of reinforced steel and strikeouts? We can see no data points to the contrary.Most of the time, it’s better to build your understanding of the world out of big, grounded truths even as anomalies zip in and out of the frame. The MLB postseason asks you to forget about the broad view for a month or so, but we aren’t very good at doing that. We try to hold both in our heads, and frequently get dizzy trying to pull it off. Is the Yankees’ roster construction inherently worse than that of the Rays, or was the roster as constructed just worse last week?With the Brewers up 2-0 on the Dodgers in the NLCS and the Guardians victors over the Rays in Game 1 of the ALCS, here are some observations that are true at least for today.Last year, the NLCS meeting between the Dodgers and the Brewers was a decisive drubbing in which Shohei Ohtani batted .357/.500/1.143 and tossed six scoreless innings for good measure. It was the magnum opus for an all-time player in an all-time season.Conventional wisdom doesn’t change quickly. So it mostly holds that the Dodgers still have the brighter and higher-potential stars, despite Milwaukee again running up the best record in baseball. It’s true the Dodgers have the more famous lineup card, but the Brewers now boast the top talents. By regular season production, the Brewers have the two best players in this series — Jacob Misiorowski and Brice Turang — and by on-field pop in these playoffs, we’d have to add red-hot catcher William Contreras to the list ahead of any performer in Dodger blue.Observation No. 2: The pitches are fast and freneticOf course, the condensed talent pool of the playoffs also means these aren’t just any fastballs.More than 41% of all pitches thrown this postseason have been 94 mph or faster — with a few sizzling offspeed pitches even making the cut — and the increased exposure to velocity is not helping. Hitters are registering the worst October results off those fast pitches since 2013, when 94+ mph offerings comprised only 29.5% of their diet.A full 17% of all pitches thrown have been fastballs up and out of the zone, with hitters managing only a .201 against them. While his dirt-scraping golf homer deservedly got the wows, perhaps revived Guardians avatar Jose Ramirez’s tomahawk blast off 99.9 mph heat at his eyes was the more impressive shot.Observation No. 3: The pitch not challenged could make all the differenceBefore Jake Bauers’ 12-pitch battle drained Yoshinobu Yamamoto in the disastrous third inning of Game 2, the Dodgers pitcher wanted to challenge a 3-2 call that gave Brice Turang a walk, but seemed to defer to catcher Will Smith’s inaction.It’s not a sure thing that challenge would have been successful …But the potential reward — a second out, which was followed by a Contreras flyout — would have changed the complexion of the game. Of note: The Brewers are also concluding each game with an average of 1.2 challenges remaining, compared to the Dodgers’ 1.0. An early challenge should spring from a confident position, but they are no less important than late challenges.Observation No. 4: Relief aces are being worked hardNo one on the Milwaukee Brewers has thrown more postseason innings so far than Aaron Ashby, the lefty who, you’ll note, is not a starter. Six games into this playoff run, Ashby has appeared five times, with four of those appearances stretching more than an inning. In NLCS Game 2, he secured a five-out save, meaning he has now gotten one more out than starter Logan Henderson and three more outs than Misiorowski, the presumptive NL Cy Young.Meanwhile, the Guardians have deployed lockdown closer Cade Smith in all six of their games, asking him for more than three outs on three occasions (though he tired in one of them, prompting manager Stephen Vogt to bring in Gavin Williams).Though pitchers are often tasked with unfamiliar challenges in October, Ashby and Smith are relatively seasoned going multiple frames. Ashby did it 23 times in 2026, tossing the second-most innings in relief in MLB.Smith recorded at least four outs to finish a game 11 times, sixth most in the majors this season (and really second among high-leverage relievers).They probably can’t keep this pace up forever, but they are at least accustomed to the situation.Observation No. 5: It’s Rays all the way downThe original architect of the Rays’ ways, Andrew Friedman, now runs the Dodgers. The next in line, Erik Neander, still runs the Rays. Another one-time Rays executive, Matt Arnold, runs the Brewers. And Kevin Cash, longtime manager of the Rays, came up as a coach with Cleveland under Terry Francona.It’s hard to say if there is a consensus understanding of the Rays’ edge, the things other teams try to emulate. I would sum up The Rays Way, as practiced in various forms by the Friedman executive tree, as an ethos of maximizing the potential of the organization in every direction, a constant stance of fluidity and openness to experimentation.Among the many things lost in the often-disingenuous discourse tornado around “analytics” is the fact that the secret sauce of the supposedly new school Rays edge is essentially optimized scouting and coaching. The tactics and transactions are evidence based — they’re not selling jeans — and probabilistic, but inside the system, it’s a human touch that keeps developing and unlocking the best version of players.Each branch of the Rays tree has its own twists on this now. The Dodgers need no further explanation. Arnold’s Brewers have earned their own reputation for building the boat out of athletic, fundamentally sound position players and turbocharging them from there.What’s increasingly clear is that efforts to distinguish small ball or Brewers baseball or the Rays way or old school or new school are sort of chasing shadows. With some caveats about how some free agent spending or salary bumps can and could be both beneficial and fan friendly, this is just how to run a good baseball organization now.Every other club’s aspirations aren’t hidden in the details. They are plainly on display when Jacob Misiorowski winds and fires, when Brice Turang uncorks a swing, when Drew Rasmussen saws off yet another batter, when Josue De Paula waits in the wings for a call. Inspect and dissect as much as you like, but you’ll find the same signals in every deep-diving search. Someone who works or worked for the Rays will probably be building something new on top by spring. ⚾An arbitrary Bandwagon fan ranking of the remaining teamsEvery remaining team ranked by the team member for whom a World Series win would feel like a lifetime achievement championship:Guardians: Jose Ramirez is getting a statue in Cleveland regardless of whether he ever grasps the Commissioner’s Trophy. Even better if he whacks a key hit and gets to describe the pitch afterward.Brewers: Christian Yelich’s emergence as an MVP-level player invigorated the Brewers to start this era of dominance. As Sam Miller covered in his newsletter this week, he hasn’t had many postseason moments to add as a cherry on top, but he’s getting a chance to add those now.Dodgers: Tarik Skubal is the top candidate I suppose, but he’s not particularly close to the end, or particularly tied to the club just yet. I’m not even sure winning a ring with this Dodgers team would eclipse his put-the-team-on-my-back postseason excellence in Detroit.MLB proposed a return to a 154-game schedule, a number last used leaguewide in 1960 (and in the NL in 1961). This would give players a standard weekly day off (Monday), theoretically creating some health benefits and potentially some attention-economy scheduling wins. It would certainly give your friendly neighborhood baseball newsletter writer a nice little window to breathe, reflect and write, but I’m nonetheless against the idea on the grounds of playoff creep.The whole concept of fewer games, which I suspect actually does broadly appeal to players, is of course tied to the salary cap, like every other proposal MLB is throwing around for useless public relations points.This is all a charade for now, but in the months when the fun is gone, you can see the start of what the sides might be discussing outside of the salary cap showdown.It’s fair to seek some accountability for the Yankees being so mistake-prone so repeatedly on defense. There are good questions to be asked about how Cashman stuffs the roster with powerful but lumbering (or virtually immobile, in the special case of Giancarlo Stanton) hitters whose athletic limitations often tie his manager’s hands.Then again, the Yankees’ track record of making the playoffs — even in what is often the league’s toughest division — and justifying high expectations is a very real high-wire act that could very much go awry with the wrong overreaction.I expect not nearly as much will change in the Bronx as disappointed fans want right now, and the rearview mirror take on this post-2024 pennant era will be colored almost entirely by Cashman and the club’s success or failure in finding a next wave of position players to support Aaron Judge and roll ahead with Cam Schlittler.Ben Rice looks like one building block, but he’s in the same offense-first (offense-only?) vein as every other recent titan. Is George Lombard Jr. a mainstay? Is Spencer Jones a real fixture? Is an external piece finally the missing, long-term piece that Jazz Chisholm, Trent Grisham, Paul Goldschmidt, et all just weren’t?For now, the plan is probably to wait and see. At some juncture, though, best will lose its grip and will take the wheel.After a massively disappointing season, Blue Jays star Vladimir Guerrero Jr. had eye surgery …… which certainly raised my eyebrows.The part where I ask for your supportThis is a project by and for the passionate. It’s undertaken on mornings, nights and weekends. On trains and planes and holidays. Around the responsibilities of a full-time job.I recognize the building subscription creep, the proliferation of good writers operating independently and charging independently in an unforgiving industry. I don’t expect The Bandwagon to be your only destination for baseball writing, but I hope it makes your emotional investment more enriching.

item.title: So Many Different Mes
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: Japanese photographer and artist Tomoko Sawada works primarily in self-portraiture. For her first project, she visited ID photo booths to take hundreds of photos of herself, dressed, posed, and presented differently. Eugenie Shin of Tokyo Weekender calls that 1998 project, ID 400, “a dizzying grid of strangers who are all actually the same woman”.For subsequent projects, Sawada says she’s continued to “examine the relationship between outer appearance and inner self through different concepts”.

item.title: I Met The Twee Bird That Ruffled Kelly Clarkson’s Feathers
item.author: Sabrina Imbler
item.content:encoded: Before we get to the feud, let's start with the facts. Molly, the wooden crank-operated automaton made by the artist Bliss Kolb, is a beauty. Although Molly is made of basswood, cherry, and teak, with glass eyes and steel screws, its buttery yellow body and dusky brown wings recall the northern yellow warbler, a melodic whistling songbird found across the U.S. and Canada. Molly is a beautiful singer. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VNZ4RysiN3A It is also true that Kelly Clarkson is a beautiful singer. Or maybe beautiful is understating it. Clarkson is considered one of the great vocalists of her generation and one of the greatest singers of all time. She instantly proved the premise of : that a reality show could, in fact, find the best singer in the nation (and arguably could have ended once they found her). For seven seasons, Clarkson belted out unbelievable covers during the "Kellyoke" segment of . Her performance of her most-requested song ever—"Golden" from , in the original, staggering key—features YouTube comments that are the dictionary definition of diva worship, for good reason.

item.title: WNBA Capably Solves Logistical Problem
item.author: Maitreyi Anantharaman
item.content:encoded: The WNBA was staring down the following issue: After the first two games of the Finals, beginning Saturday at the raucous 18,064-seat building which the Golden State Valkyries have sold out for two straight years, the series would move to Atlanta, where the Dream’s primary arena, Gateway Center, seats just 3,500. The Dream have so far played their three home playoff games at the larger State Farm Arena, the approximately 17,044-seat venue where the Hawks play. (The two teams do not share an owner.) They also played five sellout games there in the regular season: two against the Las Vegas Aces, two against the Indiana Fever, and one against the Chicago Sky, Angel Reese's former team. Last week, the team announced that they’ll play all their home games at the larger venue beginning next season. But with a Sombr concert scheduled for the night of Game 3, and the Hawks home opener scheduled for the night of Game 4, it looked like the Dream might have to play these games in their usual smaller building—kind of a bummer for the WNBA Finals.WNBA teams have often been caught in such scheduling pickles. This year, the Valkyries got a Doja Cat concert bumped by a week when they made the Finals, but last year, they played their only home playoff game in San Jose because their home arena had already been booked for the Laver Cup. In 2021, the Phoenix Mercury bopped around alternate venues to start the playoffs because of a scheduling conflict with Disney on Ice. Later that postseason, when it seemed like the Mercury might again be displaced to accommodate a Lakers-Suns preseason game, the Suns moved their preseason game up a few hours and played the games as a doubleheader. On Sunday, reported that efforts to move the Finals games to even Georgia Tech’s 8,600-seat arena or another 13,000-seat arena nearby had “hit a roadblock.”

item.title: What The Steve Ballmer Scandal Says About Sports Media
item.author: Patrick Redford
item.content:encoded: The NBA season is one week away, and there's one game I can't stop thinking about. On Nov. 2, Kawhi Leonard's Toronto Raptors will travel to Los Angeles to play the Clippers, his former team and the subject of the NBA's harshest-ever punishment over the cap shenanigans they did to sign him back in 2019. The spectacle of Leonard, back in L.A. in a Raptors uniform, will be so weird, and I'm curious to see how the basketball media will cover it.Speaking of basketball media, that's the true subject of this week's episode of . If you've read Defector's coverage of the story, you're probably familiar with the many media angles to the scandal: how investigative podcaster Pablo Torre broke the story, how ESPN helped Clips owner Steve Ballmer run cover, and how the Worldwide Leader duffed its big scoop about a supposedly light punishment for the team. This is the most interesting part of this story, so we pulled in Torre himself to talk it though and reflect on the role of the media in the whole saga. He spoke about whether he could have done this story at ESPN, what he makes of the theory that this is a mostly victimless "crime" that only really indicts the salary cap, and the potential conflicts of interest around an outlet charged with covering the league also paying them a ton of TV money. It was a fun episode! https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jcLPF0tAJ5Q

item.title: It’s All Happening Right Before Our Eyes
item.author: David Kurtz
item.content:encoded: The Retribution: Ilhan Omar EditionIt’s easy to get tripped up by the sheer volume of Trump II depredations — the corruption, the retribution, the destruction, and the absurdity of it all. Add in the proximity of the midterm elections, and there’s a risk of falling into the pedantry of category distinctions.What’s an election interference gambit versus an appeal to racism? What’s a fit of retribution versus an attack on the constitutional order? What’s an abuse of power versus conspiracizing? One easy framing adjustment is simply to use “and” or “all of the above.”The unparalleled early holiday morning search by federal agents of the D.C. home of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-MN) three weeks before the election perfectly captures the importance of allowing for an “all of the above” category. Otherwise, you can’t truly make sense of it all.An overt investigatory step against a sitting member of Congress up for election in three weeks is an astonishingly brazen abuse of power. The DOJ norm to refrain from such actions within 60 days of an election doesn’t quite do justice to how out of the ordinary this search was.The DOJ norm was put in place before the widespread use of mail-in ballots stretched out Election Day from a single date to a rolling two-month election, which would caution restraint even farther out. And in fact even in the old days, notable developments in investigations, in my experience, tended to slow by the summer, after the primaries had locked in the candidates for the general election.This is precisely the kind of pre-election ugliness we talked about Friday.An Attack on Naturalized CitizensThe purported basis for the investigation of Omar is immigration fraud — based on a persistent but baseless far-right conspiracy that decades ago, when she was 12, her now-deceased father schemed his way into the country illegally.The search warrant, as described to the New York Times, lists “potential immigration crimes under investigation, including false statements and fraud in immigration paperwork, as well as a general conspiracy charge.”The underlying theory of the case, such as it is, is that Omar should be denaturalized. It makes the citizenship of all naturalized citizens contingent and dependent on who is holding power at any given time.Black women — see, e.g., Lisa Cook, Fani Willis, Letitia James — are a favorite target of Trump. Omar is Black and Somali and from Minnesota, a trifecta of Trump race-baiting, smearing, and dehumanizing. The search of her home came just a few days after Trump tried to instigate Minnesotans into a race war against Somalis. The message is so rancid: Omar doesn’t belong here, conned her way in (as a child), defrauded her way to financial prosperity, and has no right to be here, let alone in Congress.The executive branch enforcing the law against members of the legislative branch has always required a delicate balance of constitutional imperatives. There is nothing delicate or well-balanced about Trump’s ongoing attacks on Congress’ constitutional role. The Omar investigation is another in a series of threats against all members of Congress and against the legislative branch’s constitutional role.An Attack on Elected DemocratsThe Omar search is made worse because it comes after President Trump targeted her for years and publicly announced in January that a criminal investigation of her was underway. He has made the retribution element abundantly clear. It’s part of his broader attack on elected Dems — not merely a rhetorical attack but an abuse of his office to unleash the power of the federal government against his political foes.It is all of the above — and more.One other notable element of this retributive investigation: It is being helmed by Homeland Security Investigations, which is part of DHS, not DOJ. HSI has been in the lead on some of the most glaring retributive investigations in recent months. With a bloated budget, DHS, across its many component agencies, has police and investigatory powers that lets the Trump White House bypass or sideline DOJ. The FBI and DOJ aren’t sidelined completely. HSI can’t prosecute cases without DOJ, and DOJ had a role in obtaining the search warrant for Omar’s home (which, dismayingly, a D.C. federal judge signed off on). But this adds to the evidence that DHS is Trump’s favored tool of authoritarianism.If there was any doubt that the Omar case is being run out of the White House, the administration did little to hide it. A senior Trump administration official told the Washington Post that in addition to Attorney General Todd Blanche and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services Director Joseph Edlow, the investigation involved White House deputy homeland security adviser Anthony Salisbury. I can’t emphasize enough how far over the cliff’s edge we are with White House-directed investigations.The worst predictions of what a second Trump term would be like are coming true right before our eyes.The Retribution: Full Court Press EditionIt’s not just Ilhan Omar. You can feel the ramping up of retribution from President Trump as the midterm election draws closer:: In another in a series of targeted attacks on the press by the Trump administration, the Trump DOJ has purported to launch an antitrust investigation against ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News and NBC over their pool coverage of the White House. The move comes after the networks banded together to boycott President Trump’s ban of CNN from the White House.: President Trump renewed his effort to remove Lisa Cook from the Federal Reserve Board, establishing a committee to “investigate” the bogus mortgage fraud charges the administration has ginned up against her.: The Trump administration imposed sanctions on the ​International Criminal Court on Friday within hours of one of its former judges winning the Nobel Peace Prize.The Lawlessness: Defiance of Judges Edition: U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes of D.C. damned near lost her mind in an emergency hearing over the Trump administration’s holiday weekend removal of more than 400 trees from a National Park Service golf course in the nation’s capital that President Trump wants to redesign unilaterally. Reyes had previously ordered that the Trump administration provide notice to the plaintiffs before any major changes were made to the course — and time for the court to address them. Instead, the administration provided notice at 5 p.m. on the Friday of a three-day weekend and removed the trees on Saturday. Reyes became the latest federal judge to rue having trusted the administration and given it the benefit of the doubt. “I trusted you all not to do precisely what you have done,” she said.: The Trump DOJ apologized to a federal judge in Manhattan after pro-Trump TV ads paid for by the federal government continued to air after the court ordered an immediate halt to the ads on Sunday evening. The DOJ lawyer told the judge that he emailed her temporary restraining order blocking the ads to DHS counsel 72 minutes after it was issued, but DHS counsel didn’t see the email until the next morning. Notably, the Trump DOJ had stopped short of defending the legality of the ads in court, arguing instead that the ads were already scheduled to stop running so the case was moot.: After losing its last two chief prosecutors, the “grand conspiracy” investigation in south Florida is now being run out of Main Justice, the Wall Street Journal reports: “Lawyers in the deputy attorney general’s office are now directly overseeing the Florida-based investigation from Washington, officials said.”: “[M]ore than 60 people charged in the past few months as part of a surge by the Justice Department to prosecute as many noncitizen voters as possible before November’s midterm elections,” the WSJ reports.: A federal judge sanctioned a DOJ attorney in an immigration case for making a “factually baseless” accusation against the immigrant’s attorney. The DOJ lawyer was ordered to undergo at least one hour each of continuing legal education on (i) the special role of U.S. attorneys; and (ii) the need for evidentiary support for all factual contentions.: To celebrate the arrival of 2025, Ken Paxton partied in Dubai with his girlfriend and two fugitives from the U.S., the WSJ reports.: The Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC for the Senate GOP leadership, is pouring in another $8 million to save Sen. Pete Ricketts (R- NE), bringing its total spend in the race to $15 million.NYT: Inside Elon Musk’s $276 Million Midterm Rescue Mission for RepublicansTrump Mocks Protester Assaulted at His RallySurveillance video captured an ICE agent appearing to strike a fleeing immigrant Saturday morning near Houston. The man, who was apparently not the initial target of ICE, reportedly suffered two broken legs in the incident.No More Kimberly Guilfoyle to Kick AroundEven as President Trump was publicly dangling the possibility of firing Kimberly Guilfoyle, the WSJ was cranking out another in its series of wtf stories on the U.S. ambassador to Greece: “At Davos, Kimberly Guilfoyle Boasted of Private Jet Trips, Luxury Stays.”The WSJ didn’t just have witnesses to Guilfoyle’s grasping at Davos in January. It had a recording of her, too. Some of these quotes, y’all:To an American businessman whose help she wanted getting into a dinner thrown by Greek House Davos for Eric Trump: “You know, I can deliver the world to you. Which you deserve. … “I’m going to make you a lot of f—ing money.”Furious that she wasn’t invited to the dinner: “You don’t have the f—ing U.S., you know, ambassador to Greece not come. She should be kissing my f—ing ass.”Bragging on her ties to Greek shipping tycoon Nikolas Tsakos: “I see Nikos every f—ing day. … I’m flying with him to Paris. I’m with him for a f—ing week. … He loves me. Honey, I spent Christmas with him. New Years. OK? Gstaad. Like, everywhere.”Alas, we learned this morning from the White House press secretary that President Trump has asked Guilfoyle to resign. It was fun while it lasted.

item.title: Christine Brennan Has Not Fully Lost It, According To Christine Brennan In Two Baffling Phone Calls
item.author: Tom Ley
item.content:encoded: Thank you for your email and my sincere apologies. This went to a spam folder and I just saw it now. As you might know, I’ve covered the WNBA since it began in the late 1990s and have fought very hard for it to get attention from the male-dominated mainstream sports media and national media for whom I work, including USA Today, CNN and ABC News. You can find a lot about my coverage of the WNBA and its incredible advocacy in my book, On Her Game: working to get BG home; being a month ahead of Colin Kaepernick protesting the killing of Black men; working to get Sen. Warnock elected, etc. To have the opportunity now to get that attention and coverage is something I never thought would happen in my lifetime. And then to witness the rudderless “leadership” of Cathy Engelbert at this crucial moment…well, that’s why I continue to speak out.As you can see on my social media and in my book, I believe the great Dr. Harry Edwards had it right about preparing for Caitlin Clark’s arrival. I also believe Adam Silver finally needs to engage; this is his legacy too. There are things big and small I’d love to speak with you about: for instance, immediate investigation of the messages Kelsey Mitchell and other players say they are receiving. That should be the highest priority of the new commissioner: investigate everything happening to the players and take the appropriate action. As we know, that happened with Clark’s stalker, who is now in jail.Also, the W needs a transgender policy. As I’ve said on some recent podcasts, it is the only major sports league or organization without one, as far as I know, which creates the massive controversy we’ve seen the past few months. The W needs to address this issue. It’s not easy but the commissioner needs to be taking this on, not leaving it to the players.

item.title: ‘Fallow’ Explores A World Where Big Tech Has Disrupted Pregnancy
item.author: Jade Gu
item.content:encoded: The practice of surrogacy can be said to date back to the Bible; in Genesis 16, Abram is promised descendants by God, but his wife Sarah is unable to conceive. Sarah then instructs Abram to lay with her handmaid, who is then able to bear his child and fulfill God’s promise. This story begins at the issue of infertility. Yet the practice today has evolved to address a myriad of motivations: the pro-natalism push, the desire to preserve one’s body, gay couples endeavoring to start a family. The heightened demand for surrogates has fueled a robust industry, including reduced-cost options via agencies that have sourced surrogates specifically in “countries blighted by poverty.” One novel motivation for using a surrogate that has emerged is that of some form of careerism. Celebrities like Lucy Liu, who cited the pace of her career as her reason, have welcomed children via surrogates. Carrying and delivering your own children is beginning to join the ranks of services that can be outsourced to others out of sheer convenience. Sarah Anderson’s shrewd, satirical debut novel follows a woman named Natalie who is employed at a workplace grievance call center. She comes across a mysteriously lucrative opportunity: a position with a tech company called “The Company” offering a “GENEROUS SALARY WITH BENEFITS,” the only apparent requirements being a “healthy lifestyle, birthing hips, and discretion.” After a few white lies regarding substance use in the job interview, Natalie receives an offer from The Company to participate in their Genesis program. The program was conceived by The Company to combat the decreased emotional investment and productivity associated with maternity leave, allowing for female executives to instead employ an in-house surrogate. Natalie’s contract renders her responsible for seven viable pregnancies over the course of 10 years, while not disclosing the nature of her vocation to any of her personal associates. At the end, she is entitled to up to $60,000 in desired “reconstructive” surgery. Natalie, dazzled by the salary and the idea of freedom from the tedium of conventional work, signs the contract. Natalie’s existence goes on to consist of becoming an optimal body to carry the babies of various female executives. She spends her days walking “aimlessly” on her treadmill, getting driven to the doctor, chiropractor, and acupuncturist, watching foreign language films for the fetus to internalize. Her first pregnancy and delivery go smoothly, largely unconcerning up to her physical postpartum symptoms of hives and severe body odor, which abate after a few weeks until she feels like a “looser, wetter version of herself.” An employee thanks Natalie, bemoaning her first terrible first pregnancy and her “relief” toward Genesis as a program.

item.title: Racist imbecile depletes National Strategic Reserve of Racism
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: You’d think in a county as big as the United States that there would be enough racism to go around — and most of the time, there is. You want racism? We’ve got racism up the yin-yang. Racism was baked into our Constitution. Remember the Three-Fifths Compromise?But there’s one greedy piece of racist shit in our nation, who, every time he opens his rancid anus-mouth, gloms it all for himself — to the point where we actually have to dip into our precious National Strategic Reserve of Racism.“In Somalia, where they don’t have— PANTS to wear. They come here, they go in BMWs and Mercedes, and— they like that. Somalia, love Mercedes. They come in, they have nothing. And they’re the number one buyers of Mercedes-Benz and BMWs in the state of Minnesota. The WHOLE THING is crazy. It’s crazy. Low-IQ people. If you want to stop Ohio from being plundered, ransacked and destroyed like Minnesota’s being destroyed, we’re gonna stop it, just like we did with Springfield. We’re gonna stop it. We’re not gonna let it out.”Preznit Fuckwit sure has a bug up his ass about Somalia, doesn’t he? Bro, show us on the doll where the Somalis hurt you.Donny can’t, because they haven’t.For sure, Dear Leader is the vilest racist ever to crap a diaper in the Oval Bordello. But Somalia is just a convenient scapegoat to distract from Dear Leader’s own clownfucktacular failures as president. He hasn’t lowered prices. He hasn’t fixed the economy. item.title: There Is Some Mighty Weird Stuff Going On Up There
item.author: Barry Petchesky
item.content:encoded: The technical term for them is Transient Luminous Events, and it's a good term. Transient, because they last just a few milliseconds. Luminous, because they light up the sky, but also because they invoke the radiant immanence of an Old Testament manifestation. Events, because—well, imagine you saw this. You would agree this was an Event.The most commonly observed TLE is a red sprite, an enormous electrical discharge shooting from thunderstorm clouds, usually a blood-red color due to the excitation of nitrogen atoms. Below is one of the finest images of sprites ever recorded, by nature photographer Florian Riou last month: https://www.instagram.com/p/Dd1japWjrkl/
