item.title: Who really controls Greg Abbott?
item.content:encoded: Greg Abbott is worried. After three terms as Texas governor, the Republican had every reason to believe the office was his as long as he wanted it. But Abbott is now seeing his Democratic opponent, state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, get uncomfortably close to him in the polls. Suddenly, the governor has to be mindful of negative press, something he’s lost practice at in the decade-plus he’s been in office. Abbott avoided a recent campaign stop from Donald Trump, lest he be seen in the vicinity of the unpopular president or Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general who appears to be facing an uphill battle in his own Senate race against state Rep. James Talarico. The governor is so concerned about his re-election prospects that he recently reversed his position on data centers, which have grown increasingly unpopular, and is now calling for moratoriums and restrictions on their construction. But one issue Abbott hasn’t budged on is his all-out war on public education.Schools in Texas are wildly underfunded, with hundreds having to reduce students to four days a week. This is very much by Abbott’s design. As Jessica Grose of the New York Times explained on Oct. 7, the governor signed into law a voucher program whose entire purpose is paying parents to take kids out of school and put them into unregulated “alternatives” — such as private schools or homeschooling — that have no real requirements to offer children an actual education. Since local school funding is tied to student head count, this has created a backdoor way to funnel money out of already-struggling public schools. Watching the governor concoct elaborate schemes to siphon money from beloved local institutions into unregulated religious programs and homeschooling is enraging people, so much so that some lifelong Republican leaders are announcing they will be voting for a Democrat for the first time ever.Even in deeply conservative rural and suburban areas, Abbott’s policy is unpopular; a June 2026 University of Texas/Texas Politics Project poll found that only 33% of Texans approve of his performance on education. As Grose notes, public schools are the heart of many Texas communities, especially when it comes to high school football. (As a native Texan, I can attest that the “Friday Night Lights” lifestyle is real.) Watching the governor concoct elaborate schemes to siphon money from beloved local institutions into unregulated religious programs and homeschooling is enraging people, so much so that some lifelong Republican leaders are announcing they will be voting for a Democrat for the first time ever. It helps that Hinojosa, whose entrance into holding office was being on the Austin school board, has made saving Texas schools the centerpiece of her campaign. Considering education is the issue that could sink Abbott, it raises the question: Why not back down? After all, he shifted gears on data centers. But when it comes to this policy, which is undermining and could even start closing beloved local schools, the governor will not budge. To the contrary, he has burned a lot of bridges within the GOP in his war on public schools, backing primary opponents of anti-voucher Republicans in the legislature until he’d tilted the scales to get this done. Money is the likeliest answer. As Grose notes, Abbott’s war on education is backed by three powerful Texas billionaires — and major conservative donors — Tim Dunn and a pair of brothers, “If you ever wonder why state laws and policies are more radical than most Texans would prefer, Through his Midland Bible Church, Dunn founded Midland Classical Academy, which offers a glimpse of his preferred curriculum: anti-science Biblical literalism that will leave kids unprepared for living and working as adults in the real world. The school teaches “the authority of God over every area of life” and structure education along a historical timeline “from the garden to Mesopotamia, from Greece and Rome to the Reformation and beyond.” The intense parental involvement required by the academy sounds incompatible with allowing mothers to have jobs outside of the home. Abbott’s war on education isn’t just financial or limited to K-12. Republicans “Abbott himself doesn’t read as a Christian fundamentalist like Dunn or Wilks. While the governor hits his minimum Republican allotment of God talk, he has also managed to evade a reputation as a rabid evangelical, despite his support for abortion bans and for forcing the Ten Commandments into classrooms. Part of it is his affect, which feels more old-school Republican than Bible-waving preacher. As a Catholic, Abbott has also managed to keep a discrete distance from the evangelicals who are the backbone of the Christian nationalist movement.But whatever his personal beliefs, Abbott has emerged as one of the GOP’s most loyal soldiers in a movement to turn America into a far-right Christian nation. His benefactors have singled out public education as the biggest obstacle to an illiberal theocratic agenda — and with good reason. Education is power. It’s not just that kids who learn to read and think critically often leave conservative religions, though that is a big fear driving the war on public schools. It’s also that education empowers the majority of Americans who don’t subscribe to fundamentalist Christianity. If Wilks, Dunn and other far-right billionaires can break public schools, leaving the only options as religious education or none at all, they will turn America into a hellscape. Modern people need education to hold down decent-paying jobs, and civic participation depends on the ability to read, write and reason. A population without the benefits offered by public education would largely be left intellectually, financially and spiritually impoverished — and easier to control.

item.title: Quoting Geoffrey Huntley
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: If the agent isn't using my diagnostics library, I could introspect and update AGENTS.md, but there's still a delta, and it'll drift. Instead, I write a pre-commit hook that checks the git diff for direct calls to observability modules that bypass my diagnostics module. Boom: fail the commit, inject a prompt telling the agent to use the diagnostics library. All of a sudden it's ten out of ten.

item.title: Sex Bomb
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: Imagine you've traveled to a market fair somewhere in Jolly Olde England around 1500. Among the farmers and craftsmen selling their wares, there are also jugglers, puppeteers, and singers to keep the crowd around. A four-man choir performs in harmony, but what are they singing? It's Tom Jones' 1999 hits "Sex Bomb" which was a big hit in Europe, but was never even released in the United States. German music theory professor Jonas Wolf has a particular thing for Renaissance music. He has made a hobby of translating modern music pieces into different historical styles. This one is a one-man project, with Wolf singing four parts. While the song is quite pleasant, the real interest is the incongruity of the tune and the subject matter. However, from what I've read, performers in the Middle Ages could get pretty bawdy at times. (via Metafilter)

item.title: The Brewers Are Walking Down Their Wounded Prey
item.author: Chris Thompson
item.content:encoded: I like to imagine a wised-up contrarian reading Ray Ratto's blog about the Milwaukee Brewers' Game 1 victory over the Los Angeles Dodgers, which identifies a formula in the way the Brew Crew are progressing through the National League playoffs. It's not a vague, vibes-based formula that Ratto describes, either: He says Milwaukee's opponent scores first "but cannot make a big inning out of its opportunity"; he says the Brewers "catch up quickly" then nose ahead; he says Milwaukee's starter "goes four innings" then hands it over to Milwaukee's bullpen; he says the bullpen slams the door, making a narrow margin on the scoreboard feel approximately as vast and daunting as a snow-bound glacier-capped mountain range.I like to think of this hypothetical smirking contrarian—I even have the face and voice of a former shit-eating acquaintance in mind as I type this—rolling their eyes at this so-called "formula." Sure, but this is baseball, and there's too much variance in baseball for formulas, says our contrarian, then somehow wedges the word "orthogonal" and an Ayn Rand reference into an unwanted sermon on randomness and regression. I like to imagine this contrarian then watching Milwaukee's 7–4 victory in Game 2 and becoming so flustered and irritated by the process and outcome that they call out of work the next two days, just to delay their own reckoning.It was downright spooky how closely the Brewers followed their formula Monday night. The Dodgers scored runs in the first and third innings, each time to go up a run, but failed in both cases to extend and exploit their opportunities, both times when an observably unwell Shohei Ohtani made the third out. The Brewers answered both runs with runs of their own, yoinking momentum back their way and chipping away at Dodgers starter Yoshinobu Yamamoto, who needed 25 pitches to get out of the first inning and another 22 pitches to record the first two outs of the third. Milwaukee nosed ahead on a two-out, two-run third-inning single to center, and chased a gassed Yamamoto from the game. Milwaukee's own starter Logan Henderson completed the requisite four solid innings but gave back the lead at the start of the fifth, and was yanked. The Dodgers again failed to put together a sustained rally, and the Brewers immediately countered with another run of their own.

item.title: Tuesday, October 13, 2026
item.author: Jack Baty
item.content:encoded: I've felt a little off for a the past few days. Tired, lethargic, headache. I took an hour nap after lunch yesterday and woke up a whole new person. Felt 100%, just like that. I'll take it!I've had a Withings scale for years. Their app has been basic, but easy to use. And by "was" I mean back then. Now, it gets worse with every update. The latest might be the final straw. There's a "Complete your profile" overlay on every screen that takes me to a permissions screen asking to allow them to send my health data to their "AI infrastructure". I'm not doing that, and I can't find a way to disable the button. On top of that, they're about to charge a $99/year subscription in order to sync my data to Apple Health. I'm definitely not paying for that. It's a bathroom scale, fer cryin' out loud.. Back to logging my weight by hand, I guess.My grandson gets cuter and funnier every time I see him. He just turned 3, which is a great age. Right now it's all about monster trucks.

item.title: 64 cases, zero proof: Putting Bannon’s lie to bed
item.author: 1axceynr3fctrz2of4p6mg8658sin53im00kbn@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: This weekend, in an interview with Ted Koppel on CBS’s , Steve Bannon confirmed what I have been saying for years: “The core belief of the MAGA movement is [Trump] won the 2020 election.”When confronted with the fact that Trump and his allies lost more than 60 court cases challenging the election results, Bannon resorted to a familiar GOP tactic. He falsely suggested that the cases were thrown out on technicalities: “We can go debate this another time, but we didn’t have standing. We never even got into court.”Even worse, Koppel told viewers that Bannon was “technically correct; they didn’t have standing. They couldn’t find a judge who thought they had a significant case worth hearing.”Koppel may have meant that the cases failed because they lacked merit. But what he said is simply wrong.Trump and his allies found plenty of judges willing to hear them out, in many cases through hours or even days of testimony and argument. Those judges listened, weighed the evidence and ruled against them.I know, because I was the lawyer who helped Joe Biden defeat those cases one by one.Correcting the record matters as we approach another election in which Trump and the GOP are once again spreading lies. So let me put this one to bed, once and for all.

item.content:encoded: People who are blind can become very good at negotiating the world by touch, but that presents real hazards while cooking, specifically sharp knives and burning heat. item.title: Organising my cross-stitch patterns
item.author: Alex Chan
item.content:encoded: I have a lot of digital cross-stitch patterns and until recently they were a mess. My “collection” was a series of several hundred PDFs, disorganised and spread across my disk.Recently, I was looking for a pattern and it took me several minutes to find it. I had a brief moment of panic, thinking that I’d lost it, and the website this pattern came from is long since gone. Fortunately it did turn up, but it was clear I had to organise my pattern collection.The patterns are arranged in a masonry layout with a preview thumbnail for each pattern, which is normally the first page of the PDF. If a pattern has multiple files – for example, different files for colour and black-and-white printing – there’s a list of links below the thumbnail. I can also add a source link to where I bought the pattern, if I want to find more patterns by the same author.Internally, it’s structured like my other static websites. The metadata for the patterns is stored in a JavaScript file, and then I have an HTML page which renders that metadata in this visual design. My pattern collection doesn’t change very often, so I’m adding new files by hand.There are no sorting or filtering options, because my collection is small enough that they’re unnecessary. I can scroll through the entire list in less than a minute and find whatever I need.I’d like to start making my own clothes soon, and I expect to copy this design to store clothing patterns.This collection now sits alongside my saved bookmarks, podcasts, TV shows, and more. I can keep all my patterns organised, and I won’t lose them in the depths of my hard drive.There are a couple of technical pieces I’m quite pleased with in this process: I love the cascading grid style of a masonry layout, and I think they’re great when you have variable-sized content – like my pattern cards. I’ve been using them for over a decade; screenshots of my early web apps show my experiments with David Desandro’s Masonry.js library.Masonry layouts are now a native feature of CSS called “Grid Lanes”, which is simpler and more performant than the JavaScript approach. I’m excited to use these layouts in even more places. Most digital postage patterns are shipped as PDFs, and I’m creating the thumbnail images with my create_thumbnail tool.I had to extend my tool to support PDFs, which turned out to be straightforward with the pdf_oxide crate. I’d not come across Oxide before, but it’s a cross-language library for working with PDFs, and I can imagine using it in future.A coloured stripe for the palette. In the metadata for each project, I have the complete list of DMC thread colours and the pattern dimensions. I have a lookup table that converts DMC thread colours to hex codes, and then I’m able to create a linear gradient in CSS to render a coloured stripe of the pattern colours.Here’s an example from a pattern with four colours:border-bottom 12px solid transparent border-image linear-gradient to right #7a451f 0 #7a451f 25 #985e33 25 #985e33 50 #e4bb8e 50 #e4bb8e 75 #361f0e 75 #361f0e 100 1Building the HTML, CSS, and JavaScript was very quick – I have notes on how I build my media sites, and I’ve done it plenty of times before. I threw together the initial prototype in less than 15 minutes. The longer part was finding all the PDFs scattered across my disk – but now that’s done, and I know exactly where to find my patterns.

item.title: Improving Conversation on KDO
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: I’ve been really pleased with how KDO comments are working lately — you folks have been lively, informative, fun, and pushing conversations beyond what I can individually manage. And the vibe of the threads are more closely matching the vibe of the community guidelines. All good! The one-size-fits-all-ness of social media has its advantages, but some are looking for quieter spaces and more orientation around community and shared sensibilities. Through the comments, KDO has been growing into one of those places.In order to give us a few more tools to facilitate conversations, I’ve been working on some new stuff over the past few days and some of it just went live: More compact (not so much indentation) and better on mobile especially. I feel like some of the spacing isn’t quite right yet, but that’s easy to tweak as I see how it works on real threads. I spent a lot of time trying to get the right mix of simplicity and info into the comment design, so I hope it works. You can add images/photos to your replies now — just paste or drag them into the comment editor or use the image button in the toolbar. You get two images per comment. From the community guidelines: “Posting images and embeds (video and audio) should safely err on the side of utility. I love Phillip J. Fry waving a wad of cash and saying ‘Shut Up And Take My Money!’ as much as the next person, but we’re not doing reaction GIFs/images/videos here.” Animated gifs will not work. Pasting a link to a YouTube video, Vimeo video, or SoundCloud audio will embed the appropriate player right into your comment. You get two embeds per comment. You can reply to individual comments now. Threading is still only 1 level deep (i.e. there are “top” comments and replies indented under those top comments) but each reply now tracks the comment you’re replying to. (This is difficult to explain! But hopefully easy to understand when you’re looking at a comment thread.)Better reply tracking in “latest” and “popular” sorts. When comment threads reach a certain number of comments, you’re able to sort them reverse chronologically or by number of faves. Previously, it was difficult to distinguish “top” comments from replies to comments (which often read as incomprehensible outside of their context). Now, each reply shows a) who it’s in reply to, and b) a snippet of the replied-to comment (which you can click to read in the thread). Again, difficult to explain (we’re firmly into “how the sausage is made” territory here… eyes are glazing over re-reading this…) but easier to use — I hope! You can mention another member in a comment. Typing “@” and a couple of characters will bring up a list of members who have been recently active on the site — select the one you want and their name will appear in your comment. Their name will have a dotted line under it and hovering over it will bring up their profile bio (if they have one). I hope this will be useful in referencing and connecting replies in threads (e.g. “I love what Franklin G. said in his comment and will be thinking about Maggie W.’s reply as well…”) and also between threads (e.g. “This reminds me of something Darcy Wong wrote last week…”).Reposting social media posts. I’ve been able to do this in threads for quite awhile (here’s a recent example) and I just opened it up for everyone else. Post a public Bluesky or Mastodon link as the only thing in the comment box and it will automagically expand to a repost (including up to two images from the post). No idea if anyone else will use this! But it’s there. I reorganized how the profile page works. (If you’re a member, you can access your profile page in the menu under your name at the top-right of the page.) There are now three tabs: Comments (lists the most recent comments you’ve made on the site), Faves (list of posts and comments you’ve faved), and Mentions (list of comments you’re mentioned in and replies to your comments). For comments in the Comments and Faves views, I’ve also made it easier to see what’s being replied to.Ok, I think that’s it? At least for the public-facing stuff. I’ve also been tweaking the KDO post editor (Movable Type is now completely out of the loop, RIP to a real one) and it’s getting goooood. I’ve been streamlining the posting process, especially for adding images and doing Quick Links, and it’s really a pleasure to create posts now. More to do on this front as well.Anyway, feel free to try some of the new stuff out in the comments — I’m hoping this will make conversations easier to follow, both for participants and readers. I’ve got some ideas for further improvements, but I wanted to get these out here for now. As always, your comments and suggestions are welcome! And thanks for your membership support — it means I can spend time making improvements like this.

item.title: Troma Tuesday: Squeeze Play
item.author: Schill
item.content:encoded: There are movies that make you think. There are movies that make you laugh. And then there are movies like , where the main challenge is simply accepting that someone actually got all of this into a finished movie.Released in 1979, is a low-budget sex comedy built around softball, romance, rivalry and enough questionable decision-making to fill several respectable movies. It comes from that wonderful era of exploitation filmmaking when a movie didn’t necessarily need a huge budget, a complicated plot or even particularly convincing acting. It just needed a poster that looked interesting enough to make somebody hand over a few dollars at the theater.And definitely knows what kind of movie it is.The basic setup is wonderfully ridiculous. A group of women put together a softball team to take on a men’s team, turning an ordinary recreational game into an excuse for competition, flirting and a whole lot of sexual comedy. The plot is less concerned with realism than with getting everyone onto the field and finding increasingly silly ways to create romantic complications.It’s basically if someone removed the inspirational speeches, replaced the budget with pocket change and decided that subtlety was an unnecessary expense.The softball angle is actually one of the movie’s better ideas.There is something inherently funny about taking a completely ordinary suburban activity and treating it like a life-or-death sporting event. The movie understands that its audience isn’t necessarily here for the finer points of baseball strategy. Nobody is going to be breaking down defensive shifts after watching .The game is simply an excuse to put a bunch of characters together and let the movie’s various romantic and comedic situations develop.The movie is very much a product of its time. Its idea of comedy is broad, its sexual humor is unapologetic and its characters are often less like fully developed human beings and more like walking setups for the next joke.That’s not necessarily a criticism.Actually, it’s part of the charm.Movies like weren’t trying to win awards. They were designed for audiences who wanted something light, cheap and a little bit naughty. The whole thing has the unmistakable atmosphere of a movie that could have been discovered on a late-night cable channel years after its original release.The production itself has that low-budget late-’70s look that makes everything feel slightly more authentic than a polished studio comedy would.The locations don’t feel glamorous.The costumes don’t feel expensive.The characters don’t appear to have unlimited wardrobes.And nobody seems particularly concerned with making the whole thing look bigger than it is.That gives a strange charm.It feels like a movie made by people who knew exactly what they had and weren’t going to waste time pretending otherwise.The biggest problem is the humor.Some of it works surprisingly well, especially when the movie leans into the absurdity of the situation. But a lot of the jokes are firmly locked in the late 1970s. What was considered outrageous or hilarious at the time can occasionally feel more awkward than funny today.The movie also isn’t particularly interested in subtle character development. People fall for each other because the plot needs them to. Rivalries appear because the movie needs a conflict. Romantic complications arrive exactly when the screenplay needs another complication.You don’t watch because you need to know whether these characters will undergo meaningful personal growth.You watch because you want to see what ridiculous thing happens next.That’s an important distinction.And honestly, there is something refreshing about a movie that doesn’t pretend to be more important than it is.Modern comedies often feel like they need to have a message. has no such problem.Its message is basically:Get a softball team together.Make everybody attractive.The movie’s biggest strength is its willingness to embrace its own silliness. It doesn’t have the polish of a major studio production, but it has personality. There is a particular kind of charm that comes from watching a movie made during the period when exploitation films could still find an audience simply by being weird, cheap and entertaining. also benefits from being short on pretension. It doesn’t ask the viewer to admire its artistry or contemplate the human condition. It just wants to entertain you for a while.There are stretches where the movie feels repetitive, and some of the comedy hasn’t aged especially well. The pacing can also drag when the movie isn’t actively moving toward another joke or softball-related complication.But when it hits the right tone, becomes exactly what it should be: a goofy, low-budget snapshot of late-’70s exploitation comedy.It’s the kind of movie where you can almost imagine the pitch meeting.“It’s about a women’s softball team.”“And there are romantic complications.”That’s basically the entire business plan. isn’t a lost cinematic masterpiece. It isn’t secretly one of the great sports movies. It isn’t going to make anyone rethink the possibilities of the romantic comedy.But that’s missing the point.It’s a movie from an era when filmmakers could make something cheap, silly and mildly outrageous, throw it into theaters and see what happened. That kind of filmmaking has largely disappeared, which makes movies like more interesting today than they probably were when they were released.It’s occasionally ridiculous.And it’s exactly the sort of movie that becomes more entertaining when you stop expecting it to be good and simply enjoy it for what it is. is not a great movie.But it is a wonderfully goofy example of late-’70s exploitation comedy, and sometimes that’s all you really need. Put it on, don’t expect sophistication, and enjoy the strange little time capsule that emerges from the other side.

item.content:encoded: Grandpa Yoshitaka is well-known in Japan and has gone viral elsewhere for his lovely photographs with his cats Chouchou and Miko, and their beloved predecessor Wolf out in nature. Yoshitaka always has a beaming smile that competes with the cats. Or almost always. Getting two cats to get along long enough for a photo shoot in a flower garden isn't always easy. When they are good, they produce serene and beautiful images, but when they are bad, they are just funny. item.title: Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: Python 3.15 is here! Here's the essential What's new in Python 3.15 guide, this year curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11.First, some highlights from Python 3.15.The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows.My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. I had to recommend manual lazy imports in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost. [[, ], [, ], []] [] [{, }, {, }, {, }] {} [{: }, {: }, {: }] {} Python's existing tracing profiler has been renamed from to profiling.tracing, and has been joined by an exciting new sampling profiler called Tachyon, aka profiling.sampling.Sampling profilers work by periodically capturing stack traces from running processes, then using those to calculate which functions have the most time spent inside of them. They're very low overhead and can provide a deep insight into running systems, without needing to instrument those systems first.If you have the PID of an existing Python 3.15 process you can start gathering samples by running this (I had to use on macOS):sudo uv run --python 3.15 python -m profiling.sampling attach 1234Interact with the main program a bit, then hit Ctrl+C to stop gathering and see a report, which looks something like this:3.15 isn't much faster than 3.14Miguel Grinberg investigated How fast is Python 3.15? the other day against the 3.15.0rc3 release and found performance to be mostly the same as 3.14, with the exception of the experimental JIT. The JIT gave a 1.2x boost over the standard 3.15 interpreter (on a Fibonacci test), the first time Miguel observed a meaningful JIT performance increase.Miguel's explorations of 3.14 last year found significant boosts against Python 3.13 across many more categories.Upgrading to Python 3.15 with uvI used the following sequence of commands to get to use Python 3.15 on my Mac. First I had to upgrade itself to ensure it knew about the new release:Then I installed the stable 3.15 release:And told that I wanted that to be the default for every command, unless the project itself pinned a different version:uv python pin --global 3.15Now the following reports 3.15 as the version:I already have a bunch of tools installed using . I reinstalled them to use Python 3.15 like this:uv tool upgrade datasette --python 3.15Then I can confirm the version like this:datasette --get /-/versions.json jqHighlights from Python 3.11The release of 3.15 means that Python 3.10 (released in 2021) is officially no longer supported.My policy for my main open source projects is to keep them working in every supported Python version. I can now drop 3.10 and start using features that were introduced in 3.11. is a new in 3.11 alias for .Python's SQLite support got some significant upgrades in 3.11, including:create_window_function() lets us create custom window functions in Python, as a class with , , , and methods.blobopen() provides an efficient mechanism for partial reads and writes of large binary values stored in a SQLite row.You can now call to remove a SQLite authorizer. Datasette had a workaround for this!I plan to land Python 3.11 improvements to a bunch of my projects over the next few weeks. Here's my first Datasette PR removing that workaround.

item.title: ‘Saban’ Has Nothing To Say About Its Subject Or The World He Helped Create
item.author: Israel Daramola
item.content:encoded: At times it really does feel like time is moving faster than ever, and even things that happened a year ago might as well have happened 10 years ago. But it is important to maintain perspective, and understand that time and history have to play their parts before we can properly recognize moments for what they meant at the time they happened. With that said, it can feel a little strange to begin reevaluating the legacy of Nick Saban, football coach, and the Saban era of Alabama football a mere three years after his surprise retirement from the team and college football in general. The man is just started getting comfortable as on-air ESPN talent, finding time to evaluate games and banter with human Red Bull can Pat McAfee, in between his actual work as minister of propaganda for archaic college sports bills.The truth is we aren’t removed enough from the Saban era to understand what his time there meant for the sport, that particular team, or the city of Tuscaloosa at large. But the content machine needs to eat constantly in order to maintain value for an increasingly shrinking number of investors, and so it must be fed. So Nick Saban, come on down for your glossy, incredibly long, fussy, overproduced, myth-making, hagiographic sports documentary project.The new six-part ESPN documentary, , is the officially authorized story of Nick Saban as championship coach of the Alabama Crimson Tide, alongside some other stops at Toledo, Michigan State, and a national championship at LSU. If you’ve watched enough modern sports documentaries, and Lord knowswe have, then you already know what to expect: a lot of inspiration-core, thinly veiled sponcon in which the product is the star of the documentary themselves.

item.title: Dominance Politics, Elite Gatekeeping and Jon Ossoff
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: I’ve been in a conversation over the last few weeks about a possible piece I might write for another publication about Democrats and the politics of masculinity and power, particularly how this relates to how young men have shifted to the right in the Trump era. I mostly think that this is an issue that affects Democrats generally, and is not just narrowly about this or that demographic group. This has been a theme in lots of conversations at TPM over the last 20 months when it comes to the extra-ideological division among Democrats between “fight” and accommodation and civility. Going back even further, to late 2004, I’ve been writing about what I call “dominance politics,” or, originally, “bitch slap politics.” I thought of this this weekend because there was a blip of attention to comments from David Brooks on The Newshour. “The insinuations that El-Sayed is involved in terrorism because he’s Muslim, ridiculous. Jon Ossoff, my advice to him is, if you start calling your political opponents Nazis, maybe it’s time to shut up. That’s just not what we do here in this country.” There are a slew of problems with this. Not least of which are false equivalence and appeals to ethnic hatred and bigotry. Ossoff didn’t call Mike Collins a Nazi. What Brooks is referring to is Ossoff’s debate swipe when he told Collins, “You’ve hired half the Third Reich to staff your congressional office and you have promoted neo-Nazi content online.” This isn’t some random swipe. It’s been one of the biggest stories of the campaign season that week after week reporters keep finding members of Collins campaign, political operation or family who are associated with far-right or neo-Nazi individuals and organizations or who distribute anti-Semitic propaganda. This is merely an aggressive statement of facts that are unambiguously in the public record. But it’s not the specifics of Ossoff’s attack or Brooks’ tut-tutting I want to focus on here. It’s the more general and more important issue of tut-tutting, elite gatekeeping and how this relates to how Democrats operate in the public sphere.

item.title: The X is Off-Target
item.author: Ernie Smith
item.source: Tedium: The Dull Side of the Internet.
item.content:encoded: Is X good again? That's probably the wrong question. The right one: Are we past the era when a single social network needs to be everything to everyone? but I simply don’t have time to devote to every single social network. I don’t have the energy to post to Threads and Instagram and TikTok. I would much rather post a couple places I know are worth my time and then focus my energy elsewhere.But if your job is watching the zeitgeist as a blogger like myself presumably might, you may feel like you’ve spent the last couple of years with one hand behind your back. No one network covers the conversation anymore, and if you’re posting about tech or AI, you might feel like you’re missing something important by not being on X.I see more interesting posts on X than I do on Threads, Bluesky, and Mastodon combined. I wish that weren’t so but it is. Most people don’t want to think about politics so they don’t. Those people, when they want to participate in a Twitter-like social network, go to X.And I can’t blame anyone. The only network that compares to X, size-wise, is Threads — but Threads’s algorithm is weirder than X’s now, and the content I see there is relatively boring. My Threads timeline is full of engagement bait without being engaging. And if you want to judge a platform by its owner, “I’m grossed out and/or appalled by Elon Musk so I’m going to Mark Zuckerberg’s joint” isn’t a way to avoid being grossed out and/or appalled by the owner. Bluesky and Mastodon are too small for most people to care about — and, worse, they are the networks where politics are, in my experience, unavoidable. You can have a discussion about cool new use cases and tools for AI on X and people just discuss the tools and use cases. On Bluesky and Mastodon it’s difficult to have such discussions without arguments from people who (a) believe all use of AI is unethical, and (b) will shove their viewpoints into your replies.As a guy who also blogs, I sympathize with the perspective that chatter about politics and anti-AI sentiment has perhaps made smaller networks like Bluesky and the fediverse less fun for some curious nerdy tinkerers. If you don’t feel like you can share your excitement about an emerging technology because it breaks a social norm, you might feel like you’re in the wrong spot.(And it would sure be nice if the famous people didn’t post on the biggest network.)But at the same time, just because a social network feels like it’s good in one sense doesn’t mean it’s good in numerous others.For one thing, I’m going to forever associate the mess that was the Trump administration’s first 90 days, the DOGE of it all, with X. Much of what was happening was publicly highlighted there, and for a time, it felt like X was an appendage of a government that many felt had taken the country in a dangerous direction. Eventually, Musk extricated himself from the federal government, but not without lingering questions about “why.”And for all the weaknesses of Bluesky’s moderation capabilities—anyone who has appeared on a public list that they don’t understand knows what I’m talking about—it is a network that tries to do to protect its users. X has made it possible for users to appear on your timeline even if you’ve blocked them, or vice versa.The fact of the matter is, as Anil Dash has frequently emphasized over the years, X is not a welcoming place anymore and in fact comes with more brand harms than brand goods. (Many of the arguments he has made about Substack more or less apply to X. Just because good things happen there doesn’t mean those good things cancel out a platform’s harms.)We’d probably be happier with smaller, more focused networksBut I think this discussion also opens up another, related question: Do we to live in a world where every network is the biggest thing ever? Can you have a thriving community without your primary platform being a zeitgeist machine? Gruber’s framing on the issue seems to suggest that Twitter circa 2009 is the ideal. But what if that moment has genuinely passed? The Threads algorithm that Gruber points to specifically goes out of its way to discourage the very kinds of interactions that a 2009 Twitter once allowed. The fediverse’s server-oriented setup favors interactions in smaller communities even if, in practice, people still tend to favor the larger ones.If anything, the tension that folks see on Bluesky, a network (unfortunately) seeded with people who intentionally quit X, shows how a single network for everyone may be a pipe dream at this point. People need communities that touch on specific areas, but the problem has always been discovery and embrace. Threads attempts to solve that by connecting those latent lines together using algorithmic imperfection. Bluesky tries solving it with the use of starter lists and custom feeds. At this point in its history, X prefers a “let things fall where they may” approach.I think the problem we have right now is not that all the excitement is happening on bigger networks; it’s that we want smaller, more niche communities, but our options for getting those come with a lot of baggage either technical or cultural. Some people just want to post, no bullshit. Other people don’t want to deal with the bullying and othering that poorly moderated networks carry.On top of all that, these networks can push you off the path you’ve chosen to focus on. You want to post about tech or weird stuff, but all of a sudden, you’re posting about a guy you didn’t know existed 10 minutes ago. In that sense X is an easier network to enjoy if you want to just passively have a conversation about something, and that it’s easier to keep track of zeitgeist-defining conversations and viral posts.But at the same time, none of this really takes into the fact that, for all the political chatter that has taken place on Bluesky in the past two years, the real-life effects of each network are by no means comparable. (I struggle to see a political scandal from the fediverse or Bluesky that gets anywhere near what we’ve seen from X in the past two years.) X has made room for interesting discussions about AI that appeal to a certain audience of techies. But there are a lot of people that feel left out by these discussions. They deserve the room to find their own places to converse.Perhaps we don’t need one large overarching network anymore. Maybe we just need one or two places where we feel comfortable to talk about the things that really appeal to us. (If I were Bluesky, I would look for ways to niche in.)For lots of people, X probably isn’t it. And that’s OK.“As much as the AI hype all around us pretends that OpenAI and Anthropic are unique and special, they’re not.” Micah Lee’s take on AI encourages you to look beyond the obvious players, who mainly just want to get bigger. on his latest film, Columbus Day. Finally, every holiday has its own dedicated romantic comedy. for a green tea chai burrito bowl, I have some bad news for you.By the way, did you know we launched a new newsletter? It’s called , and it focuses pretty tightly on mini PCs, with a mixture of modern and offbeat tech. (Here’s the latest.) You may dig it if you like our nerdier Tedium posts.And if you host a website you’d like to keep around for a good long while, give foreverhost.ing a look.

item.title: What Kind Of Villain Will Manchester City Be?
item.author: Tom Ley
item.content:encoded: The lead-up to Sunday's game between Liverpool and Manchester City could not have felt more strange. Here were the two teams that have defined approximately the last decade of the Premier League, who have been each other's fiercest rivals while setting new standards for excellence on the pitch, meeting in a meaningless game. It was meaningless in a figurative sense, in that the primary reason for anyone tuning in was to see how the Anfield crowd would greet their guests in their first game since City was found guilty of 114 financial rule breaches. It was likely meaningless in a literal sense, too, as the points City gained from its 3-0 win are likely to be wiped out by whatever considerable punishment the Premier League eventually doles out.Due to this year's supersized international break, Premier League fans have had nothing to do but use the last three weeks to stew in their feelings of grievance. Spend enough time thinking about those 114 guilty verdicts, and the £900 million in phony sponsorship money which City used to establish itself as lords of the competition, and it's hard not to come away feeling that everything about the last decade would have been different—especially for team—if not for these fraudsters.This game eventually had to be played, though, and once it started, so much of the venom that built up over the last few weeks seemed to dissipate. The visiting City fans, defiant and armed with their inflatable bananas, entered the stadium via police escort. The Liverpool fans provided plenty of roaring and chanting early on, but eventually there was just a soccer game to watch. And a fairly boring one at that: A cagey first half in which neither team created many chances ended 0-0, and the game was eventually decided by Ryan Gravenberch's sending off in the 62nd minute, which gave City's attackers all the space they needed to eventually put three goals past Liverpool's defense.

item.title: The livestreamed executions will continue until morale improves
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: If Preznit Fuckwit and Piss-Drunk Pete Kegstand get their way, they will soon be inflicting upon the world the barbaric spectacle of livestreaming a public, state-sponsored execution — and in response, the entire world has pretty much risen up to ask, ‘what the fuck is wrong with you?’Margaret Brennan: “Nidal Hasan is in a wheelchair. Doesn’t the administration risk livestreaming this and making him a martyr? Couldn’t this be a risk to the homeland?”Markwayne Mullin: “No one has to watch it.” Brennan: “Well then, why are you livestreaming it?”Mullin: “The president is restoring American values.”I’m sorry, but what ‘American values’ are being restored by turning a death sentence into public entertainment? When was that ever an ‘American value’? Did I blink and miss it? Was there some early draft of the Declaration of Independence that I’m not aware of, extolling the virtues of ‘life, liberty, and the pursuit of gunning down some fuckface in a wheelchair’?Oh, and thanks for clarifying that ‘no one has to watch it,’ Marky Two-Names. I was really worried there that you shitheads were going to go all Clockwork Orange on us.That’s Marky’s answer to a disgusting violation of human rights — ‘just pretend it’s not happening.’Oh yeah, that’ll work. Just look away, and try not to think about how this savagery is being perpetrated in our names. Awesome idea, Marky. Thanks for your contribution to the national discourse. You’ve really done us all a solid.Margaret Brennan has it exactly right in that clip. Donny and Petey are going to turn some asshole who murdered a bunch of soldiers into a . They’re going to turn him into a Did not one of these nitwits think about what could happen next? Did they not game that shit out? Of course they didn’t. These are the morons who quite famously act first and think never. It’s as if you took two eight-year-old boys, pumped them full of sugar, and set them loose making policy.“Let’s kill him! Yeah, let’s kill him! FIRING SQUAD! ON TV! YAY!!!!!!”It’s this kind of lack of foresight that’s landed us up to our necks in an unwinnable don’t-you-dare-call-it-a-war on Iran that’s raised the price of everything, killed more service members than our piss-drunk Secretary of Death is willing to admit, and destroyed our nation’s ability to defend itself. “We don’t have an acceptable base in Qatar because minutes into the war, the Iranians took those bases out. Donald Trump was so fundamentally unprepared for this war that within days of the war starting, our billion-dollar air bases and naval bases in the region were obliterated by the Iranians. Every single American should be furious about that. Not just because Americans died, but because their taxpayer dollars, at scale, were wasted.”Now these dumb-asses are going to take that mindset and apply it to the public spectacle of a livestreamed death — and who knows what might happen next?Economies, foreign policies, human rights — all this shit is interconnected in ways that are too complex for thimble-brains like Donny and Piss-Drunk Pete and Marky Two-Names to ever comprehend. It’s like some huge fucking Jenga tower, and these nitwits are just pulling out blocks at random.It’s the most fucked-up version of the Butterfly Effect ever.The entire world is a tinderbox right now, for no good reason at all — and it’s happening because a handful of imbeciles back in Washington DC decided it would be fun to see how quickly they fuck that Jenga tower’s shit.And we get to watch it take place, in real time, in the most fucked-up livestream, ever.I cannot wait for the adults to be back in charge in America.And when I say adults, I don’t mean New York Times columnist David Brooks.David is very very very sad right now, because that mean old Jon Ossoff is being — — uncivil. . Jon Ossoff, my advice to him is, if you start calling your political opponents Nazis, maybe it’s time to shut up. That’s just not what we do here in this country.Oh, please — fuck straight off into the ocean, David. Don’t you dare presume you can lecture us on You want to talk about uncivil? Have you met the asshole who heads your party right now? He started this shit.Here’s a prime slice of advice: if you don’t want to be a Nazi, don’t a Nazi. Clean up your act. Start with the government storm troopers rounding up undesirables and disappearing them into slave-labor camps. Nazism doesn’t get any more Nazi than that. Nazis perfected that shit.Oh, and maybe don’t fucking livestream executions. You know who would have loved that, if the tech had been available in 1933? The Nazis, that’s who. They would have gone ape-shit over that stuff. Don’t tell me they wouldn’t have.And now, here’s a heartfelt drama that recently played out in three acts. You’ll never guess what happened in Act Two: Russian bot traffic cratered. Troll accounts with user names like ‘ChristianPatriot34545674543’ suddenly went silent.“According to Cloudflare Data Explorer the amount of russian bot traffic has dropped to 49% after Ukraine struck a yandex data center.”“And when our strikes reached Yandex data centers, it suddenly became a little easier breathe, on many social media platforms. A lot of people, a lot of people, noticed it. And there was less hate, less division, a fewer provocations — because there were fewer bots. And it’s pretty clear where those bots were coming from.”A massive drop in Russian bot traffic, three weeks before the midterms? Shoot that shit straight into my veins.Now we come to Act Three, in which the proprietor of the world’s largest Nazi Bar and Child Porn Emporium completely loses his shit.“Zelenskyy has gone too far.”Boo fucking hoo, Space Nazi.Now comes the part where we throw our heads back in laughter.Hey, it’s time for a little Daily Claudia.Today, let’s play a vigorous round of Jeff Can’t Be Bothered To Pay Attention. This one’s from Half Moon, on January 4, 2025.And here we are at Shadows on the Hudson, on July 28, 2024. Hey, maybe I wasn’t just being a jerk. Maybe I was doing something important, like calculating the tip.Anyway, look how quickly I sprang into action and became An Attentive Husband™, the second I realized that photos were being taken.Have a great Monday, everyone.here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: The Brewers Will Just Keep Doing This Until Someone Stops Them
item.author: Ray Ratto
item.content:encoded: The idea that the Milwaukee Brewers can keep playing the same game over and over again and getting the same result is an interesting one. It's probably not a sustainable one, because baseball does not tend to operate that way, but you keep watching for something different from them, and it always turns out the same.This would be a problem for them if they were somehow failing at this playoff thing, but rather they seem to have it down pat. Through five games, the formula is simple: Starting pitcher goes four innings, the same four relievers maintain the status quo, the hitters make three runs stand up in victory, and then everyone goes to the clubhouse for a beer and shower and comes back again the next day to do it again.Surely this cannot be sustained, if only because at some point Abner Uribe's arm will accordion back into his chest cavity. At some point in this postseason they either have to break out a 10-run game, get blown out the same way, have the bullpen melt into slag ... or maybe Jacob Misiorowski throws a three-hit complete game shutout just for giggles and candy.

item.title: Trump hates me personally. Now he’s taking it to the Supreme Court.
item.author: 1axclmoswx0laweygwujfiy434hzby2f7wrfmr@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: When I tell people that Donald Trump hates me, they often assume I mean it in a generic sense — that he hates Democrats and people who fight him in court. No, I correct them: he hates me personally.On Friday, he took that hatred to the U.S. Supreme Court.In 2022, Trump sued me, along with Hillary Clinton and several others, for racketeering. A federal judge dismissed the case and sanctioned Trump and his lawyers, ultimately ordering Trump and his lead attorney to pay nearly $1 million.On appeal, a unanimous panel of the conservative 11th Circuit, including a judge appointed by Trump, upheld both the dismissal and the sanctions.Now Trump wants the Supreme Court to revive his suit and throw out the sanctions.His lawyers argue that he deserves extra time to sue because he set the case aside while serving as president. They also claim the Court must step in to protect the presidency from judges who punish its lawyers.Trump filed this suit as a private citizen, between his two terms. The 11th Circuit found his claims not only too late but “otherwise meritless,” and it agreed that many of the legal arguments he and his lawyer made were frivolous.I became a defendant in this lawsuit because, in 2016, I represented Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaign.When Russia hacked the Democratic Party and the campaign, my role as general counsel required me to understand what happened. That required assessing Russia's interest in interfering in the campaign, weighing legal options and risks.At a news conference in July 2016, Trump said: “Russia, if you’re listening, I hope you’re able to find the 30,000 emails that are missing. I think you will probably be rewarded mightily by our press.”On that point, Trump was right.The legacy media basked in every email leak. The fact that they were the product of a foreign government’s effort to swing the election did not matter to them or their corporate bosses.“But her emails” became shorthand for that coverage, and the legacy media has never reckoned with it.That failure, like its coverage of the Iraq War in 2003, is part of the reason Democrats’ confidence in the legacy media has eroded. I believe it is also why independent outlets like Democracy Docket have grown while the legacy media struggles.Once he became president, Trump waged a multi-year war against me and others who worked for the Clinton campaign. During his first term, his supporters spread lies and misinformation. Ultimately, his Department of Justice appointed a special counsel to pursue us.Anyone who thinks weaponization started in Trump’s second term has forgotten John Durham’s appointment and the partisan witch hunt that followed.After three and a half years of nonstop investigation, Durham charged just three people. One was an FBI lawyer with no connection to the campaign. He pleaded guilty to altering an email and was sentenced to probation.The other two were charged with lying to the FBI, went to trial and were quickly acquitted. One of them was a former law partner of mine.Durham clearly hoped to dig up dirt on me, but in the end, he failed. I was never charged.The experience left me with a keen understanding of how Trump can turn his army of supporters against someone while casting himself as the victim.

item.title: Windy & Carl
item.author: Flow State
item.content:encoded: Today we’re listening to Windy & Carl, an American space rock duo consisting of Windy Weber and Carl Hultgren. We recommended the husband and wife pair for the first time last year. Windy & Carl came up in the Michigan indie/experimental scene in the ‘90s by applying many effects to guitars, creating shoegaze-adjacent ambient pieces. They just released a new LP, Windy&Carl Meet Optigan Conservatory, in September. It’s a collaboration with their longtime friends Frank Rotondo and Fred Thomas, who contribute electric keyboard and synths over the guitars in largely improvised sessions. We’re also playing , which was originally self-released in 1994 and is being reissued by Kranky; that one showcases their early experimentation with stretching, distorting, modulating, and looping guitar sounds.We wish you a great start to your week.
