item.title: What kind of shithole country livestreams executions? Our kind.
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: For We the People, life continues to out of control.Basic goods and services remain unaffordable. Inflation and unemployment are on the rise. Our food is unsafe to eat. Our government lies to us. Our once-staunch allies hate our guts, and openly mock us. Masked, trigger-happy federal thugs roam the streets of our cities. Our hallowed national monuments have been shuttered, or bulldozed to rubble.Our detached, demented president has completely checked out of fixing any of this shit, preferring to focus on useless vanity projects in honor of his own crappy self.But We the People getting one very special thing, and it’s just for us. Know what that one thing is? Get ready for it: Public executions.Hegseth on Nidal Hasan: “He’s gonna get a firing squad of soldiers. As it should be. We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it. That it’s public. Because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”Seriously, what the damn?Did you notice how completely fucking excited Piss-Drunk Pete was, in that clip? He was absolutely as he burbled away at a mile a minute about how the military was going to publicly kill the shit out of someone. That’s insane. happy about meting out death — and nobody who’s that over-the-moon about killing should be put in charge of the lives of others.We’re going backwards as a country. The last public execution in the US was the hanging of some dude named Reiney Betha, on August 14, 1936. After that, states came to their senses, realized that kind of spectacle was barbaric, and stared passing laws against it.And now, Piss-Drunk Pete wants to bring it back, because he thinks that shit’s awesome. As always with these fuckfaces, Hey, you know what other country also does public executions? Iran. Isn’t Preznit Fuckwit always telling us how we’re more civilized than they are? That’s such a cute story, Donny, tell it again.Oh, but at the same time we’re going backwards, we’re also going forwards. We’re bringing public executions into the twenty-first century. Check out this abomination.The public will be able to watch the execution of a former US Army major by firing squad, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has said.A Defense Department official told the BBC the execution of Nidal Hasan, who shot dead 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, would be livestreamed.It is believed it would be the first public execution in the US in almost a century. The decision to livestream it is “unprecedented in the modern era” and “on uncertain legal terrain,” said John Mills, a lawyer who works with inmates sentenced to death.Oh, come on. Are you fucking me?! Who’s going to watch a livestream of someone getting firing-squadded to smithereens? Cultists? More importantly, who’s going to provide the livestream stream? Netflix? Amazon? Facebook? What corporation wants to be complicit in this barbarity? You’d hope the answer would be , but I can think of a few tech bros who would be that horny to curry favor with Dear Leader, and volunteer to host that shit for free.Is this who we want to be, as a nation? Do we really want to be known as the country that broadcasts state-sponsored death? Count me out. I want no part of this fuckery.It’s so much fun being a rogue nation, isn’t it?Ten days ago, the state of Tennessee tried to execute Christa Pike by lethal injection. If you’ve been following that story, you know that they fucked it up royally. Instead of dying, Pike spent hours moaning and crying in pain, and ended up in the hospital in a coma, with severe burns to her arms and shoulders.Imagine if that shit-show had been livestreamed.Maybe it should have been. Maybe the public outrage over that obscene level of cruelty would have started a national conversation about the death penalty.Now here’s something Dear Leader shat out onto his crappy app yesterday. It’s one of those posts that, when it shows up in your social feed, you go, ‘oh come on, that’s fake as fuck, not even Donny is crazypants’ — .The White House considers anyone that uses the term, “Artificial Intelligence,” as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, “Super Intelligence,” THE ENEMY! President DONALD J. TRUMPWho even talks like this? Just because we don’t agree on what to call the janky, six-fingered plagiarism robots, we’re now the all-caps ENEMY? How can any one person be that infantile?I’m so tired of him. I’m so tired of the relentless dumbfuckery. I’m so tired of the bone-crushing stupidity, and the childish if-you-don’t-agree-with-me-you’re-a-poopy-head mentality.And I’m fucking exhausted that there’s now an entire infrastructure devoted to making this utter failure feel good about his own shitty self.Did you know that Donny was awarded another Emotional Support Trophy yesterday?But Donny’s minders also did this: they took a genuine award that Donny’s uncle — the actual MIT professor, John G. Trump — had won in 1983, stuck it behind some chintzy gold frame, and with great fanfare, presented it to Donny, so that he could stand there, beaming, and pretend that he had somehow earned it all by his own Big Boy self.Look at this preening asshole. He’s just so eternally embarrassing. Put that shit down, numb-nuts, you haven’t won anything. And now, speaking of actual awards that Donny will win— “Thank you very much. If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump.”Really weird how there’s currently no Truth Social post from Donny, congratulating Navi Pillay for winning. What’s up with that?Well, it’s Friday, and — — we made it through another week in one piece. Let’s reward ourselves with some Daily Claudia and get out of here.Here are a couple more pics of Katie and her mom. These photos are undated but they’re obviously from the early 1990s.Have a great Friday, everyone. here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: The Not-So-Great Defector Bake Off Has A Gem Of A Time During Biscuit Week
item.author: Chris Thompson
item.content:encoded: The Not-So-Great Defector Bake Off, where Kelsey and Chris attempt to complete the technical challenges from the newest season of The Great British Bake Off in their own home kitchens, with the same time parameters as the professional-grade bakers competing on the show.When I was a child, there was nothing I loved more than preservatives. I loved soda. I loved fast food. I loved the kind of packaged treats that you get in a box at the grocery store, where each of them is individually wrapped in plastic, and the sugar content is so high that they make your teeth hurt. In particular, I loved Little Debbie's Nutty Buddies. The stacked wafers layered with chocolate and peanut butter called to me when my household had them. It was always a special treat. I can feel the crunch of the thin wafers between my teeth even now, probably 25 years since my last Nutty Buddy. I would eat one tomorrow. Such is the draw of childhood nostalgia and sweet treats.

item.title: A new feature for my blog, built using my voice
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: I shipped a new feature for my blog today: the Newsletters page, which offers an index of all of the newsletters I've sent out, both my free weekly Substack and my monthly sponsors-only updates. I built the feature almost entirely using my voice, chatting away to my laptop while I cooked dinner.I used the ChatGPT desktop app for this, in the Codex tab, using the voice conversation mode, running against a local development environment. Here's what that looks like:Start dev server and open in browserThis gave me a preview of the site that it would be working on, and meant that I could later ask it to show me the new pages so I could visually track its progress.Then I clicked the "Start new voice chat" button - that's the microphone button, it's the one to the right of it - and set my laptop up in the kitchen so I could talk to it while I cooked.I had a pretty good idea of what I wanted to build, and it's a simple enough Django feature that I was certain the model (in this case GPT-6 Astra High) would be able to do it. A new model, a migration, some view code, templates, and a couple of import functions to populate the database from external sources.Here's an extract of my voice transcript that was captured by Codex:Um, they do not. Um, this is going to be a new type of content. Um, it's not going to show up... Oh, hold on. Yeah, no- I do not want this to show up in my, um, tag pages and date archive pages and... Actually, no, I think... I don't want it on the tag pages. I don't want it on the, um, blog index page. But I think I do want it to show up on the date-based pages. You know, if you navigate to September the 19th, and I sent a newsletter on that page, I think I want that to show up. So... this is- so I think we probably need a new model. The other thing is that I want them searchable, uh the Substack ones are not searchable, because those are actually just copies of other s- on content on my blog. These monthly ones do contain unique content, and spe- and once they're... published, like once they're made public a month after they've gone out, I want them to show up on my search results.Apparently this was clear enough that the model knew what I wanted to build! You can read the full transcript, disfluencies and all, in this Gist.We went on like this for about half an hour (the time it took to cook dinner). The model would reply and occasionally ask clarifying questions, then get to work modifying the code.We got a surprisingly long way entirely by voice:A new model and migration to represent imported newsletters in Django, plus Django Admin configuration for thatFour working imports: The most recent Substack items via RSSEvery other Substack item via their undocumented API, which GPT-6 Astra knew about (it tried directly) and then ran a search to figure out how to paginate it and found this article by Karen SpinnerMy most recent private sponsors-only newsletter from a private repositoryNewsletters showing up on day and month archive pages too, but not on tag pages or my homepageWeekly Substack newsletters link to Substack; archived monthly newsletters have their own pagesIntegration with my site search engineIt was ready to ship. The catch was the imports: Astra offered to export data from my local copy so I could import that into production, but I wanted it to work like my other import scripts. Since some of the data lived in a private GitHub repository, this would involve creating a new API key, and for that I knew I'd have to sit at the keyboard for a while.Finishing it with a reviewOnce I had finished cooking and judged it mostly feature-complete, I had Codex create a branch and open a pull request.I reviewed the code in the GitHub PR interface. It was nearly what I needed, except it had chosen to use Git in a subprocess for one of the import scripts. I needed one of the imports to pull from a private Git repository, so I figured the API would be a better bet. I switched to typing and had Codex swap that out for an API-based import instead.You can see the changes I made during the review in the extra commits on the PR. I fixed the import mechanism and made a few tweaks to the display of those public pages. It took an additional half hour of typing-based prompting to get to the point where I was happy to deploy it to production by landing the PR.The index page shows my most recent Substack weekly newsletters and GitHub sponsors monthly newsletters mixed together in reverse chronological order. Further down the page are links to my by-year archive pages.GPT-6 Astra designed the page, and then tweaked that design based on my vocal feedback from glancing at the local preview across the kitchen.Better for multi-tasking than as a daily driverOpenAI using voice-driven demos like this one for things like DevDay - and they do work well in that environment. I don't think this is going to be a daily driver for me though.I've written before about how much "work" I get done using ChatGPT voice mode on my phone while walking the dog - mostly research and brainstorming, but occasionally actual development work by having ChatGPT write and test out snippets of code.This feels different. The addition of the visual preview, plus being able to type or paste things in via the keyboard when I need to communicate something that doesn't work vocally, makes this a much more powerful way of interacting with a coding agent.I still switch back to typing once I get down to the details of things though. Being able to paste in examples and error messages, or directly highlight the code or feature that needs changing, remains more efficient than trying to describe it in words.I mainly work from home, which is good because there's no way I'd want to talk to my computer like this in a shared workspace!The killer feature for me is the ability to multi-task. I usually cook with a podcast or TikTok running; now I can actually build stuff instead.

item.title: Who will stop Trump now from seizing voting machines?
item.author: 1axb2a54qx7g67d6wvvnght97tmq66zafeh1ur@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: Convicted criminal and former Mesa County Clerk Tina Peters is pushing a scheme to give the Trump administration control over voting machines. In August, she called on the Department of War “to go in and demand to have these machines in their custody.”More recently, her lawyer, election denier Peter Ticktin, suggested that Peters’ plan was to “get control over the ballots as soon as the machine spits them through and then do a recount.” And on Oct. 5, according to Trump ally Ed Martin, Peters met with Trump in the Oval Office to discuss election security.We have been here before.In December 2020, a group of conspiracy theorists sat in the Oval Office arguing that Donald Trump should declare a national emergency and order the secretary of defense to “seize, collect, retain and analyze” voting machines, equipment and electronically stored election information.The motley crew of election deniers pushing this approach included attorney Sidney Powell, Trump’s former national security adviser Michael Flynn and former Overstock.com CEO Patrick Byrne. The day before the meeting, Flynn had suggested that the president could invoke martial law and use the military to “rerun” elections in swing states.More important than who advocated seizing voting equipment was who opposed it. The White House counsel, his deputy and the staff secretary all helped stop Trump from signing the order. So did Attorney General William Barr. Even Rudy Giuliani opposed using the military.Those guardrails no longer exist.

item.title: ttok 1.0
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: I released ttok 0.4, ran , piped a file into the new version... and realized that it was defaulting to the GPT-4 tokenizer when it should very clearly default to GPT-5/GPT-6 instead!I figured switching the default was a reasonable excuse to finally ship a 1.0.OpenAI haven't actually confirmed that GPT-6 uses the same tokenizer as the GPT-5 family yet - there's an angry issue about it - but I found this commit by William Liu which reports on an experiment he ran confirming that the tokenizers are likely the same:All seven GPT models (5.5, 5.6 Sol/Terra/Luna, 6 Astra/Sol/Luna) report 44,794 tokens and match each other on every one of the 31 fixtures. GPT-6 introduces no input-count change on this corpus.

item.content:encoded: New Hampshire’s GOP officials asked an appeals court to overturn a lower court’s ruling that barred the state from fully enforcing a prohibition on election officials accepting student IDs for voting.Voting advocates argue the ban burdens students, especially those who are low-income or lack transportation.The Trump administration refuses to say whether it'll send ICE to voting sites, but a FOIA lawsuit forced it to disclose 166 pages of documents about its plans.While the records contain talking points and value statements, they leave the main question unaddressed…The new challenge says the Department of Homeland Security diverted $20 million meant for border-security commemorations to pay for the spots.Voting for some Kentucky residents got easier after Jefferson County announced plans for a vote center with a drive-through option.“This initiative will expand accessibility for residents with disabilities who may struggle to vote at traditional polling locations,” the county clerk said.Early voting opened Monday, and mail ballots will start flowing to voters Friday. The state is a battleground for fights over voter access.Just this week, Montana saw big wins for voters with disabilities and for direct democracy. But other groups, including student voters, still face significant access barriers.A federal appeals court declined to rehear Minnesota's defense of its law seeking to combat election misinformation, voter intimidation and harassment.The denial comes after a panel of appeals judges ordered the lower court to block enforcement of the law.The exchange, unearthed from government documents, comes after New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D) disclosed in July that a software failure incorrectly registered over 6,000 noncitizens to vote.

item.title: Quoting Carson Gross
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: Computer programming is, fundamentally, about two things:Problem-solving using computersLearning to control complexity while solving these problemsI have a hard time imagining a future where knowing how to solve problems with computers and how to control the complexity of those solutions is valuable than it is today, so I think it will continue to be a viable career even with the advent of AI tools.

item.title: Oh Hey, More AI Stuff — Is This Our Reliable Narrator?
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: Yet another update on the running AI discussion.Here’s an interview Ezra Klein did with a guy named David Robinson. And that interview is about a piece Robinson, a member of the Open AI safety and safety documentation team, wrote in The Atlantic announcing his resignation from OpenAI — a decision and announcement he is self-aware enough to note has become something of a cliche. I found the interview interesting and edifying, largely on the front I mentioned earlier about finding reliable narrators.Robinson isn’t a data scientist or a programmer. His role at OpenAI was essentially being the conduit between the teams building the LLMs and the knowledgable and interested public, specifically the people who write the documentation — what does this model do, how does it work, what are the possible safety risks. As is usually the case in any highly technical space, the people doing the work aren’t going to be writers and they’re usually not going to speak a language outsiders can necessarily understand. So you have people who are close enough to the work and the workers to understand what is happening and also able to speak human so they can communicate it to everyone else. Robinson led the team that served in that role.

item.title: Action Alert: Speak Out Against Taxpayer-Funded Political Ads
item.author: bounce_75b4552d-49c3-f111-bf5b-000d3a4fbe83_prod@bounce.myngp.com
item.content:encoded: This administration’s “flood the zone” strategy continues with actions that raise serious concerns about constitutional principles and the rule of law. As disheartening as these actions can be, we must meet them with informed engagement and expectations for a better future.Today, we are issuing our latest Action Alert, asking the public to speak out against the misuse of federal resources for partisan political promotion. The administration recently spent nearly $12 million in taxpayer funds on television ads promoting the President, with millions more allocated under a $20 million contract for additional ads selected to run during major broadcasts in the critical weeks before the midterm elections. Following widespread criticism, the President announced that the remaining ads would be paid for via his MAGA Inc. Super PAC.Both approaches raise serious questions under federal law, including restrictions on the use of appropriated funds for unauthorized publicity or political propaganda, the Hatch Act, and federal campaign finance laws. Shifting the payment method from taxpayer funding to privately raised Super PAC funds does not eliminate the need to comply with applicable legal restrictions. Our Action Alert outlines four steps you can take today. LDAD is grateful to our many volunteers who continue to help document important developments, raise concerns, and defend the rule of law. They do this in a variety of ways, for example:LDAD volunteer, Professor Mark Gordon, recently moderated an important election-related program co-sponsored by the Minnesota State Bar Association and LDAD entitled: Rules and Procedures for Voting in the Midterm Elections in MN.Lawyers Defending American DemocracyP.S. Thank you for your ongoing support of LDAD. Please help us protect the rule of law and the freedoms we hold dear by volunteering for our Meeting the Moment initiative and donating to our work.

item.title: Let’s Deconstruct Photoshop
item.author: Ernie Smith
item.source: Tedium: The Dull Side of the Internet.
item.content:encoded: A quixotic new project takes an AI-first approach to battling Adobe, and while it’s unclear where it leads, it raises important questions about what happens when companies ignore their users.I am not a unique flower. Like many creatives, I had a good relationship with Adobe that, over time, went belly up.The first sign something was wrong was when the company more or less ignored Mac design conventions in a way that made its software harder to use. (All you had to do was support full-screen apps in Mac OS X Lion, dudes!)Then it turned its subscription plan into the only real option. Then it kept raising prices. Then it changed its offering in a way that suggested it only really cared about customers who could pay them for hundreds of licenses each year.On top of that, it failed to keep up with where I was going as a user, along with many other users. Despite the fact that a huge contingent of power users have been decamping to Linux, it more or less ignored those users. Meanwhile, AI changed the definition of what software could be.That perhaps explains why I’m not particularly surprised that some programmer decided to rebuild the Creative Cloud suite using clean-room techniques in a vibe-coded environment. It solves many of the issues that upset power users—the lack of end-user responsiveness, the high cost, and the ability to use it on the platform of their choice. Adobe, as a public company, has often been tethered to the desires of the stock market, which has meant a lot of AI stuff, even when many creatives have made clear they do not want them.So now, we have ArtCraft out here Robin Hooding every single one of the key Adobe apps.Do they work particularly well? On the surface, yes. Opening up these apps in AppImage shows that these apps, programmed in the Rust programming language, are not only fast, but relatively small. Rather than hundreds of megabytes, these apps load in tens of megabytes. They detected my discrete GPU right away. And within a couple of minutes, I was manipulating an image.A lot of finicky, below the surface stuff did not work so well. Color pickers and secondary menu boxes were rough, not elegant. It did not detect my fonts in DesignCraft until I downloaded an update published just a few minutes before I downloaded it. And while I could set a color with a hex code in PhotoCraft, I could not do the same in DesignCraft.But it was familiar. I could see myself building a zine with this tool, or using it to access old files that I cannot otherwise open without a Creative Cloud subscription.Is an open-source vibe-coded creative suite really worth cheering on? I think so.There are real reasons to cheer on something like this, even if you otherwise hate AI. The spirit of this evokes a Robin Hood-like mindset, in that it exists because of real ethical and economic issues around Adobe that many end users have long been stuck with. In one sense, it is “fighting AI slop with AI slop.” And even if you don’t end up using these tools, the techniques that these projects land on will ultimately inspire open-source projects that actually rely on craft. There are other apps that have emerged in the past couple of years that hope to bring design to Linux; this open-source tool may have opened up a shortcut for these projects.Let’s talk about “craft” a second here: I think it’s a bad name to build around for this project, as cool and interesting as it is. Craft implies that a lot of heart was put into the code, that it was built by an expert. Which may be true of the artists and creatives that actually use this thing, but does it really speak to what the vibe coders are actually doing? Probably not. It’s really easy to not give critics something to point to, so don’t give it to them.Another thing that they’re likely to point to is the inherent security issues that might come with a tool like this. The decision to use Rust as the language is likely to help with stability, but it’s not like any regular user is going to be looking at the code here.But AI coding techniques are likely to change our relationship with open source for good, as seen with the recent AI-based fork of Asahi Linux. And in fact, it may change how companies like Adobe think of open source and vibe coding.Who knows how legal this is? This feels like one a legit lawyer should probably weigh in on. But some of the language creator Brandon Thomas has used on forums and the ArtCraft website evokes the spirit of Napster, an icon of tech rebelliousness that is not exactly very rebellious in 2026. Napster was not legal, but it still changed everything. That’s a better place for AI in the cultural conversation than “everyone making the worst signs you’ve ever seen.”And even if ArtCraft’s wild deconstruction project fails, it feels clear others will try to take its place. Which is exactly what happened with Napster.So the Ellisons own Warner Bros. Discovery, which I don’t love. But you know what I do love? That the anti-animation monster named David Zaslav isn’t in charge anymore.The fact that a political candidate turned a famous sketch into a very effective political ad is the kind of world I want to live in.I’m getting sent a lot of single-serving sites at the moment. Here’s one that’s an iPod-themed music game that you might enjoy.Find this one an interesting read? Share it with a pal! PhotoCraft, by the way, doesn’t support animated GIFs just yet, but it does have the Save for Web legacy menu, which I was able to use to make today’s header. Not a bad start.

item.title: New Details Emerge on Stephen Miller's Meddling at the Trump DOJ
item.author: David Kurtz
item.content:encoded: The Tip of the Politicization SpearSince the dawn of Trump II, Stephen Miller has been the barely hidden hand running the Justice Department from the White House. Now a new report from CBS News adds quite a bit more detail to the level of influence and control that Miller exerts over the Trump DOJ.The story is framed around an apparent conflict of interest. Miller attended an counterterrorism training session at FBI headquarters on Sept. 29 that was focused on President Trump’s notorious NSPM-7 on domestic terrorism and political violence. Miller urged the federal agents in attendance to be more aggressive in pursuing threats against government officials and their families — at the same time he was an alleged victim and potential witness in a case of alleged threats to his wife, Katie. Miller was reportedly frustrated by the pace of the criminal investigation into the allegedly threatening communications.“In his comments, Miller spoke about the need for federal law enforcement agents to be more proactive in investigating threat cases and told them that no case is too small, whether the threats are directed toward a congressman, a spouse, friends, loved ones or a speaker at a college campus, the senior FBI official said,” according to CBS News.The top two FBI agents in the counterterrorism division of the FBI Washington Field Office were demoted last month over “frustration shared by the Miller family” that the Katie Miller case was moving too slowly. Their demotions reportedly factored into the resignation of FBI co-deputy director Andrew Bailey, although the FBI publicly dimissed that reporting as “fake news.”Two days after Miller spoke to federal agents at the training session, a Massachusetts man was indicted for cyberstalking on Oct. 1 — despite reported concerns from career prosecutors in Boston that his communications to Katie Miller didn’t amount to a federal crime. He was charged with using interstate communications with the intent to harass and intimidate by sending her at least 40 calls, voicemails, and text messages in August and September, some of them crude and profane.But a glaring conflict of interest is just one element of this story, and probably not the most important one.Notably, this episode appears to be a subset of the Trump administration’s broader push to lump all threats together with legitimate political opposition and brand them as domestic terrorism. The criminalization of political opposition to Trump is one of the darkest through-lines of his second term.In this episode, two things jump out: (i) Miller picked a counterterrorism training session to urge more aggressive action in cases involving threats and harassment, citing the assassination of Charlie Kirk; and (ii) Katie Miller’s alleged cyberstalker was “arrested by members of the F.B.I.’s joint terrorism task force, an unusual show of force for a cyberstalking case,” the NYT noted last week.In other words, what might have normally been a local law enforcement matter is now federalized and turned into a counterterrorism investigation. The Trump White House went so far as to defend Miller’s presence at the training session on domestic terrorism grounds, telling CBS News that Miller is tasked with carrying out the NSPM-7 mandate to “investigate, disrupt, and dismantle all stages of organized political violence and domestic terrorism.”The other big picture issue is the one Morning Memo keeps coming back to: the mind-blowing fact of an unabashedly political White House aide addressing federal agents at FBI headquarters. The DOJ, including the FBI, being run out of the White House remains the defining corrupt act of the Trump II presidency.The CBS News story — co-bylined by Sarah N. Lynch, a superb reporter on the DOJ beat — goes quite a bit further in revealing how involved Miller is in the running of the Justice Department:In an earlier episode, Miller pressured the DOJ to take action against a Virginia political activist who protested outside of the Millers’ Arlington home and distributed their address on flyers. A federal magistrate judge twice rejected search warrant applications in the case, CBS News previously reported.In the Virginia case, Miller asked FBI counterterrorism agents in his neighborhood’s political activist group and regularly called the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the the Eastern District of Virginia for updates.Miller has been holding monthly meetings with the heads of federal law enforcement agencies about the deployments of the National Guard and federal agents to D.C. and Memphis in Trump’s “violent crime crackdown.”“Miller is also in touch multiple times a week with the Deputy Attorney General’s office to discuss fraud and immigration cases, according to sources with direct knowledge of the matter,” according to CBS News. The DAG is essentially the chief operations officer at DOJ and runs the department day to day.Miller’s meddling (which may be too weak of word) at DOJ is truly unprecedented. He is the tip of Trump’s spear aimed at politicizing the Justice Department.Kurt Olsen Reportedly Failed a PolygraphKurt Olsen — the Big Lie proponent who stepped down as the lead prosecutor in the bogus investigation into a “grand conspiracy” by the Deep State to deprive Donald Trump of his civil rights — had his DOJ security clearance terminated last month after failing a polygraph test, Reuters reports.‘I Can Do Whatever I Want, If I Want’The American Prospect: In an important development, U.S. District Judge John C. Hinderaker, a Trump appointee in Arizona, has ordered DHS to “facilitate” the return to the United States of an Egyptian man that it deported to Equatorial Guinea, a country where he has no ties. As reporter Gillian Brockell notes, the ruling “could have far-reaching implications for thousands of others subjected to the Trump administration’s third-country removal scheme.”Washington Sun: In a ruling this week, U.S. District Judge Gary R. Brown, a Trump appointee in Brooklyn, condemned ICE agents for falsifying records to cover up a pair of bad arrests. “The evidence suggests that ICE attempted to support their unsupported misidentification argument through false or misleading documentation and testimony,” Brown concluded.CNN: ICE told agents nationwide on Tuesday to increase immigration arrests by 1,000 people per day, returning to a previous goal of 3,000 daily arrests.“On Monday night, it was our understanding that Christa was brain dead and that life support would be removed the next day. But on Tuesday, to the shock of everyone, including me, including her team, including the medical team, Christa woke up and began talking.”—Randy Spivey, a lawyer for Christa Pike, on her recovery from Tennessee’s attempted executionThe Corruption: Kimberly Guilfoyle EditionThe WSJ manages to outdo its remarkable story last month on Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece and former fiancée of Don Jr., with a follow-up bombshell.I started to summarize the highlights, but I really can’t do it justice. Just go read it.

item.title: Steve Hilton is convinced he's going to win. Hahahaha.
item.content:encoded: There’s a midterm election coming on Nov. 3, which includes a race here in California to determine who will replace Gov. Gavin Newsom. On the blue side of the ticket is unremarkable Democrat Xavier Becerra, whose chief positive attribute is that he is not a Republican. On the red side is Steve Hilton, an immigrant from the U.K. who gained U.S. citizenship in 2021. Hilton’s most high-profile political experience came back in the early 2010s, when he served as an adviser to then-U.K. prime minister and alleged porcine enthusiast David Cameron. But that experience, plus a lengthy stint as a commentator for Fox News, was enough to convince Hilton that he not only should run for governor, but that he WILL be the state’s next governor.On the surface, he makes for an attractive candidate. Hilton is good company, and when I met him, he was as good at explaining the issues, as you would expect a seasoned broadcaster to be. He’s even reaching out to the gay community, albeit in somewhat awkward fashion. Listen to the man talk and you might come away thinking he’s a Democrat.But Steve Hilton is not a Democrat. He’s a Republican, one who plans to give tax breaks to the wealthy, massively increase funding to the police and let artificial intelligence companies do basically whatever they want without fear of California regulation. Most importantly to me, he is backed by President and aspiring dictator Donald Trump. So, Hilton can’t run as a Republican, especially not in a state as firmly blue as California, without having to answer for that party’s standard-bearer. But God bless Hilton, he gave it a try, repeatedly, when I met with him in August. This was true right from my opening question, when I asked him why he wanted to run for governor here at all.Article continues below this ad“I love California and it’s obviously not working,” he told me. “Sixteen years of one-party rule, it’s a disaster. So we’ve got to turn things around.”“OK,” I shot back, “but why would I trust a Republican to change any of this, in this administration?”At this, Hilton feigned ignorance. “In which administration?”Article continues below this ad“The Trump 2 administration.”“I don’t see the relevance of that to California.”Hilton acknowledged none of those things. Instead, he continually portrayed himself as a heroic outsider. “I’m not the president,” he insisted, with a showman’s vigor. “I’m not him. I’m me.”Article continues below this adWhen I brought up the president later in our conversation, he complained to me, “I don’t know why you keep talking about Trump.”“That’s why I’m here,” I told him. “Because you’re a Republican. I want you to explain to me how you could possibly exist as a functional Republican with the standard-bearer of that party exercising a ridiculous amount of influence over the party and being a general, omniscient presence over the entire country, California included.”“Well, I think that description, it just doesn’t match the facts,” Hilton told me. The polls at the time implied that voters did not agree. When I met Hilton in August, he was trailing Becerra badly, so I asked him why he was running a campaign that was doomed to fail. “That gap [in the polls] is shrinking,” he said to me, with no lack of confidence. “The gap went from 25 to 18 in the Berkeley poll. What was the next one? Our own internal poll, down to 14 points. There’s a poll that we’re hearing about next week where the gap will be under 10%.” Article continues below this adHilton didn’t mention that he was quoting polls from before and after the primary, and the gap fell from 21 not 25, which is VERY much a Republican thing for him to do, but I still gave him the benefit of the doubt.“Let’s say the poll numbers hold and you don’t win the election,” I said to him. “Where would you go after this?”At this, he laughed. “I don’t know. I haven’t thought about it. I’m planning to win. I do believe that I’m going to be the next governor. I can see it. I believe it.”Article continues below this ad“Is that your ego talking? Have you convinced yourself?”“No, it’s California talking. It’s the conditions in our state.”“It’s not the polls talking.”“Yes, but we’re just at the start of the campaign. No one really pays attention until after Labor Day anyway. Everything points to this being a change election in California. That means that I will win the election. That is my strong expectation.”Article continues below this adBut that confidence only holds if Hilton pretends the Trump factor in this race isn’t significant. Surely the voters he’d met along the trail had told him as much. That’s why I asked him, “Have you not had voters talk to you specifically about what the president is doing?”That answer floored me. “Never?”Article continues below this ad“Literally never comes up,” Hilton boasted. “It’s ‘What are we going to do about the gas prices?’ Right now in California, you’ll see gas prices in the $5 to $6 range. If you go to Texas today, they’re in the $3 range. Same country, same president, same Iran war going on, vastly different gas prices. That’s entirely due to the policies that Democrats have pursued in California.”He’s partially correct, given that California’s gas prices are high partially because the state has the highest gas tax in the country, and its fuel standards increase costs for producers. But he again fails to acknowledge the role the Trump administration has played in driving up prices nationwide. It’s a form of denial that he’s shown many times over, from asking voters to ignore Trump’s endorsement of him after he accepted it, to attempting to soften his affection for other members of the MAGA herd, including the late Charlie Kirk. Hilton came to our meeting sporting a wristband honoring the fallen white supremacist. I asked him why he had it.“He was a good friend of mine, and someone gave it to me,” Hilton said about that. “So I just kept it.”Article continues below this ad“Did you like his way of going about things, because he was rather open about his views on race.”“I’m not sure what you’re referring to.”“Well, he was a friend of mine. I’m sure we all agree that we are friends with many people. That doesn’t mean we agree with 100% of everything they’ve ever said or done. You can still be friends with someone, just as I am with many Democrats. Don’t agree with them, but we’re friends.”Article continues below this adDo not count Becerra, the Democratic candidate, as one such friend. Hilton made sure to get in his jabs at Becerra in between all of my nagging questions. “We haven’t even talked about all the disqualifying factors for my opponent, who, in the words of [former Biden official] Susan Rice is ‘an idiot.’ You can’t have an idiot as governor of California.” I asked if he thought Becerra was especially idiotic given the current level of stupidity in the Trump administration, but he quickly sidestepped. “I don’t know. You’d have to ask Susan Rice. I don’t know why she called him an idiot.”Article continues below this ad“Well, you just said it was a great quote about him, so you must think he’s an idiot, too.”“I’m just telling you what people who have experience of working with him say. She also called him a ‘bitch-ass,’ whatever that means exactly.”“I think you know what a bitch-ass means.”“I actually, truly don’t know exactly what that means.”Article continues below this adHe must have learned in the interim. Because one week ago, Hilton faced off against Becerra in the only televised gubernatorial debate prior to the election. There, he brought up the “bitch-ass” comment from Rice directly to his opponent. He also constantly took umbrage anytime Becerra tried to link him to the president.“All you ever say is ‘Trump, Trump, Trump,’” he admonished Becerra. “That’s nothing but an insult to every Californian who is desperate for something to change in this state.”Article continues below this adIf voters here are desperate for a change, they’re not buying Hilton as the face of it. Two weeks after Labor Day, he is now down against Becerra by 25 points. I don’t think he’s going to win this election. Because when you’re a Republican, there’s no hiding it.

item.title: This work takes persistence
item.author: 010001a11bfb1945-9bf3b7a6-52b8-4359-b28f-cdfae9c3a117-000000@amazonses.com
item.content:encoded: It hasn’t been an easy year for religious freedom. Across the country, politicians are pushing religious doctrine into public schools and government, while the Supreme Court continues to reshape the constitutional protections that have guided this work for generations.But thanks to supporters like you, no matter the moment, Americans United will always show up and take action whenever and wherever we can.In Arkansas, our legal team secured a permanent injunction blocking a law that would have required every public school classroom and library to display a government-chosen version of the Ten Commandments. In Texas, 28 families represented by AU and our allies have asked the Supreme Court to stop a similar law. Across the country, we’re helping students, parents, teachers, and federal workers understand their rights and know what to do when they’re threatened.This work takes persistence. It takes attorneys who know how to build a case, advocates who know how to move lawmakers, organizers who can unite us, and a community of supporters who make it possible for Americans United to keep showing up. If you have money set aside in a donor-advised fund, consider using it to support Americans United. Your generosity keeps this work moving forward at a time when it matters deeply.Thank you for being part of this movement.With gratitude, Americans United

item.title: We’ve endured ten long years of this shit. Lucky us.
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: In her most recent post, the indispensable Heather Cox Richardson reminds us of a fact that somehow had completely flown under my radar. Yesterday marked ten years since the release of the Access Hollywood tape, confirming in our minds the thing we all already suspected: that the racist game show host running for president was also a misogynistic piece of shit.That tape — in which the racist game show host literally bragged about grabbing women ‘by the pussy,’ — should have consigned him to the rotting dustbin of history, but for some maddening reason, it didn’t. As a result, every day for the last ten years, the racist game show host has been — — inflicting himself on us.You’re welcome, America. Lucky us.“I could have done very bad things to Hillary Clinton. I could have done very, very bad things to Joe Biden. I could have done very bad things to Barack Hussein Obama.… I can do whatever I want, if I want.”Well, , then. That’s certainly good to know. Thanks for sharing, Donny. Tell me, what are we supposed to with this information? File it away for future reference? Fear this idiot ? He’s already the world’s most tiresome asshole.Who talks like this? It’s so unpresidential. Our Predator-in-Chief is unfit for office, and growing worse by the day.‘I can do whatever I want, if I want.’Why does everything that seeps out of Preznit Fuckwit’s rancid anus-mouth sound like something that he or his dead pedo bestie Jeffrey Epstein would have said to one of the Motel-a-Lago ‘spa girls’?What was the context for this boast of how awful Donny could be, ? From what point A did we get to this point B? Yesterday’s Oval Bordello dog-and-pony show was ostensibly held so that Dear Leader could brag about how he had automatically enrolled every child in America — — into his dodgy new ‘Trump Accounts’ scam. How did we get from to ‘I could fuck everyone’s shit but good, if I wanted to’?For heaven’s sake, there were in the room.Trump to children in the Oval Office: “You stay there. You’re so good looking. The press can admire you.”Eww. Shut the fuck up, Piggy. “There’s never been anybody in the history of the Nobel Prize that deserves it more. I settled eight wars. I stopped the total obliteration of the world.”Oh. My. God. An entire year has passed, and this colicky little piss-baby is still whining about not getting the Nobel Peace Prize. Donny has such a ginormous back-catalog of grievances that I’d completely forgotten about the Nobel.Could Grudgie the Whale please stop bellyaching for five consecutive seconds? Would that be too much to ask?Which brings us to Dear Leader’s other public event from yesterday, a campaign rally in San Antonio, Texas — because you’ll never guess what the stupid shit did. He doubled down on the dumbfuck.“Let them hit a missile into San Diego or Los Angeles on the way. You want to see a horror show? Let them hit San Diego. Let them hit Los Angeles. You want to see some bad things happen?”No, we don’t. No one wants to see bad things happen. What the fuck is wrong with you?“I can do whatever I want, if I want.”Yeah, we know. You keep saying that.Just you watch. Nuking California is now going to become a centerpiece of every one of Donny’s speeches. It’s going to turn into a laugh line, because MAGA Donny has the emotional maturity of a toddler. His goal is to be the center of attention, and it doesn’t matter how he gets it. Whatever works. He knows that the grown-ups are annoyed by his antics, so he’s going to keep on doing it — because any kind of attention is good.But let’s circle back to yesterday’s Oval Bordello dog-and-pony show, because I know there’s one question you’ve been dying to ask. ‘Hey, Uncle Jeff, as soon as someone else started talking, did the narcoleptic old fart factory fall fast asleep and crop-dust his Emotional Support Flunkies — without their consent — with the pungent aroma of ass music?’Remember, Donny can ‘do whatever he wants, if he wants’ — and that includes sleeping his way though his entire failed presidency.Now, let me turn it around. I have a question for , dear readers.Forgive me, but Ms. Dell seems higher than a kite. Is there something in the water at the White House? I feel it’s a legit question to ask, because I’m pretty sure that Susan Dell has joined Space Nazi aboard Forkship One, and is somewhere out in deep space right now.What do you say we consent to some Daily Claudia?I remain fascinated that so many of the selfies on Ms Spouse’s phone that I had assumed were static images, are actually what Samsung calls ‘motion photos.’Here are two vids that I’d previously posted as still photos, of Ms Spouse and Bestie Kathy, at Half Moon, on May 29, 2025.Have a great Thursday, everyone. Thank you to all of you who emailed or commented in support of the Daily Claudia. Don’t worry, it’s not going away at any time in the near future. I mean, eventually I will run out of photos — but we’'ll cross that bridge when we come to it.here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: The AI Panic and the Hunt for Reliable Narrators
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: This is an update to my post from Tuesday about the “existential risk” panic. A good friend of mine reached out to me and said, in so many words, yes, all that techno-babble is weird. But that doesn’t mean these risks aren’t real. And as I tried to make clear in my piece, I agree with that, at least to the extent that if Group A isn’t made up of reliable narrators, I’m not clear who the reliable narrators are. He pointed me to this recent report put out by the Rand Corporation, which is kind of the original think tank and has always been closely tied to the U.S. government and for lack of a better word the U.S. military-intelligence-industrial complex. It’s an interesting report. Or at least I found some interesting and I think sensible prescriptions in it once I got through the first half or two-thirds of it, which contained very Randian decision trees, definitions and a lot of what seemed like assumptions about existential risk and coexistence with AI that I didn’t understand. It eventually sets out a sensible if hard-to-execute approach which generally amounts to a safety-first regime of governing AI (make sure new things don’t endanger us before we build them or make them widely available) and, critically, open the decision-making up to public institutions with public accountability.

item.title: Trump is doing family separation but without the backlash
item.author: delivery_20261008060502.47827077.141@bounce.slate.com
item.content:encoded:
Children are almost always treated with special deference in American law, because lawmakers understand and respect the significance of adolescence and the necessity of parental guidance. President Donald Trump has upended this long-standing, universal understanding in a particularly insidious way during his second term. For the first time in our nation’s history, tens of thousands of children are being separated from their parents, who, at the hands of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, are being violently arrested inside of the country, then detained, and quickly deported without their kids. These children are essentially left to fend for themselves or are placed with an unknown caregiver, which in some cases has led to horrific endings. Although this may sound awfully similar to Trump’s 2018 “zero-tolerance” policy, it is worse, because there is no explicit family separation policy this time around, making it harder to challenge in court. Instead, family separation has become just another devastating consequence of the president’s mass deportation agenda.
Under past administrations, ICE policy held that any detainees who were parents should be reunited with their children before being deported, or agents must get confirmation that there is a designated caregiver in place for their children in the parents’ absence. Last year, upon Trump returning to the White House, ICE revised this policy to make it only applicable “when operationally feasible,” which gave agents all the leeway they needed to ignore the historical guidance in order to prioritize mass deportations. “This loosening of guidelines, combined with scaled-up immigration enforcement, has resulted in the detention of thousands of parents, many of whose minor children are U.S. citizens,” a recent analysis by the Migration Policy Institute concluded.
Under Trump 2.0, the Department of Homeland Security no longer provides reliable data on its immigration enforcement, but the Brookings Institution estimates that as of April 2026 about 205,000 children have likely experienced a parental detention since Trump began his second term and about 145,000 of these children are U.S. citizens. Mothers in particular seem to be affected, with ProPublica finding that the Trump administration is deporting about four times as many moms of U.S. citizen children per day as the Biden administration did, most of whom have minor or no criminal histories at all.
Stories of these children are playing out across the country, like in Minnesota, where three children have been separated from their father for nearly 10 months after he was yanked out of his car and violently arrested on his way to work. And in Alabama, where one woman has been caring for an old co-worker’s 2-year-old for nearly a year since ICE picked up the baby’s mother while she was on a grocery run. In Illinois, a college senior found himself the sole breadwinner of his family after ICE arrested and detained his uncle. Three sisters in San Francisco were among a lucky few who were reunited with their mother after she was detained for almost a year, leaving the eldest sibling to take care of the household while juggling college classes and navigating a complicated immigration system for her mother.
Then there are the children who ICE arrests with one or both of their parents. Although the U.S. government has historically allowed families to remain in detention together, the Trump administration has quietly been separating children by giving their parents false promises that they’ll be able to stay in touch with them. In reality, as detailed by Mother Jones, oftentimes children are sent to the Office of Refugee Resettlement and reclassified as unaccompanied minors—they are not; the U.S. government knows their parents are in detention—and sent off to live with foster parents. ORR does not track these types of cases, so it's unclear how many children are being reclassified, but Mother Jones estimated they now make up a “huge chunk” of ORR’s caseload. Under normal circumstances, unaccompanied minors are defined as children who arrive at a U.S. border alone, with no parent or guardian.
Regardless of how the Trump administration chooses to manipulate immigration law, the National Immigration Law Center says parents and legal guardians who are detained by ICE have a legal right to make decisions about their minor child’s care. They are also allowed to see their children while in detention, upon written request, whether that’s in person or over a video or phone call. And if a parent faces deportation, they also have a legal right to make decisions about what happens to their children, which usually comes down to either allowing the child to remain in the U.S., regardless of the child’s immigration status, or to be deported alongside the parent. All of these decisions are supposed to happen with a lawyer, but even this is no longer happening, due to financial constraints, the administration’s attacks on legal aid for minors, and its extreme hostility toward immigrants, leaving parents with little to no recourse when ICE does not follow protocol.
Children do not get to choose their parents’ immigration status, yet their families are being torn apart over it. The consequences are clear, with studies showing that children who lose a parent to sudden, forced deportation experience anxiety, anger, aggression, isolation, and depression. It also often leads to housing instability, academic withdrawal, and family dissolution. Yet, the president is unbothered by this; in fact, he’s doubled down on efforts to eliminate immigrant children from the U.S. altogether, evidenced by his birthright citizenship executive order. Despite the Supreme Court categorically rejecting it earlier this year, Trump has since introduced yet another executive order targeting birthright citizenship. The Trump administration’s assault on immigrants has been cruel at every turn, but what it’s doing to immigrant children could be its worst act by far.

item.title: I told you I was tired. Then I read about ICE.

item.content:encoded: By last spring, ICE was already laying the groundwork to interfere in the midterms. Explosive new documents show that it had investigated groups that register voters, considered infiltrating some of them with undercover agents, and amassed tens of millions of voter records.For months, I have been sounding the alarm that ICE will be used to suppress voters and block people from casting their ballots. These records show that, behind the scenes, it is already carrying out Trump's orders.None of this is an accident. When President Donald Trump returned to office, he set out to build an army ahead of the midterms — one that would answer to him and only him.

item.title: Heathered Pearls (Interview)
item.author: Flow State
item.content:encoded: Today we’re listening to Heathered Pearls, a Polish-American electronic musician based in Brooklyn. He was born in Częstochowa and moved to Michigan with his parents as a kid, growing up in the Detroit exurbs. He gravitated toward beatless electronic music, but also found influences in the local Detroit scene – from which he highlights two memorable tracks below. Jakub Alexander started the project Heathered Pearls to collect ambient electronic music that are minimal in style, with focused attention on the details of the synth loops, their effects, and interplay. “When I make music,” he told us, “I think of it as the prettier side of the noise scene.” We’re first playing his new album, , which came out in March, followed by his 2012 LP, , which is more atmospheric. A conversation with Jakub follows the streaming links.What’s your earliest memory of music?Watching my mom and her friends up late at night listening to The Police’s through the cracked open door.How were you first introduced to ambient music?In the early mid-90s, Deep Forest, Enigma, and Orbital were probably the firestarters. I wanted more of the beatless moments, so I went down a few different avenues and found trance and local Detroit dub, which were enough subgenres, but they opened up a can of worms for me. What early listening most influenced the direction of your sound?For Heathered Pearls specifically, which was the aughts, so probably just what I have had listed for years on my Facebook in 2010: Gas, Casino Versus Japan, High Wolf, Dettinger, Maurizio, Markus Guentner, burger/ink, Lawrence, Kaito.What acts / tracks in the Michigan scene inspired you the most and stick with you to this day?This Juno track my friend Danny Scales played for me when we lived together.And this Underground Resistance cut:Both together, I think, marry the spectrum of music I make but come from different sides of the sound that comes from Michigan’s scene.As Heathered Pearls, you’ve oscillated between ambient and more four-on-the-floor music. Tell us about that journey, and maybe some of the similarities or differences between those production modes.I wish I could make music for the dance floor; when I make music, I think of it as the prettier side of the noise scene. If I were talented enough, I’d just make IDM. I’m not a piano player; I can’t strum a guitar, keep a beat on a drum kit, or have the balls to write lyrics, but if you leave me with your melody and let me affect it, then I feel at home.You’ve also been on the other side of the table as an A&R. Tell us how you approached that job, how you assessed demos and such. Did that experience affect you as a musician at all?Rarely do I sign a lot of the music that aligns with the lane of music that I make. I think I do my job really well because I can relate to everyone involved. I’ve made myself do the work that some people find boring or shitty, and I’ve seen enough outcomes in so many different scenarios in the last 30 years that it gives me more compassion than most. If it’s in the studio, before a show, over dinner, or just a phone call, I feel like I understand it better than most when people start asking the tougher questions. Listening to the music is the fun part.What was your studio setup for ? What instruments/gear/software did you use to make the record?Reason and no samples. I know it’s not the prettiest answer or the answer that you might’ve wanted to read, but I try to push what the program comes with to make it my own.How do you discover new music these days? Any recent notable finds?YouTube still. I’ve recently been on a newer jazz kick, sitting on a lot of trip-hop I found over the last few years, and I like what the kids are doing with shoegaze.Name an underrated artist from the past 50 years.What are you working on next?I’ve been dealing with dizziness for a couple years now, which has kind of shrunk my world a bit if anyone out there also battles with it. This sort of hinders the part of me that can make ambient music, since I find most sounds like what I wanna put out, but I’m feeling slightly better very recently. I hope to make a few more singles or an EP next year and then eventually another album which I’ve already sort of collected the influences which is a process that I love to do before making new music.

item.title: Forgotten Band: The Muffs
item.author: Schill
item.content:encoded: There are bands that disappear because they were terrible. There are bands that disappear because they had one hit and nothing else. And then there are bands like The Muffs, who somehow managed to release a stack of excellent records, build a devoted following, influence plenty of musicians, and still end up in the musical equivalent of a forgotten drawer.The Muffs were never completely unknown. Alternative-rock fans who were paying attention in the 1990s knew exactly who they were. Their music appeared in movies, television shows and video games, and their version of “Kids in America” introduced them to an even larger audience.But compared with the amount of talent in the band, The Muffs should have been much bigger.They were loud, catchy, funny, messy and completely uninterested in pretending to be cooler than they actually were. They could sound like a punk band one minute and a ridiculously infectious power-pop band the next. At the center of it all was Kim Shattuck, whose voice could go from sweet to ferocious in the space of about three seconds.And that’s probably the best way to describe The Muffs.They sounded like they were having fun.From The Pandoras to The MuffsThe story of The Muffs starts with Kim Shattuck and Melanie Vammen, who had previously been members of the Los Angeles garage-rock group The Pandoras.After leaving The Pandoras, Shattuck and Vammen formed The Muffs in the early 1990s. Ronnie Barnett of The Muffs’ eventual classic lineup joined on bass, while Roy McDonald became the drummer.The band quickly developed a sound that was impossible to mistake.There were punk influences everywhere, but The Muffs weren’t interested in making relentlessly aggressive music. They understood the value of a great melody.Their songs were short, loud and packed with hooks.That combination helped separate them from many of the alternative and punk bands around them.They could be abrasive without becoming exhausting.They could be poppy without becoming manufactured.And they had something else that a lot of bands lacked:The band’s self-titled debut arrived in 1993.It immediately established what The Muffs were all about.The songs were fast, distorted and catchy, with Shattuck’s vocals constantly bouncing between melodic singing and her trademark screaming.That scream became one of the band’s defining characteristics.It wasn’t the polished, carefully controlled kind of screaming that eventually became common in alternative rock. Shattuck sounded like she might actually lose her voice halfway through the song.That unpredictability was part of the appeal.You never quite knew when a sweet pop melody was about to explode into a furious yell.The Muffs followed the debut with in 1995, which remains one of their essential albums.If the first album established their sound, demonstrated just how good they could be at writing ridiculously memorable songs.Tracks like “Sad Tomorrow” and “Oh Nina” showed that underneath all the distortion and attitude was a genuinely gifted pop songwriter.Then Came “Kids in America”The Muffs’ biggest exposure came when they recorded their own version of Kim Wilde’s “Kids in America.”Their version appeared on the soundtrack to the 1995 movie .Suddenly, a band that had been operating in the alternative underground was being heard by a much larger audience.The song fit perfectly with the movie’s energetic teenage aesthetic.And it sounded unmistakably like The Muffs.For a moment, it seemed like the band might finally break into the mainstream.But that’s where the story takes a familiar turn.The Muffs never became massive.They never became one of the defining bands of the decade.They remained a cult favorite.And, in hindsight, that may have been both a blessing and a curse.The Problem With Being Too Good for the MainstreamThe Muffs occupied an awkward musical space.They were too punk for mainstream pop.Too melodic for hardcore.Too scrappy for polished alternative rock.Too weird to be packaged neatly.And yet they had the songwriting ability to produce genuine pop hits.That combination should have made them huge.Instead, it made them difficult to categorize.The 1990s music industry loved categories.The Muffs didn’t fit perfectly into any of them.They simply sounded like The Muffs.That is usually great for artistic longevity.It isn’t always great for selling millions of records.They Never Really Went AwayThe Muffs continued recording throughout the 1990s and 2000s, releasing albums including , Alert Today, Alive Tomorrow, and .They never completely disappeared.They just became one of those bands that you had to know about.If you were digging through alternative-rock playlists or looking for great punk-pop records, eventually you would stumble across them.And when you did, there was usually the same reaction:“Why didn’t I listen to these guys earlier?”That’s one of the strange things about The Muffs.Their music hasn’t aged particularly badly.In fact, some of it sounds better now.The production might sound unmistakably 1990s, but the songs themselves are timeless little blasts of power pop.They don’t require nostalgia to work.They’re simply good songs.Kim Shattuck Was the Secret WeaponIt’s impossible to discuss The Muffs without talking about Kim Shattuck.She wasn’t simply the singer.She was the personality of the band.Her voice could be sarcastic, vulnerable, hilarious, furious and sweet, sometimes within the same song.She also had an instinct for keeping songs from becoming overly polished.The imperfections were part of the charm.Shattuck later became a member of The Pixies for a short period and also continued performing with The Muffs.Her death in 2019 at the age of 56 was a devastating loss for fans of the band and the wider punk and alternative community.The Muffs continued after her death through archival material and releases, but there was obviously no replacing the person who had given the band its unmistakable personality.Why Did We Forget The Muffs?A memorable soundtrack appearance.And enough albums to build a substantial catalog.They simply never became part of the standard story of 1990s alternative rock.Mention Nirvana, Green Day, The Offspring, Weezer or Hole and most people immediately know what you’re talking about.Mention The Muffs and you might get:“The Muffs… wait. I know that name.”Then you play “Kids in America.”A band you forgot you loved.The good news is that The Muffs are incredibly easy to rediscover.Start with and . Then work through the later records.You’ll quickly discover that “Kids in America” isn’t some isolated novelty.It’s just the song that happened to escape the cult.The real appeal of The Muffs is the combination of melody and chaos.They could write a gorgeous pop song and then scream their heads off in the middle of it.They could sound polished for thirty seconds before deliberately blowing the whole thing apart.They were punk without being miserable.They were pop without being fake.And they were funny without turning every song into a joke.That’s a pretty difficult balance to pull off.The Muffs deserved a much bigger place in the history of 1990s alternative music.They weren’t just a soundtrack band.They weren’t just another punk-pop group.They were one of the most consistently entertaining bands of their era.And if you’ve forgotten them, don’t feel too bad.That’s basically the story of The Muffs.They’ve been waiting patiently for you to remember.And once you do, you’re probably going to wonder how the hell you forgot them in the first place.

item.title: Quoting Ben Affleck
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: I've always been kind of into computers since I was young. And then when film started to move from analog film to digital, I became more interested in that aspect of it. And the visual effects workflow for many years has included machine learning.So I can write like pretty shitty Python scripts and stuff like that because with convolutional neural networks, which were the sort of precursors to what the transformer can do, which is just much more computation simultaneously, you would do things like look at what's called a tensor, which is just the numerical translation of a visual image in numbers — like the batch number, the frame number, the red, green, and blue values of each pixel in each frame. And a tensor, you use a convolutional neural network to identify patterns in that that would reveal what's called edge detection or feature extraction, which is just identifying patterns enough to know like this is where the window ledge is, so we can more easily take the green screen image out and replace it with something.

item.title: Pete Hegseth’s holy war on “weirdos” targets most Americans
item.content:encoded: Pete Hegseth is odd. This isn’t just a personal opinion, though there’s no doubt that he gets widely mocked for his carefully cultivated public persona, which is a mix of megachurch preacher, gym rat and Robert Duvall’s napalm-huffing character in “Apocalypse Now.” The fact that the defense secretary is different is simply a statistical reality.It’s not just that he’s a white evangelical Christian, a group that, according to PRRI, makes up only 13% of the population. Hegseth’s church, the Communion of Reformed Evangelical Churches, is extreme even for the right, with a leader who argues against women’s suffrage and teaches that slavery was the height of “mutual intimacy and harmony” between the races. Even within MAGA, those remain fringe positions, despite great efforts by some Christian nationalists to reignite “debate” on such long-resolved issues. All this means it’s hard not to laugh when Hegseth pontificates about his hatred of “weirdos.” Although he has a war to fight in Iran, somehow he finds time to focus his attention on what he clearly sees as the greater battle: remaking the military according to the demands of his very white, very male, very right-wing vision.““Wimps,” “radicals” and “weirdos” are more ambiguous pejoratives, but Hegseth’s recent actions suggest his definitions are expansive enough to cover the vast majority of Americans. He’s been on a firing spree, demanding a 20% cut of the Pentagon’s top brass in an apparent effort to expunge those he deems “woke.” The move comes after nearly two years of blocking promotions for and pushing out Black and female military leaders. Hegseth also rewrote the list of religions recognized by the Pentagon, narrowing from over 200 faith categorizations to a mere 31 — 22 of which are Christian. He claims this is to simplify the bureaucracy, but his motives are likely more disturbing: to stigmatize non-Christians and restrict the definition of “Christian.” The Air Force is already forcing service members to register their religious beliefs under the truncated list, drawing criticism from atheists and others whose belief systems are not included as options. Last week, Hegseth upped the ante by announcing the formation of the Office of Religious Affairs “to strengthen the moral, ethical and spiritual readiness of our warfighters.” Despite boilerplate claims that this action will not “compel religious participation” or “diminish the free exercise rights” of service members, both the policies and pomp surrounding the announcement made it clear that the goal is to promote Hegseth’s version of Christianity — and shame anyone who does not adhere to it. The office will be run by the defense secretary himself and, in ominous language, promises to fund “research, technology, and analytical tools to support and assess spiritual fitness,” which sounds like a data-gathering operation to ensure troops meet Hegseth’s esoteric views on proper religious practice. “Taken together, this purge helps clarify what Hegseth means when he’s talking about “weirdos” and “wimps,” as well as other slurs like “t******s.” He’s hostile to women, the LGBTQ+ community, people of color and anyone who doesn’t adhere to his vision of conservative Christianity — although it’s worth noting that with his message of peace and love, Jesus Christ himself would not be accepted by Hegseth as a Christian.The secretary may have gone to Princeton University, but he hasn’t yet grasped the concept of irony. The people he deems “weirdos” far outnumber those in his narrow category, presumably of non-weirdos, many times over. Hegseth has tried to justify his position and rhetoric by arguing that a proper military should only contain “the real 1%” of supposedly superior people. But as Eliot Cohen of The Atlantic notes, this claim is ignorant of history. You need large numbers to win wars, which inherently means that armies can’t be elitist institutions.Hegseth has a real math problem on his hands. His “real 1%” of alleged non-weirdos is just not enough people to staff a modern military, especially in times of war. His solution appears to be to hit the road, trying to recruit more mini-Hegseths to enlist. On Sept. 19 he embarked on the Send Me Tour in an effort to reach out to people in white evangelical-heavy parts of the country with a Bible-heavy pitch about how Jesus wants them to fight for their country. Both the tour’s name and the secretary’s stump speech rely heavily on In a response video, Sen. Raphael Warnock, the Democrat from Georgia who is also an ordained minister with multiple theology degrees, didn’t mince his words. “Pete Hegseth is busy twisting the scriptures yet again . . . Those objectives, of course, are not remotely Hegseth’s. His creation of a hierarchy that places white, straight men at the top and relegates everyone else into an underclass of “weirdos” and “wimps” ignores the Bible’s historical context — and actual meaning. Anyone who doubts that can simply examine his behavior in office and his monomaniacal focus on sorting America’s service members into a worthy-unworthy dichotomy, based solely on how much they adhere to his own self-serving ideals of what a soldier should look like.

item.title: Claude Haiku 5.5
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: The previous Haiku, 4.5, was very much showing its age. It came out almost a year ago, and was priced at $1/million input and $5/million output - relatively expensive even back then, and a full 10x the price of OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna, released last month.The new Haiku exactly matches the price of GPT-6 Luna - $0.10/$0.50 - up to 100,000 tokens. Beyond 100,000 tokens the price increases 5x to $0.50/$2.50. Luna itself has a price increase at 272,000 tokens but only to $0.20/$0.75.Haiku 5.5 also uses a new, less generous tokenizer. My Claude Token Counter tool shows that the same long prompt uses around 1.25x as many tokens with Haiku 5.5 compared to Haiku 4.5, so there's a hidden price increase there.If your workloads fit in 100,000 tokens, Haiku is the same price as Luna and reports higher benchmark scores. Above 100,000 tokens, Luna looks like a much better deal.llm install -U llm-anthropic llm anthropic refresh llm -m claude-haiku-5.5 "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" -o thinking_effort low This effort pelican (with a reasoning trace that starts "This is the classic pelican-on-bicycle SVG test...") took 5 minutes 9 seconds to generate, but still only cost me 3.3826 cents:For comparison, here's the pelican I got a year ago from Haiku 4.5 (for 0.7583 cents - Haiku 4.5 did not support reasoning levels). It at drawing pelicans:And a generous API credit scheme for subscribersIn addition to Haiku 5.5, Anthropic announced today that they are halving the price of cache reads for Sonnet 5.5. They've also added API credits to subscription plans:Second, this week, we’ll roll out a new monthly API credit to all Max and Team subscribers for use on the Claude Platform. Max 5x users will get $100 in credits per month, Max 20x users will get $200, and Team subscribers will receive up to $500, pooled across their users.Claiming this is pleasantly easy: navigate to Settings -> Billing and select the API organization that should benefit from the credits every month:The API credits exactly match the cost of the subscription itself. This is really generous - it makes it much easier for subscribers to use the API. Anthropic also let you disable auto-reload for the API, with the consequence that "API requests will stop when your balance runs out" - exactly what you want if you're planning to burn through those API credits without risk of a nasty billing surprise.OpenAI still allow you to use your Codex subscription for personal API use, which works out as a better deal for heavy API users. This new credit scheme goes at least some way to overcoming that difference.

item.title: Trump Rages, Rages Against the Dying of the Light
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: This is the weekly, free edition of The Backchannel. If you’d like to receive the free edition of The Backchannel in your inbox, you can subscribe here.Donald Trump’s manic building and naming spree has been a core feature of his second term in office. And that’s saying something. Because if nothing else, you can’t say Trump hasn’t been active. There are wars, blowing up the international trade regime, the on-going attempted authoritarian takeover of the state, the bust-out rush to wrest as much money out of the presidency as he can, his significant role energizing the AI boom (and possible bust). But with all these things, the building and naming spree stands out, especially in 2026. I focus on this today. I return to this today because of news that Trump wants to turn his West Palm Beach golf club into a new Camp David, a permanent presidential retreat.The details here are important. If Trump had some secluded property he wanted to donate to the federal government for this purpose, there might be some logic, though it’s hard to imagine Democrats wouldn’t put it up for sale at their first opportunity. What he wants to do is different. His plan is to donate a parcel of land at the private club for the Florida Camp David. So it’s really that future presidents would have there own private bungalow at Trump International Golf Club in Palm Beach. As an additional, rather comical, sweetener the club’s legal counsel, who is presenting the idea to Palm Beach County officials, says that future presidents will even be offered comped memberships to the club.

item.content:encoded: Right-wing crazies from around the world are starting to find him useful. That’s more than a little dangerous.
